News.title: Brit tourist, 41, found dead at Phuket hotel by staff who went into his room on day holidaymaker was due to check out
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

HOLIDAY TRAGEDY Brit tourist, 41, found dead at Phuket hotel by staff who went into his room on day holidaymaker was due to check out

A BRITISH tourist has been found dead in a Thai hotel room after a “Do Not Disturb” sign was left hanging on his door for several days.

Horrified staff made the grim discovery after entering his room on Monday morning when he was due to check out.



The holidaymaker, 41, had checked in on July 24 for a 10-day stay.

Staff said the room was last cleaned on July 27 – and since then a “Do Not Disturb” sign had been hung up on his door.



It is understood that no one had entered the room for several days as employees respected the sign.

On Monday, the manager of the hotel in Patong went to check on the UK national but received no response.

He opened the door before finding the Brit dead inside at approximately 11am.

Police and emergency services rushed to the scene.

There were reportedly no signs of a break-in or struggle, according to local media.

The tourist is understood to have died 12 to 24 hours before his body was discovered, a forensic doctor ruled.



But authorities are conducting a full autopsy to determine the exact circumstances of his death.

His body has been transferred to Vachira Phuket Hospital for examination.

News.title: Huge fire spreads to ten homes with thick smoke billowing into air & gardens scorched after ‘barbecue sparked blaze’
News.content:
A MASSIVE fire reportedly caused by a BBQ ripped through ten homes and left four in ruins.

The blaze erupted at 2.40pm yesterday, with eight fire engines scrambling to the scene.



Flames quickly tore through the buildings in Ash Keys, Crawley, with locals urged to keep their windows and doors closed.

West Sussex Fire & Rescue Service rushed to bring the inferno under control throughout the afternoon.



Pictures show the devastation wrought by the flames, leaving four homes gutted and burned.

In the aftermath, holes can be seen in the roofs, with the walls charred and windows blown out.



The fire service said ten properties were involved in the fire, with the blaze having also spread to the gardens.

Four were seriously damaged in the blaze.



A West Sussex Fire & Rescue Service spokesperson said: “The fire involves 10 properties, with four seriously damaged. Crews are working hard to bring the fire under control and to extinguish it.

“We would like to use this opportunity to remind people that the Fire Severity Index, which measures how severe a fire would be if one were to break out, remains very high in West Sussex due to the prolonged warm, dry weather.

“We are encouraging people to avoid using disposable barbecues and having bonfires in outdoor spaces, pick up litter if you see it, extinguish smoking materials properly, and to report any signs of fire immediately by calling 999.”

It comes after three grassland blazes spread rapidly across a nature reserve with locals urged to avoid the area.

Emergency services were called to a wildfire at Barr Beacon in Birmingham yesterday afternoon.



The another blaze started at Perry Hall Playing Fields at 12.45pm, with huge plumes of smoke seen billowing from the park.

And a third wildfire broke out at a park in Hay Mills at around 4pm.

It comes after an inferno engulfed Dunwich Heath in Suffolk on Wednesday evening.



Terrified residents were evacuated from their homes and caravans as the blaze ravaged approximately 150 acres of the scenic landscape.

Over 120 firefighters were deployed to tackle the blaze, located just three miles from Sizewell B nuclear power station.

A major incident was declared “due to the size and complexity” of the wildfire.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Chief fire officer of Suffolk’s Fire and Rescue Service, Jon Lacey described the fire as “one of the largest that I remember in the history of Suffolk”.

The wildfire crept within metres of Harry Potter actor Ralph Fiennes’ property, with shocking aerial footage showing scorched land bordering his home.

News.title: Two motorcyclists in 50s and 60s are killed in horror rush hour crash on country road
News.content:
CRASH TRAGEDY Two motorcyclists in 50s and 60s are killed in horror rush hour crash on country road

TWO motorcyclists, in their 50s and 60s, have sadly died following a horror multi-vehicle collision on a country road.

Police were called to reports of the smash on the B676 between Melton and Saxby in Leicestershire, yesterday.

A Yamaha motorbike and a Honda motorcycle as well as an Audi A4 were involved in the deadly collision.

East Midlands Ambulance service attended the crash but tragically the two motorcyclists were pronounced dead at the scene.





The driver of the car, a man in his 20s, was not injured.

No arrests have been made in the aftermath of the fatal smash with police now appealing for any witnesses to come forward.

Anyone with any information that may assist Leicestershire Constabulary with its investigation is asked to come forward.

Detective Constable Emma Neeves said: “Enquiries into this incident are continuing today and I’d like to speak to anyone who can help.

“I’m appealing for any motorists who were on that stretch of road yesterday to come forward and I’d like to speak to anyone with a dashcam.

“My appeal for information also includes anyone who witnessed the collision or saw any of the vehicles beforehand.

“Anything you’re able to provide or tell us, no matter how insignificant you think it is, could assist our investigation.”

News.title: M67 closed in both directions ‘throughout the day’ over ‘police-led incident’ as drivers face delays – see diversion
News.content:
A MAJOR UK motorway has been closed in both directions following a “police led incident.”

The M67 has closed in both directions between Junction 3 Hyde and Junction 4 Woolley Bridge, in Derbyshire.

National Highways warned drivers that the nature of the incident will likely leave the road closed throughout the day.

Contractors and emergency services are on scene assisting with traffic management.





Diversion routes are in place with no delays in the area at this time.

Drivers are asked to plan their journey ahead of leaving to avoid delays.

National Highways said: “The M67 has closed in both directions between J3 Hyde and J4 WoolleyBridge due to a Police led incident.

“Due to the nature of the incident, the road is likely to remain closed throughout the day.



“No delays in the area at present.”

News.title: Noel Edmonds faces backlash after he ‘condemns two farm shop bought lobsters to death’ after releasing them into the sea
News.content:
NOEL Edmonds has been accused of condemning to death two lobsters he bought from a farm shop to release into the sea.

The former Deal or No Deal host and his wife Liz returned the pair to the water on the Isle of Man.



Noel said they were uncomfortable seeing them confined in a tank and decided to buy them to release them.

In a social media clip, he said: “Nice clear water in Peel Harbour; there they go.



“And we know this is nice fresh water because a moment ago a seal went past.

“Wonderful place.”

But the 77-year-old was told his act of kindness was likely to backfire as the lobsters would not survive their return.

One web user said: “They didn’t have a chance the moment he removed them from tank.”



Another posted: “A lovely sentiment, but from a marine biologist perspective it’s best not to release captive lobsters.”

Meanwhile Matt Harrison, the owner of the farm shop from which Noel bought the lobsters, said he had moved their tank in response to the controversy — and was thinking of getting rid of it altogether.



He said he bought the lobsters to support a young local fisherman, adding: “The tank is still in the shop but we’ve moved it.

“I am sensitive to people’s feelings, but the vast majority want us to keep it.”

News.title: Four injured in shooting in major European city after argument breaks out as cops rush to scene
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

GUNFIRE SHOCK Four injured in shooting in major European city after argument breaks out as cops rush to scene

FOUR people have been injured in a shooting on a street in Germany.

Cops have been deployed to the area of Berliner Straße in the Mülheim, Cologne, after shots rang out on Monday around 10pm.



Police say a dispute “between several people” sparked the incident, though full details have not yet been released.

Rescue workers have taken four people – some seriously injured – to hospitals.



Witnesses alerted the police after hearing gunshots in the street.

The operation is ongoing with the area under police cordon.



Numerous officers are currently on the scene interviewing witnesses and securing evidence.

It was also not yet known who fired the shots or how many shots were fired.

News.title: Tragedy as animals die in fire at Britain’s ‘2nd-best zoo’ with staff ‘devastated’ as two people also rushed to hospital
News.content:
ANIMALS have been killed after a fire ripped through the office at Britain’s “second-best zoo” leaving staff “devastated”.

Two owners of Hoo Zoo and Dinosaur World in Hadley, near Telford in Shropshire, were also taken to hospital as a precaution.



The Shropshire Fire and Rescue Service were called to the attraction on Monday morning, August 3, after a fire was discovered in the zoo’s office.

One of the zoo’s owners Will Dorrell said in a video statement posted on Facebook on Monday evening that some animals had perished in the blaze.



He said: “We are saddened to announce that several stick insects, a snake and a hedgehog have died as a result of this morning’s fire at the zoo.

“These animals were privately owned by the zoo’s owners and have never been on display to the public.



“The owners are devastated at the loss of these animals but would like to thank Shropshire Fire and Rescue for all of their efforts in trying to extinguish the fire.”

Thanks to the speedy response by the fire crews, they were able to prevent the fire from spreading to other wooden buildings surrounding the office.



Mr Dorrell did though confirm the office had been “gutted” by the fire.

The attraction has been closed all day but it intends to re-open tomorrow, August 4.

Mr Dorrell asked that visitors “please bear with us and sort of excuse the mess” as they try to clear up and cordon off the area affected.

An earlier statement had said: “Our team have been monitoring the animals across the site to ensure that they all remain safe and well.

“If you had booked tickets or an animal experience for today, then please email info@hoo-zoo.com to re-arrange your visit for an alternative date.



“Please quote your order reference number and preferred new date in your email. Thank you for your support and understanding.”

Hoo Zoo and Dinosaur World was rated the second best in the UK by users of travel website Tripadvisor.

It’s the second year running Hoo Zoo and Dinosaur World had been able to claim the runner-up prize.

Earlier this year it was also voted the ninth-highest rated zoo in Europe.

The site, which used to be a farm, had been in the hands of the Dorrell family since 1988.



Chester Zoo was rated the top-rated zoo in the UK by Tripadvisor users in the same survey.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Mr Dorrell said the achievement was surprising because there were “some fantastic zoos in the UK and in Europe”.

The ratings are based on customer reviews on the tourism website.

News.title: Lucy Powell’s anti-Tory obsession is no substitute for a serious education policy
News.content:
Loopy Lucy

IF Westminster gossip is to be believed, Lucy Powell was Andy Burnham’s THIRD choice to be Education Secretary.

The new PM may already regret not having a fourth option.



Powell’s claim that ex-Tory minister Michael Gove’s drive to raise academic standards in schools contributed to more than one million young people being out of work or training is as dangerous as it is patently wrong.

The Sun has argued for years that there needs to be better apprenticeship opportunities for kids, especially with AI radically changing the world of work.



But that CANNOT come at the expense of dropping standards and abandoning any ambition to give ALL pupils the best possible chances in life.

Not only is there NO evidence for Powell’s claims that Gove is responsible for leaving teenagers on the jobs scrapheap.



But in Wales and Scotland — where Labour and SNP-led governments refused to follow his methods, which later made English classrooms world leaders in maths and science — youth unemployment is HIGHER.

Labour’s catastrophic tax rises on business have done the real damage to young people’s prospects.

Allowing a ballooning of mental health benefits claims has only made that worse.

Powell’s depressing diatribe is rooted solely in her tribal hatred of Tories rather than educational fact.



Our kids will pay a high price for her wilful moronism.

Zero clue

ANDY Burnham says he “cannot ignore” the impact of Labour’s Net Zero policies on the cost of living.

So why is new Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh insisting that green levies don’t increase bills for households, when they so obviously do?

Fanatical Fahnbulleh, a disciple of Ed Miliband, also downplayed the prospects of significant new drilling in the North Sea.

The lack of honesty over the estimated £40billion a year cost of Net Zero has been staggering.



It seems there’s also not much chance of a straight answer about what, if anything, the Government is going to do about it.

Liddle giant

ROD Liddle knew what Sun readers’ lives were like – and they loved him for it.

Proud of his working class roots and his country, Rod wasn’t afraid of laying bare the hypocrisy of left-wingers spouting concern for ordinary folk while being firmly part of the Establishment.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Funny, fearless and staunchly committed to a free Press, no topic was off limits — he knew exactly what he thought, and did not hold back.

One of a kind and one of our own, he will be sorely missed.

News.title: Hazmat team descend on woman's house after 'smelly' Shein parcel arrives at door
News.content:
Hazmat team descend on woman's house after 'smelly' Shein parcel arrives at door

EXCLUSIVE: Courtney Davies ordered products from Shein for her online business - but their arrival prompted the emergency services to have to intervene due to fears over the safety of her parcel

View 4 Images A mum claims hazmat firefighters descended on her home when she fell 'dizzy and unwell' after a Shein parcel arrived covered in a 'strong-smelling' liquid (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

A mum says hazmat firefighters descended on her property after she became "dizzy and unwell" following the delivery of a parcel from Shein. Courtney Davies had ordered products for her online business from the online retailer including bookmarks, magnets, and stickers.

‌



But when the 28-year-old opened the parcel on July 28, she said there was a strong "chemical" odour that left her feeling lightheaded, before she spotted all her new items were covered in a white liquid. Courtney said some of the substance spilt on her hoodie and jeans, resulting in them changing colour almost instantaneously.

‌



She quickly took the parcel outside and called 999, resulting in a hazmat team and ambulance arriving at home, which had to be evacuated as a result.

‌



The mum-of-two said the team deemed the liquid to be a 'hazardous material' and subsequently disposed of it – but they couldn't determine what exactly it was.

View 4 Images Courtney began to feel 'dizzy and unwell' following the delivery

Courtney added that she and her partner had to be monitored for an hour in an ambulance, with paramedics testing their bloods, heart rates and for any evidence of burns.

‌



The couple both reported having a headache for the next two days that even painkillers couldn't shift. "I ordered bookmarks, scrunchies, stickers and a few magnets [from Shein]," Courtney, from Devon explained. "As I opened it up there was this really strong chemical [smell] all over the parcel.

"It got on my clothes and they immediately started changing colour. It was similar to bleach but so powerful it almost felt like it was burning your nose hairs. My partner said 'we need to take this outside, it's starting to make me really light headed'."

She continued: "My eyes were watering and my nose was running - it was so strong. I rang the [emergency services] 10-15 mins after. They could still smell it when they arrived. We had to dispose of it and they got rid of it.

‌



"Everything was coated in this liquid, all in the inside of the parcel, it had a white consistency. We still don't know what [it] was. I washed my hands immediately because of how fast it changed the colour of my clothing, I was scared of what would happen when it got on my skin.

"It was strong enough that within seconds my jumper was changing colour. There's been a few times bleach has splashed up my trousers and it probably takes around an hour for it to change colour, this was immediate.

"We sat in the ambulance for an hour outside my house because they had to observe us. They had to check our throats to see if we had any chemical burns. We had blood tests and our fingers pricked."

‌



View 4 Images An apparent chemical from the package changed the colour of Courtney's hoodie (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

Courtney said the parcel's stench was so bad it stunk out the house and that doors and windows had to be open for two hours after she opened it.

The mum, who suffers from anxiety, said the incident caused her to have a panic attack. "I have massive anxiety and it brought on an anxiety attack, I had a panic attack over it," she said. "We were told to not touch anyone, not eat or drink, just stand there and hope that everything was okay. It was scary.

‌



"All my windows and doors had to be open for two hours because my house stank. They should investigate it so it doesn't happen again. This can happen to someone who has a lung condition or asthma and something like this could hospitalise them."

Courtney went on: "We had a headache for about a day-and-a-half. Not only have they affected my income, they damaged my personal belongings. I couldn't work the day after because I had a really bad headache. Not even painkillers were getting rid of it."

View 4 Images Devon & Somerset Fire & Rescue Service later confirmed the bizarre call-out (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

‌



The mum said Shein requested 'substantial' proof and that she sent them the hazmat team report, but claims she was ignored before having her case closed. However, Shein have since offered a full refund and are investigating the matter.

Courtney has since vowed to never shop from Shein again.

Devon & Somerset Fire & Rescue Service confirmed the incident details.

Article continues below

A Shein spokesperson said: "We take any report of this nature seriously and we are conducting an investigation in line with our safety protocols. Our initial review has not identified any obvious issues with the package or its contents during the warehouse packing process.

"Incidents of this nature are highly unusual and, along with our logistics partners, we are working to establish what occurred. We have contacted the customer directly and issued a full refund for her order as a gesture of goodwill."

News.title: Devastated groom left at Gatwick Airport after easyJet overbooks honeymoon flight
News.content:
Devastated groom left at Gatwick Airport after easyJet overbooks honeymoon flight

Devastated groom left at Gatwick after easyJet overbooks honeymoon flight

View 3 Images Honeymooners Andy and Katya Wedlake were unable to fly together

A newlywed couple have revealed how their honeymoon got off to a terrible start at the hands of unforgiving easyJet staff, who refused to let both of them board despite being en route to their honeymoon.

‌



Londoners Andy and Katya Wedlake arrived at Gatwick Airport on July 26 with time to spare for their 8.25am easyJet flight to Montenegro. They had booked the romantic getaway months in advance and were keen to enjoy their honeymoon - until they went to check-in.

‌



The reason why the newlyweds had not been able to check in online the night before was now clear: easyJet had overbooked the flight. Mr Wedlake told the Telegraph: "They could only give us seats once boarding had closed – and if other people didn't turn up to the flight."

‌



Overbooking flights is common practice across in aviation. Aircraft carriers often sell more tickets than there are seats in order to maximise the number of bums on seats in the air, and therefore to bring down fuel and operational costs.

View 3 Images The reason why the newlyweds had not been able to check in online the night before was now clear: easyJet had overbooked the flight. (Image: Getty)

As per rules determining the rights of air passengers, airlines must first ask for volunteers willing to travel on a later service in exchange for compensation. easyJet did this and there was one volunteer, and so the couple thought that their early-morning headache was over.

‌



Mr Wedlake said: "There was one volunteer, opening one seat on the plane. They said that either my wife or I had to take that seat otherwise we would count as a 'no show' and would lose all rights for rebooking and any compensation."

They were essentially being held at ransom, so the newlywed husband chose to stay behind.

Mrs Wedlake flew alone to the Adriatic resort and her husband returned to the couple's home in London. 21 hours later, they were finally reunited in Montenegro.

‌



View 3 Images Andy Wedlake

When asked about the cruel debacle the couple were forced to endure, an easyJet spokesperson said in response: "We are very sorry for Mr and Mrs Wedlake's experience and the difficulty this caused for their honeymoon. Like most airlines, we sometimes overbook a very small proportion of flights and in the significant majority of cases do not result in denying boarding as we use data to select flights with a history of customers not travelling. By filling these seats, it helps to keep fares lower for everyone.

"In the rare event a customer can't travel, we take our responsibilities seriously and seek volunteers to travel on a later flight in exchange for compensation. Where this is not possible, a decision is made based on order of check in."

‌



They added: "Whilst a seat was available for one passenger, we are sorry that an exception was not made on this occasion to book an alternative flight for them together, especially as it was such a special trip. We have since reached out to Mr and Mrs Wedlake to apologise for their experience, provide the compensation due and offer a gesture of goodwill."

Under air passenger rights rules, Mr Wedlake is entitled to £350 in compensation after being denied boarding. But that does not come close to covering the actual toll of entire ordeal. He said: "For me that doesn't cover the stress, the sadness of being apart from my new wife, the loss of one full day in Tivat, or the wasted time."

"I understand easyJet's terms and conditions allow them to do this kind of thing, but I'm shocked they do it to destinations where they only put on one flight per day – and that they would not be able to predict this flight on a Sunday morning in summer would have a high attendance rate."

Article continues below

easyJet have been provided an opportunity to provide a revised comment.

News.title: Met Office names six areas facing power cuts on Tuesday and warns 'get prepared'
News.content:
Met Office names six areas facing power cuts on Tuesday and warns 'get prepared'

Met Office forecasters have warned that major disruption could be coming to six areas covered by its latest yellow weather warning, with thunderstorms on the cards

View 2 Images People have been told to prepare in advance (stock)

The Met Office has put six areas on alert for power cuts on Tuesday as they brace for thunderstorms and rain.

‌



The forecaster issued a yellow warning for thunderstorms in the whole of Northern Ireland from midday on Tuesday until 9pm. It warned that some short term loss of power and other services is "likely" as it urged people to take precautionary measures.

‌



It said: "People cope better with power cuts when they have prepared for them in advance. It’s easy to do; consider gathering torches and batteries, a mobile phone power pack and other essential items."

‌



The national weather agency explained that showers will develop on Tuesday morning and become heavy and "locally thundery" in the afternoon. These will be "slow-moving" and bring significant downpours, the forecaster said, with 20 to 30mm of rain predicted "in an hour or two".

View 2 Images A map of the areas affected by the yellow weather warning (Image: Met Office)

‌



UK wildfires live: Flames rage near Shrewsbury as major incident also declared in Wales READ MORE :

The Met Office warning states: "Strong and gusty winds and hail will also be possible with the heaviest showers. Showers should slowly ease from the west into the evening."

Besides power cuts, people in the six areas targeted by the warning have also been asked to consider whether their homes and businesses are at risk of flash flooding and prepare accordingly. People should also check road conditions before making any journeys, regardless of how they plan to travel.

The Met Office said: "If you find yourself outside and hear thunder, protect yourself by finding a safe enclosed shelter (such as a car). Do not shelter under or near trees, or other structures which may be struck by lightning. If you are on an elevated area move to lower ground."

News.title: 'I gave up job for side-hustle and now I take £2.4million a year'
News.content:
'I gave up job for side-hustle and now I take £2.4million a year'

It was during Covid that he got the chance to focus on it

View 4 Images Aaron at a football card convention (Image: PA Real Life)

A personal trainer who gave up his day job to focus on his side hustle said he made £2.4 million in revenue over the past year and urged people not to “get stuck in their nine-to-five” jobs if they have other passions.

‌



Aaron Pearce, 38, from Suffolk and living in Essex, said he had “always been interested in” collectable items like Pokemon cards and football stickers and cards since growing up in the 1990s. But when he graduated from university in his early 20s, he started working his “way up” in the fitness and leisure industry to become an area manager of several gyms.

‌



When the Covid-19 pandemic hit in 2020, Aaron said his sector “completely shut down” so he had time to explore reselling as a side hustle, including trainers, clothes and football cards. It was the latter that stuck, so Aaron searched on social media sites like Instagram to connect with other collectors and to buy and sell cards that he sold for up to £20 per item. But it was Aaron’s introduction to a live shopping marketplace website in 2023 that turned his football card business from a spare-room hobby into a full-time job by March 2025, in dedicated offices with a team of seven people.

‌



View 4 Images Aaron goes to football card conventions across the world (Image: PA Real Life)

Rather than reselling individual cards, Aaron carved out a space in the market for opening cases while livestreaming and selling spots to individuals. Aaron can buy boxes of cards for £400 or full cases of 12 boxes for £4,800, with a total of 150 cards in each box.

A Liverpool supporter might buy a £100 “spot” on a livestreamed case opening and then they would get all of the Liverpool cards that came out of it. The number of spots on offer varies between livestreams and boxes or cases opened, but he cited one evening in July that had 340 spaces filled. He made almost £700,000 in revenue in his first full year between July 2023 to 2024, then £1.2 million in his second year and now £2.4 million in the last year.

‌



Aaron said: “One of the biggest cards we’ve had is a Lamine Yamal rookie card, which was a one of one, meaning there’s only one of them in the world. Someone bought that spot in a case break for about £15 to £20… the card itself now is probably worth over £100,000.

“It’s a crazy feeling. Because we open so much product, we’re very lucky with quite a lot of big hits, which could change quite a lot of people’s lives.”

Aaron remembers collecting albums of football stickers with his father as a child, but said they got “lost along the way” into adulthood. When he graduated from university with a degree in sports and exercise science in his early twenties, he said he “progressed into the personal trainer world” and worked his way up from sales, to reception, and various levels of management.

‌



Over the years, Aaron said he tried getting into reselling trainers and clothes as side hustles, but they “fizzled over time” due to “demand dying down”, so he looked into football cards. Initially starting as a hobby, Aaron progressed to connecting with other collectors on social media and then buying and selling individual cards that appealed to him, ranging from £5 to £20 and making small profits.

View 4 Images A signed Lionel Messi football card (Image: PA Real Life)

At the start of 2023, a friend of Aaron’s suggested he try opening packets of football cards in livestreams and he was immediately “very interested” in the idea. He researched it and found the live shopping marketplace site Whatnot, so he said he decided to make a “heavy investment” and take a risk by dipping into his savings from his fitness job to buy a £4,800 case of football cards. He would then sell spots to collectors via his account, Baller Breaks UK, effectively offering them a chance to get rare cards of the specific teams they collect.

‌



Aaron said: “I was definitely nervous at the time, but I was excited too. It was a product that I would have never been able to open up myself because I wouldn’t have been able to afford it. But at the same time, I realised that it was a very good business opportunity and if that went well, it would set us up for the future, which it did.”

Aaron made £6,324 in revenue during that first livestream. In the early days, Aaron would come home from his day job and do livestreams in his spare room from 9pm until as late as 2am, to an average of 20 to 40 viewers at a time.

He said: “Across a two-and-a-half-year period, I think I had 10 days off from streaming. So it was really just driving the consistency.”

‌



Now, having moved into a new house with a separate outdoor office space for business and stock storage in the summer of 2025, Aaron can do three livestreams a day and said he could have a case of cards worth £10,000 “come in one day” and by the end of the day, it had “already been turned over”.

To help him upscale the business, he said he has hired a packaging team for the orders he sells, an operations manager, and additional livestreamers so that Aaron can “become a bit more hands off and manage the business”. The growth of his reselling business meant that Aaron could give up his full-time job in personal training in March 2025, having more time to network at international card shows.

View 4 Images A signed Lamine Yamal football card (Image: PA Real Life)

‌



Aaron said: “It just came to a point where it didn’t make sense to continue the full-time job day to day. We had an unlimited potential earning in this side hustle and it was a no-brainer.”

He said he feels “very proud” of how far he has come, especially when he helps secure rare cards for his customers, like when two people paid £10 each for a spot last year and got a dual autograph card of Lionel Messi and Ronaldinho, which they sold for £35,000 at auction. Depending on securing enough stock from wholesalers, Aaron hopes to get to a point where the business is livestreaming 24 hours a day, seven days a week to global audiences.

Looking back on how far he has come, he said: “A lot of people get stuck in their nine-to-five, but they have a passion that they want to follow. I think it’s important to try to pursue that. If you’ve got something that you really enjoy and you can put your full focus into that, you can grow something that’s going to change your life.”

News.title: Vegetable company plunges into liquidation after 87 years in business
News.content:
Vegetable company plunges into liquidation after 87 years in business

The UK based company operating in the growing of vegetables has plunged into liquidation after 87 years in business

View 2 Images The vegetable company has plunged into liquidation [file image]

A UK vegetable company has fallen into liquidation after 87 years in business.

‌



John Paine (Kent) Potatoes Ltd was voluntarily wound up, with a liquidator appointed on July 30, 2026.

‌



The Kent based business operated in the growing of vegetables and melons, roots and tubers field.

‌



View 2 Images The company was incorporated in 1939

Isobel Susan Brett was appointed the liquidator of the longstanding Ashford company.

‌



According to Companies House the company was incorporated July 14, 1939.

Edward George Parker is listed as the director, appointed in 2007.

Recent files publicly available show the firm having amounts falling due within one year of just over £5,000. However, net assets are listed as £1,162,894.

Article continues below

The news comes as the UK agricultural sector is experiencing significant financial distress. It is predicted that more than a third of UK farms could go out of business in the next five years due to changes made to inheritance tax (IHT).

The conflict in the Middle East has also created uncertainty for the agricultural industry, creating further concern for farmers as energy costs may impact stock levels.

Alongside these concerns the recent spouts of hot weather have also impacted how farms are operating and could trigger food shortages across the country.

News.title: Ryanair passengers stranded for 15 hours in Europe given £3.38 compensation
News.content:
Ryanair passengers stranded for 15 hours in Europe given £3.38 compensation

Passengers waiting to get back to Britain said Ryanair gave them 17 zloty, worth £3.38 in today's exchange rate, as they endured a 15 hour delay to get home

View 3 Images (Image: Marcin Tkaczyk)

Ryanair passengers stuck in eastern Europe for 15 hours 'were given £3.38 compensation' which couldn't even buy them a cup of coffee at the airport.

‌



It's thought 150 people were left stranded at the gates of Krakow Airport for 15 hours after the Ryanair FR6359 service to Liverpool John Lennon Airport was delayed all day. Passengers were supposed to jet off at 8:55am on Monday morning (August 3) - but records from Flight Radar 24 show it finally set off at 12:40am on Tuesday (August 4).

‌



The two-hour flight eventually touched down at 2am in Liverpool, 15 hours and 20 minutes later than scheduled. Ryanair said delays were due to "a minor technical issue with the aircraft earlier today" requiring a replacement aircraft in an update to passengers, reports the Liverpool Echo.

‌



View 3 Images A Ryanair aircraft [file image] (Image: Peter Byrne/PA Wire)

Marcin Tkaczyk, 47, from Lancaster, is one of around 150 people who has been waiting in departures since early this morning.

He said: "We're waiting next to the gate. We could leave, but then we'd have to go through the whole procedure again, and there is nothing around the airport so there's really no point.

‌



"People are upset. There's no one in person here to explain things to us. We were supposed to arrive in Liverpool at 10.40am [on Monday]. Now we don't know. If we do depart at 12:30am, it should be 3am [on Tuesday]."

View 3 Images (Image: Marcin Tkaczyk)

Flight updates sent to passengers read: "Your flight FR6359 from Krakow to Liverpool is delayed due to a minor technical issue with the aircraft earlier today. We organised a replacement aircraft to operate your flight, but this caused a delay."

‌



A further message read: "Since your flight has been delayed, please enjoy a snack or beverage on us by presenting your boarding pass to the cashier at participating outlets. We have issued one 17.00 PLN (Polish zloty) voucher per boarding pass in your booking. Please note refreshment vouchers cannot be redeemed onboard the aircraft."

17 Polish zloty is worth £ 3.38, according to Tuesday's exchange rates. Marcin, who was visiting Krakow on a weekend city break, said the price of a coffee at the airport was 21.00 PLN.

He said: "There's no one here we can talk to. We're just waiting and waiting. I'm guessing there's about 150 of us, almost a full plane.

Article continues below

"The last we heard from Ryanair was about four or five hours ago. I'm fed up and upset. Fortunately we haven't got children with us, but there are a few kids here managing with phones, smartphones and Nintendos."

Ryanair has been approached for comment by the Echo.

News.title: BBC Great British Menu star closes restaurant forever in 'devastating decision'
News.content:
BBC Great British Menu star closes restaurant forever in 'devastating decision'

Anthony Demetre, who appeared on the 2010 series of the BBC Great British Menu, confirmed that his Vermuteria restaurant has now closed its doors

View 3 Images The Vermuteria restaurant has closed (Image: Instagram)

A restaurant of a BBC Great British Menu star has shut after almost 10 years.

‌



Anthony Demetre, who appeared on the 2010 series of the confirmed that his Vermuteria restaurant - which opened eight years ago - has now closed its doors.

‌



Demetre said in a statement on Instagram on July 31, that the decision to close the restaurant is devastating.

‌



View 3 Images Chef Anthony Demetre attends the 2008 New York Media's New York Taste event at Skylight on November 3, 2008 in New York City (Image: Getty)

"After eight wonderful years at Coal Drops Yard, Vermuteria has had to close its doors for one final time.

"We are devastated for our incredible staff, loyal customers, friends and supporters," he shared.

‌



Vermuteria, based in King's Cross's Coal Drops Yard, offered an all-day European menu. Demetre opened the restaurant in 2018 with designer Michael Sodeau.

The establishment was inspired by "eateries and cafés found in Italy, France and Spain" and offered a wide array of vermouths.

View 3 Images Vermuteria has had to close its doors for one final time (stock image) (Image: Getty)

‌



Demetre also owns the Michelin -starred Wild Honey St James restaurant on Pall Mall.

He also thanked patrons who supported Vermuteria.

"It's been an incredible journey and we are thankful that so many of you were able to join us and create lasting memories."

Article continues below

"The doors have closed on this chapter but the fire and hunger remain."

News.title: Nationwide makes change for customers from Tuesday in 'welcome move'
News.content:
Nationwide makes change for customers from Tuesday in 'welcome move'

Things are really up and down at the moment

View 4 Images Nationwide has cut rates (Image: Mike Kemp, In Pictures via Getty Images)

Nationwide has confirmed a change for customers that starts today. It said on Monday that it had cut its mortgage rates by up to 0.19% in a "welcome" move and "other lenders will follow" its lead this week, brokers claim. The lender will be cutting rates across its fixed mortgage range, including for first-time buyers, home movers and people remortgaging from Tuesday, August 4, it has announced.

‌



These latest changes will see rates reduced by up to 0.19% across two, three and five-year fixed rate products. This now means Nationwide’s lowest rate stands at 4.52%.

‌



This comes just three weeks after Nationwide increased rates by up to 0.35%. Swap rates, which mortgage rates are priced off, have fallen on Donald Trump's promise that new talks on ending the conflict with Iran would begin on Monday, after the US president called off what he said would have been "massive" strikes on the country. Global oil prices fell on Monday morning to under $85 which has allayed fears of inflation rising further, though later Iran's foreign ministry denied it was negotiating with the US.

‌



Carlo Pileggi, Nationwide’s head of mortgage products, said: “After a period of increasing swap rates, recent falls have created an opportunity for us to reduce mortgage rates, and we’re moving swiftly to ensure new and existing customers can benefit. These rate cuts will benefit a wide range of customers – first-time buyers, new and existing customers moving home as well as those remortgaging to Nationwide.”

View 4 Images The market is volatile thanks to global events (Image: Bloomberg, Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Stephen Perkins, managing director of Norwich-based Yellow Brick Mortgages, said he expected other lenders to follow suit.

‌



He added: "This is a reminder that mortgage pricing can move in both directions. Just a couple of weeks ago we were seeing lenders increase rates as swap rates rose. Now those funding costs have eased, Nationwide has been quick to pass some of that benefit on to borrowers.

"If swap rates remain lower, I'd expect other lenders to follow. The mortgage market remains highly competitive, so when one major lender moves, others rarely want to be left behind."

Justin Moy, managing director of Chelmsford-based EHF Mortgages, said the cut was "welcome".

‌



He added: "Nationwide are not normally the first to move, but this is a welcome cut after a few weeks of sharp increases in fixed rate pricing. Inevitably other lenders will follow throughout the week, this will be down to improving swap rates given the relative calm in the Middle East over the last few days, coupled with a traditionally quieter time for lenders."

David Stirling, Independent Financial Adviser at Belfast-based Mint Wealth, said he expected other lenders to follow Nationwide's example.

He added: "After weeks of lenders raising rates in lockstep, Nationwide has had the decency to go the other way. Swap rates have settled and Nationwide is moving fast, cutting fixed rates by up to 0.19% from tomorrow. Others will follow.

‌



"The mortgage market moves in herds, and right now the herd is heading somewhere more hospitable. The window is open, but it has a habit of closing abruptly, so act accordingly."

Nouran Moustafa, practice principal and IFA at Roxton Wealth, said mortgage rates were still volatile.

She added: "These cuts are modest, but the timing matters. After weeks of upward pressure, Nationwide is effectively signalling that the recent fall in swap rates has created enough breathing room to compete again. I expect other lenders to follow if swaps remain lower, because nobody wants to look expensive when buyer and remortgage demand is still highly rate-sensitive.

‌



"But this is unlikely to become a straight race to the bottom: funding markets remain volatile, so lenders may cut selectively, protect margins or withdraw deals quickly if conditions reverse. Borrowers should welcome the movement without gambling on endless reductions. A 0.19% cut can still save meaningful money on a large mortgage, but the best deal depends on fees, loan-to-value and circumstances, not the headline rate alone."

View 4 Images Nouran Moustafa (Image: Nouran Moustafa/Newspage)

Aaron Strutt, product and communications director at London-based Trinity Financial, said the 3.99% tracker from Barclays looked a better bet than Nationwide's offering.

‌



He added: "After a few weeks of mortgage rate hikes across the lenders Nationwide has announced some pricing improvements. The building society’s cheapest two-year fix is coming down marginally from 4.54% to 4.52% and the five-year fix is reducing from 4.61% to 4.53%. Its cheapest two-year tracker is staying at 4.09%.

"Nationwide has clearly been busy given the size of the previous rate hikes that pushed them out of the best buy tables. Hopefully a few more lenders will lower rates again and we can reverse the scale of the price rises we have seen recently. On Friday afternoon the lender Gen H sent a message to brokers saying after last week’s swap rate spike, things have “turned right round” meaning the lender could lower rates by up to 0.40%.

"Many borrowers are not going to fancy paying close to 4.5% for a fixed rate & they will expect that rates will come down again sooner rather than later. The Barclays 3.99% tracker seems to offer the best value at the moment even if there is a base rate hike."

‌



View 4 Images Rohit Kohli (Image: Rohit Kohli/Newspage)

Rohit Kohli, director of Romsey-based The Mortgage Stop, said he didn't expect rates to fall significantly yet.

He added: "Good news – but let's not get carried away. Nationwide's cut reflects a recent dip in swap rates, and they've moved fast to pass it on. More lenders will likely follow if conditions hold. The problem is, they might not. We're in an environment where rates can move sharply based on what politicians say and do, here and abroad.

Article continues below

"The rollercoaster isn't stopping any time soon – not while that uncertainty persists. Take this reduction for what it is: a positive moment in an otherwise unpredictable market."

News.title: Breast cancer checks missing most women under 50 who are at risk, says study
News.content:
Breast cancer is a leading cause of death in women under 50 in the UK.

About one in seven women develop breast cancer in their lifetime, yet only 5-10% of cases are linked to inherited genes.

Most cases - 96% - are in women over 40, while 25% are in women over 75.

Men can get breast cancer too, with about 420 new cases every year in the UK.

In England, guidance from Nice recommends GPs ask about family history if a woman is worried that she might have a higher risk of breast cancer, and sometimes if they are over 35 and using an oral contraceptive pill or considering taking hormone replacement therapy (HRT).

Hormones have been linked to a slightly increased risk of breast cancer, although larger risk factors include alcohol intake and obesity.

The study, by a team from Cambridge University and the Institute of Cancer Research, looks at how to predict breast cancer risk in younger women.

They used a risk calculator called Boadicea that combines factors such as family history, lifestyle, reproductive history and genetic information to give a risk score.

If all women under 50 were to have this done, they estimate about a quarter (26.5%) would be categorised as at above-average risk and referred for further assessment.

This would include a third of women under 50 (34.8%) who develop breast cancer within 10 years.

By comparison, the current Nice criteria would result in 1.4% of women under 50 being referred for further assessment, which would include just 4.4% of those women who develop breast cancer.

A main reason for the disparity, the researchers say, is because three-quarters of women (73%) under 50 who develop breast cancer within a decade have no family history of breast cancer - the key criterion in the Nice guidelines.

News.title: There's a reason child vaccination rates are falling - and it's not social media
News.content:
Twenty-week-old Grayson easily could have become one of the tens of thousands of British babies left unvaccinated against polio.

His mother, Lily, agrees with the principle of immunisation. But overwhelmed by the early weeks of motherhood, and suffering from post-partum depression after a traumatic birth, she was daunted by the prospect of a long journey to a doctor's surgery. "I've been through the trenches, awake all night. You don't want to leave the house, or go to a different town."

Weeks ticked by, and eventually Grayson missed the polio and diptheria jabs he was supposed to get at eight weeks old. By that point he was officially classed by the NHS as "overdue" for vaccination; effectively, he was on his GP's naughty list.

Then Lily realised there was a clinic practically on her doorstep - at a location she hadn't expected.

That clinic - in Keighley, west Yorkshire - runs from a vacant retail unit at the Airedale shopping centre, a 1960s-era precinct that locals say has fallen on hard times in recent years, with plenty of empty, boarded-up units. The staff who created the clinic thought: why not use one of those vacant units to administer vaccines?

"This was an empty shop; there was nothing here, the windows were all blacked out," Flora Jennings, a local charity coordinator, tells me over the sound of a baby's laughter, on the morning I visit the clinic.

News.title: Analysis: Trump challenged by cold reality from top allies
News.content:
It's been a humbling few days for Donald Trump, even if the American president is reluctant to acknowledge it.

In a series of setbacks, Trump has faced adversity in matters both large and small; two of which he cares about dearly and one that could determine his and his party's political fate for the remaining two years of his presidential term.

From a flawed attempt to renovate a Washington landmark to questions about his pick to head the justice department to increasingly complicated efforts to end his war in Iran, the president has been handling tricky issues - many of his own making.

Trump's response has been a familiar one. A first term refrain - that the president makes his own reality with "alternative facts" - is still the operative one. He sticks to beliefs even in the face of contravening evidence.

Unlike his first term, however, when many of his most notable conflicts were with dissenters in his own administration, this time around he has butted heads even with those who have proven themselves the most loyal to him.

On Friday, US Attorney Jeanine Pirro, a former Fox News host and stalwart Trump ally, moved to drop felony destruction of property charges against former Olympian David Hearn, who federal prosecutors had accused of intentionally damaging the Reflecting Pool near the Washington Monument.

"The damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism," she wrote in a 20-page court filing announcing her department's decision. She attributed her decision to prosecute Hearn as the result of misleading information provided by the Department of Interior.

Trump may embrace alternative facts, but the evidence Pirro confronted â what she would have had to defend in court, before a judge and potentially sceptical jury â provided scarce support for her case. And so she abandoned it.

Trump had enthusiastically endorsed the vandalism explanation, however, and he stuck by it. In a Truth Social post on Saturday, he criticised Pirro's decision to drop the case and did so again in comments from the Oval Office on Monday.

"She folded like an umbrella," he groused.

If the Reflecting Pool case was an instance of Trump being forced to face legal reality, up on Capitol Hill it was an unpleasant political reality that confronted him.

One of Trump's closest allies â his former criminal defence attorney Todd Blanche â was hitting stiff headwinds in his bid to become attorney general on a permanent basis.

Two Republican senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, had joined Democrats to block Blanche's nomination. They were demanding Blanche provide a letter formally disavowing any attempts to revive the proposed $1.8bn fund to pay individuals who claimed to have been the targets of politicised government prosecution.

Tillis called it a "payout pot for punks" amid concerns it could be used to compensate people prosecuted over the US Capitol riot by Trump's supporters in 2021.

In another Saturday Truth Social post, Trump wrote that he would keep Blanche on as acting attorney general and "push hard" to get Congress to pass legislation authorising the fund.

"It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done," he wrote, suggesting that no matter what the ultimate outcome of Blanche's nomination, Trump is unlikely to ever let the issue go.

The political maths in the Senate, however, was undeniable. By the next day Blanche had acceded to the senators' request, releasing two letters that Tillis and Cornyn said satisfied their concerns.

In comments from the White House on Monday, Blanche escaped the scolding that Pirro the prosecutor received. Trump said he "didn't look at" Blanche's documents. "I understand there's been a sign-off, but I don't know what they agreed," he said.

News.title: Thunderstorms and flash flood risk on final day of UK heatwave
News.content:
The heatwave impacting parts of the UK this week continues into Tuesday with a risk of thunderstorms in some parts.

Pershore in Worcestershire and Cavendish in Suffolk hit three consecutive days of heatwave threshold temperatures on Monday and it is expected more parts of southern and eastern England will reach heatwave criteria on Tuesday.

Amber and yellow heat health alerts, external are in effect across much of England until 09:00 BST Wednesday, with temperatures expected to reach more than 30C in some areas.

The intense heat will be short lived though as a change in the weather pattern is on the way from midweek.

News.title: West Ham co-owner David Sullivan advised to stay away from home matches
News.content:
The recommendation from London Stadium comes after a joint investigation by BBC Panorama and The Times revealed that seven women have accused Sullivan of sexually exploitative and predatory behaviour. He has categorically denied the allegations.

He stood down as joint chairman of the club shortly before the investigation was broadcast, saying he wanted to focus on fighting what he called "factually incorrect and entirely false, decades-old allegations concerning my personal life". He remains the club's largest shareholder.

The investigation also revealed that Sullivan has been banned from contact with West Ham's women's and youth teams for three years due to safeguarding concerns. London Stadium were unaware of the restrictions until the BBC's report.

Sullivan was banned after a historic allegation about his conduct was raised with the Football Association in 2023. He has previously said the allegation was false and that because he had never met any academy or women's team players "1-2-1" during his 16 years at the club, he accepted what he saw as a "meaningless restrictionâ¦for a quiet life".

West Ham were relegated from the Premier League in May and are due to play their first home game of the new season, a Carabao Cup match against Portsmouth, on Saturday.

Sullivan was a regular attendee at the London Stadium last season, where he was photographed watching games from the directors' box.

A spokesperson for London Stadium, the operator of the publicly owned venue, said that "following media reports at the end of the season regarding a safeguarding matter being managed by the club, London Stadium sought further information to ensure it could fulfil its own safeguarding responsibilities".

It said that West Ham had told it that the "matter was investigated and that the club does not consider there to be an ongoing safeguarding risk associated with Mr Sullivan attending the stadium".

However it said that, despite this, it had recommended the businessman stay away from games because of the "potential for demonstrations and anti-social behaviour by some spectators".

Sullivan has previously faced criticism from fans over his running of the club, with thousands joining a protest in September last year calling for his departure.

West Ham declined to comment. It is understood that the club intends to work with the stadium operators to facilitate Sullivan's attendance at games.

Sullivan has not responded to a request for comment.

Meanwhile, presenter Tony Livesey left BBC Radio 5 Live on Monday after 16 years at the station, the corporation announced.

Livesey stepped back from his weekday late night talk show in June, following allegations made against Sullivan. He had previously worked as editor-in-chief of Sullivan's Daily and Sunday Sport publications.

One alleged victim said that Livesey had arranged a meeting between her and Sullivan in 1999.

Livesey said he had "no recollection" of introducing the young woman to Sullivan and that it was "not part" of his job to do so.

He added that he had "great sympathy for a woman who may have become a victim", but rejected any suggestion that he had played "any role whatsoever in that scenario" and said he found the allegation "abhorrent".

News.title: Half-price rail travel extended to 18-year-olds
News.content:
Eighteen-year-olds will be able to buy half-price train tickets for most services when railcard rules are changed later this month, the Department for Transport (DfT) has announced.

It's an extension of the 16-17 Saver railcard which currently expires when the holder turns 18. From 17 August, they will be valid for a full year from the date of purchase.

It means 17-year-olds will be able to buy the railcard up until the day before they turn 18, making it valid until the day before they turn 19.

The existing rule meant more than 70,000 students each year were an average of Â£175 worse off than those in the same academic year who hadn't yet had their 18th birthday, the DfT said.

The 16-17 Saver Railcard costs Â£35 per year and entitles the holder to 50% off most train fares.

Rail minister Lord Hendy claimed this "common sense change" is "exactly what passengers should expect from the railway".

He said the change would "lower the cost of travel at a critical time for teenagers, whether they're pursuing further education, vocational pathways or getting their footing in the jobs market".

Jacqueline Starr, chief executive of industry body the Rail Delivery Group, said the change demonstrates the sector's commitment to "offering better value fares and delivering a more joined-up railway".

Kaynat Ahmad, vice president for further education at the National Union of Students, described the railcard as "essential for young people reliant on trains to get to college, work or training".

Eighteen-year-olds were already entitled to a 16-25 Railcard, but that only entitles them to a third off the cost of travel.

The announcement comes after the government said the cap on most single bus fares in England will be cut from Â£3 to Â£2 next year.

News.title: 'Rape list' part of misogyny girls face at school
News.content:
A group of teenage girls have said they feel "worthless" and "frightened" as a result of the extreme misogyny they regularly experience.

The students, from Tyneside, have spoken out after making a film about the language they endure at school and online.

Many comments are too explicit to share, but they include threats of violence and rape often masked as "banter". One girl described how disturbed she had been after a "rape list" was made by boys in her school.

The government said it was "taking bold and decisive action to halve violence against women and girls", with changes being introduced from September to help teachers challenge misogyny.

The North East has the highest rate of violence against women and girls in England and charities warned unchallenged attitudes could lead to abuse in early relationships.

Misogyny is defined as a contempt for, hatred of or prejudice against women.

One girl told the BBC she felt "worthless" after learning of the "rape list" made by boys in her school.

"Boys ordering girls, who they want to rape the most and then the least," she explained.

"It is frightening because you don't know people's real intentions."

News.title: Heatwaves are changing summer weddings - here's how to plan for one
News.content:
"As soon as I put my dress on, my makeup was just falling off my face."

Aimie Seale is one of hundreds of brides whose weddings landed in the middle of a heatwave this summer.

She had chosen a July weekend in the hope of avoiding any wet weather. Instead, she faced 30C heat with her ceremony in a sweltering West Yorkshire church, predominantly made of glass.

"It was just unbearably hot," says Aimie. "I remember looking at my husband at one point, and he was just dripping with sweat, so everybody kept passing him tissues halfway through the service."

Aimie and her now-husband Ryan had to book an emergency marquee to offer extra shade and an ice-cream van to keep their guests cool.

An additional cost on an already expensive day, with the average wedding in the UK costing more than Â£20,000., external

But this last-minute battle to cope with the heat is only going to get worse. Half of the years between 2015 and 2024 saw temperatures above 35C - up from one in ten - as climate change increases the risk of heatwaves.

News.title: PC Harper's mother 'devastated' his killers set for early release under revised plans
News.content:
The mother of PC Andrew Harper has told the BBC she is "devastated" two of his killers remain eligible for early release after the government revised plans to tackle overcrowding.

Prisoners who committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from the scheme for England and Wales, the government announced on Monday.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he "wanted to go even further", but that would not be possible without the prison system collapsing and putting the public "at much greater risk".

PC Harper, 28, was killed in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, his mother, Debbie Adlam, said: "It feels like we're letting Andrew down again.

"We've been through the justice system, we thought we'd done as best as we could.

"Now we're standing up to fight again... so I just feel really let down, for Andrew's sake as well as ours."

His family previously said they had received a letter from the Ministry of Justice confirming that two of the offenders who killed the officer could be included in the scheme.

The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence and would not have been eligible.

Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the car and sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter after a trial at the Old Bailey in 2020, would become eligible for release after serving half of their sentences.

Adlan said she was "devastated" by the government's latest announcement, and vowed to continue to fight for justice. "I could not sit back and do nothing," she said.

She added that Justice Secretary Alex Norris had called her to explain the situation and apologise.

News.title: France hits out at Reform UK plan to return migrants using Navy
News.content:
France has hit out at a Reform UK plan to return migrant boats using the Navy, saying the proposals would violate its sovereignty and breach international law.

Nigel Farage's party announced that if it was in power it would intercept boats crossing the English Channel and return migrants to French ports, even if France disagreed.

Opposition parties branded the plan unworkable, while a Labour minister said it would lead to "a lot of time arguing with France" instead of "actually getting to grips with the problem".

Responding to the French government, a Reform spokesperson said: "We will always stand up for British interests and protect our people, whether Emmanuel Macron likes it or not."

The spokesperson added: "Humanitarian missions do not violate maritime or international law."

Under the plans, which Reform said it would bring in if it entered government after the next election, military-crewed inflatable boats deployed from 10 Navy patrol vessels would be used to "come alongside" migrant boats crossing the English Channel.

Border Force officers and police stationed onboard would be tasked with arresting people in the boats, and they would then be returned to France or Belgium by Navy personnel or Marines.

The party said returns operations would be conducted by military personnel with Border Force officers on hand in case of "non-compliance", with a Bay Class landing ship providing "detention capacity at sea" for up to 700 people.

Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Reform's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the party would aim to get agreement to disembark arrested migrants at French ports.

He added: "If the Elysee Palace refuses, make no mistake - His Majesty's Royal Marines will disembark them safely on the very shore they left that morning".

Speaking alongside him, Farage played down the prospect of a diplomatic confrontation with the French, claiming that attitudes in France towards the idea were "softening".

But in a statement issued later on Monday, the French interior ministry said: "This would constitute a violation of French sovereignty, as well as a violation of the law of the sea and international law."

A spokesperson for the department added that measures agreed with the UK, as well as "operations deployed at the local level", had already led to a reduction in crossings so far this year compared to the same period in 2025.

News.title: Woman has pioneering womb surgery to fix 'miracle' baby with intestines outside its body
News.content:
Doctors have used ground-breaking surgery on an unborn baby to successfully correct a birth defect while he was still inside the womb.

His mother, Maisie Savage, from London, was operated on by doctors in the US while she was 26 weeks pregnant.

Baby Theo, who is now five months old and thriving, had gastroschisis, where the belly button does not develop properly, causing the intestines to grow externally.

Doctors partially exposed his mother's womb and then gently pushed his organs back inside his abdomen using keyhole surgery.

He was the third baby in the world to benefit from the first-of-its-kind clinical trial.

Maisie, 29, and Theo's father, Josh French, 36, both teachers, say they are incredibly relieved by the success of the pioneering surgery.

"He's a little miracle, isn't he?" Maisie told BBC News.

But they both know things could have been very different.

The serious birth defect affects one in 3,000 UK babies each year. In the best-case scenarios, babies can require weeks in intensive care and nutritional feeding through a tube or IV and corrective surgery.

For the most complex cases, like Theo's, outcomes are far more serious with up to six months in neonatal intensive care, multiple surgeries, IV nutritional feeding for up to two years, and a possible intestinal transplant.

Even with the highest level of medical care, one in 10 babies will die.

News.title: Newspaper columnist and broadcaster Rod Liddle dies aged 66
News.content:
Newspaper columnist and broadcaster Rod Liddle has died aged 66 after a short illness.

Liddle's children paid tribute to their father, who they described as their guide "on how to live an extraordinary life", while CEO of News UK, Rebekah Brooks, called him "an inimitable journalistic force."

Brooks added that "he challenged conventional thinking and left an indelible mark on British journalism."

Liddle, a columnist for the Sun and the Sunday Times, died at The James Cook University Hospital in Middlesbrough on Sunday evening.

A former editor of BBC Radio 4's flagship Today programme, he also had a weekly column in the Spectator, as well as a show on Times Radio.

His children, Wilder, Tyler and Emmy, said: "We're all very saddened and shocked at the sudden passing of our wonderful father.

"He raised us much as you might imagine, to be inquisitive, brave and always humorous.

"Even in hospital in the last few weeks, he consistently held the room and never let the awful situation show.

"He has left a legacy that we are all incredibly proud of, he will always be our guide on how to live an extraordinary life."

News.title: Author La Plante banned from driving for six months
News.content:
The court heard she already had nine points on her licence, from three speeding offences in June 2023 and then June and July 2025.

She told the court she believed she would have to have the dog rehomed if she was unable to drive him to his daily walks, saying: "I think the emotional turmoil of that would truly damn my career as a writer.

"It's very, very solitary and I work exceptionally hard and I would just stop."

La Plante, who is best known for creating Prime Suspect's no-nonsense Det Ch Insp Jane Tennison, admitted driving at 24mph twice, 25mph, 26mph and 27mph in the latest offences, which all happened as she was on her way to take her dog for his daily walk.

Giving evidence, La Plante said she got her dog Theo after suffering the devastation of the untimely death of another dog, Hugo.

Fighting back tears, she said she "lost it" when Hugo died and she "didn't know what to do with [her] life".

She added her new dog had helped her through the grieving process.

News.title: Farage says he discussed return to politics months before general election
News.content:
Nigel Farage has told the BBC he discussed the "potential liabilities" of returning to politics before the 2024 general election.

It comes after The Sunday Times, external reported Farage had negotiated a deal in March and April 2024 with then-Reform leader Richard Tice to return to lead the party.

Farage confirmed he spoke with Tice in spring 2024 to scope out what would happen to Reform's finances if he returned but said it "wasn't a deal, it wasn't an agreement", adding that talks came "quite some time after" he received a Â£5m gift from a billionaire donor.

Labour said Farage's remarks had "blown a gaping hole" in his argument for not declaring the gift after becoming an MP in July 2024.

Farage has repeatedly argued the Â£5m from British cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne was an "unconditional gift", was intended for his personal security, "wasn't political in any sense at all" and he was not an MP when he received it.

Reform's opponents have said he should have declared it in the MPs' register of interests when he was elected to Parliament.

The Parliamentary Standards Commissioner was investigating whether Farage broke the rules, but the process was suspended when he stood down as Clacton MP last month to force a by-election.

Farage said he took this decision as the "people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions". The investigation will be resumed if Farage wins the by-election, which is taking place on 13 August.

Farage left frontline politics in 2021 and embarked on a broadcasting career.

In May 2024, Farage was serving as Reform's honorary president but announced he would not be standing as a candidate in the general election in July of that year.

He reversed this position at the beginning of June and took over the leadership of the party.

Appearing at a press conference on Monday, Farage was asked if he had negotiated a deal on what would happen to Reform's finances if he came back as leader - in light of the report in The Sunday Times.

He replied: "I had no intention of returning to politics or as leader of Reform, but in the spring of that year I did talk to Richard Tice about what the liabilities would be if I was to come back to that position.

"And you'd be a bit of a mug, wouldn't you, to walk into a job and not find out what the potential liabilities were, and they were substantial.

"But without Richard, the party wouldn't have even survived, so that was useful for me to know. But it wasn't a deal, it wasn't an agreement, it was subject to if I came back."

He added: "If you want clarification on this, that came quite some time after the gift, which is perhaps the important point."

Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, said: "Nigel Farage has blown a gaping hole in his excuse for why his secret Â£5m 'gift' from a crypto billionaire did not need to be declared."

The Commons code of conduct states that new MPs "must register all their current financial interests, and any registrable benefits (other than earnings) received in the 12 months before their election within one month of their election".

The rules say "purely personal gifts or benefits" from family or commercial loans would not normally have to be registered.

The rules also say "both the possible motive of the giver and the use to which the gift is to be put should be considered", adding "if there is any doubt, the benefit should be registered".

A full list of the candidates standing in the Clacton by-election can be found here.

News.title: Man sniffed out by police dog while hiding behind fake wall on 300-plant cannabis farm
News.content:
A man has been jailed for six months after being found by a sniffer dog behind a fake wall on a cannabis farm.

Albert Hysaj, 42, pleaded guilty to producing cannabis and was sentenced at Cardiff Crown Court on Friday.

Hysaj was caught after a police dog named Asko located him in the commercial property on the Bowen Industrial Estate, in Aberbargoed, Caerphilly county, in May.

Gwent Police found 313 cannabis plants inside two linked units over three rooms, which included a living area with kitchen and bathroom.

News.title: Presenter Tony Livesey leaves BBC Radio 5 Live after 16 years
News.content:
Presenter Tony Livesey has left BBC Radio 5 Live after 16 years at the station, the corporation has announced.

Livesey stepped back from his weekday late night talk show in June, following allegations made against his former newspaper boss David Sullivan.

He had previously worked as editor-in-chief of Sullivan's Daily and Sunday Sport publications.

Several women have accused Sullivan, a billionaire businessman and West Ham co-owner, of abusing his power and preying on them for sex, in some cases when they were teenagers. Sullivan has strongly denied the allegations.

The claims against Sullivan were made in a joint investigation by the Times and BBC Panorama.

The BBC previously said Livesey had asked to take a break from presenting his programme while the issues raised by the investigation were being examined.

One alleged victim said that Livesey had arranged a meeting between her and Sullivan in 1999.

Livesey said he had "no recollection" of introducing the young woman to Sullivan and that it was "not part" of his job to do so.

He added that he had "great sympathy for a woman who may have become a victim", but rejected any suggestion that he had played "any role whatsoever in that scenario" and said he found the allegation "abhorrent".

In an email sent to 5 Live staff on Monday morning, the station's controller Heidi Dawson said he had now decided to leave.

"Tony has asked me to pass on his heartfelt thanks to the brilliant colleagues at 5 Live who he has had the pleasure of working with over the years," she wrote.

"I know many of you have also really enjoyed working with Tony, and we wish him well for all his future endeavours."

The award-winning presenter worked for the BBC from 2006 - the same year he left the newspapers - appearing on 5 Live from 2010 onwards, including a successful stint hosting its drivetime show.

He won radio awards - ARIA and APAs - for his reporting on how it feels to lose your mother as a child, and an ARIAS gold award after he was asked by the late Dame Deborah James to conduct her final interview.

His topical three-hour programme was broadcast on 5 Live from Monday to Thursday, featuring interviews and phone calls from listeners.

At least seven people, including three children, have been killed after a Ukrainian drone crashed onto a popular beach on the Russian Black Sea coast, according to Russian authorities.

Another 40 people were injured after a drone crashed into the busy holiday resort near the town of Gelendzhik on Monday.

Footage on social media shows the moment the drone veered towards the beach before slamming into it and causing a large explosion, which sent people fleeing from the water.

Officials said 17 people were rushed to the hospital following the incident and a specialist medical disaster team had been dispatched to the scene of the explosion.

open image in gallery ( Social media )

Veniamin Kondratyev, the governor of Russia's ‌southern Krasnodar region, which includes the resort, described the incident as a tragedy.

He said in a statement on Telegram said: “What happened today was a deliberate attack by the Kyiv regime on the civilian population, which has no connection whatsoever to military infrastructure.”

Ukraine has not issued a statement on the attack, but its military has repeatedly said it does not deliberately target civilians.

It is not clear if the drone was intercepted before hitting the beach.

The attack took place near a £1bn complex between Arkhipo-Osipovka and Gelendzhik, which has been dubbed as “Putin’s palace”.

A 2021 investigation by late opposition leader Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation linked the development to Vladimir Putin, but the Russian leader has denied any ownership.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova was cited by the TASS state news agency as accusing Ukraine of resorting to terrorism.

Three civilians were also killed in ​an overnight "enemy attack" ‌on the Russian-controlled ‌Crimean peninsula, ‌according to Sergei Aksyonov, the Russia-installed governor of Crimea.

A separate drone attack on Monday caused a fire to break at out at one of Russian online retailer Wildberries’ warehouses in the Vladimir region, which has been repeatedly targeted in recent weeks.

Officials said a young man sustained a non-life-threatening head injury and was taken to hospital following the attack.

Russia has repeatedly struck civilian targets in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities since its invasion in 2022.

open image in gallery At least nine people were killed in a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv on Saturday ( AFP/Getty )

On Monday, Sweden's foreign ministry said it had summoned ​Russia's top ‌diplomat in ‌Stockholm to protest ‌Moscow's attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure ‌in Ukraine.

It comes after Russia launched ballistic missiles on Kyiv on Saturday, killing nine people and injuring 28, including four children.

A residential building in the Shevchenkivskyi district was partially destroyed in the attack, according to Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko.

Condemning the attack, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on X: “Russians launched 35 missiles at Ukraine, including 27 ballistic missiles, as well as 185 attack drones of various types. Kyiv was the primary target, but strikes also hit the Dnipro, Sumy, Kharkiv, and Poltava regions.

“Only one ballistic missile was intercepted, simply because there are no interceptors for the Patriot systems. And it is this shortage of ballistic missile interceptors that only encourages Russia to launch such attacks that take human lives.”
