World.title: Serena and Venus Williams Set for Cincinnati Open Doubles Return
World.content:
Serena and Venus Williams will play doubles together for the first time since 2022 after the Cincinnati Open handed the sisters a wildcard into its women’s doubles draw. Venus also received a singles wildcard, alongside Sloane Stephens, Taylor Townsend, Darja Vidmanova, Elvina Kalieva, Caroline Dolehide and Lois Boisson, for the tournament running Aug. 8 to 23 in Mason, Ohio.

The pairing marks the first time the sisters will compete as a team in Cincinnati. Together they have won 14 major doubles titles and three Olympic gold medals, and their last doubles appearance came at the 2022 US Open, a defeat to Czech pair Lucie Hradecka and Linda Noskova in the tournament Serena described at the time as her step away from the sport.

Serena, 44, ended that absence this summer. She played doubles at Queen’s Club and at the Berlin Open, without Venus on either occasion, before returning to singles at Wimbledon. Her first-round loss there to 20-year-old Australian Maya Joint went three sets, and she sustained a knee injury during the match.

Her agent, Jill Smoller, said she tweaked her right knee at the end of the first set and was excused from post-match media duties by Wimbledon and WTA medical staff. The sisters had been drawn to face Camila Osorio of Colombia and Solana Sierra of Argentina, but Serena pulled out days later, writing on Instagram that she was heartbroken to withdraw from doubles. She later posted images of fluid drained from the knee, and her coach, Rennae Stubbs, said her intention was to keep playing through the US Open.

The Cincinnati entry is the first firm sign that plan is holding. Serena remains one title short of the all-time record of 24 Grand Slam singles crowns, shared by Margaret Court and Novak Djokovic, and a run in Ohio would be the clearest indicator yet of whether she returns to Flushing Meadows.

Venus arrives in a harder spot. She turned 46 in June and is still chasing her first singles win of 2026, having exited in the first round of all eight tournaments she has entered this year. Her doubles form has been marginally better, with one win apiece at two of the six events she has played, most recently partnering Britain’s Katie Boulter in Madrid and Alexandra Eala in Berlin. Her career record in Cincinnati stands at 12-10, with a semifinal in 2012 and a quarterfinal in 2019. She first played a WTA event in 1994 and has won 49 singles titles, including seven majors and Olympic gold in 2000.

The tournament opens with a community weekend on Aug. 8 and 9, with competition beginning Aug. 11 and both singles finals scheduled for Aug. 23. Draws and match scheduling are typically released in the days before play starts, so the sisters’ first opponents are not yet known. Costa Rica runs two hours behind Ohio in August, meaning afternoon matches in Mason land late morning locally.

World.title: Costa Rica Files Constitutional Reform to Widen Extradition of Citizens
World.content:
Costa Rica is preparing to make a big change to who it can send abroad to face trial. The government says it will ask the Legislative Assembly to change the Constitution so that Costa Rican citizens can be extradited for a much longer list of crimes than the two allowed today.

Right now, Article 32 of the Constitution lets Costa Rica hand over its own citizens in only two situations: international drug trafficking and terrorism. Everything else is off the table. Before 2025, even those two were off the table, and no Costa Rican could be sent abroad for anything at all.

The new proposal would add a long list. Under the text President Laura Fernández described when she presented her security package in late July, the added crimes would include money laundering, human trafficking and smuggling migrants, gun trafficking, trafficking in human organs and tissue, contract killing and murders tied to criminal groups, belonging to an international criminal organization, and computer crimes that hit national security or key state systems.

Fernández has been clear about one thing and that is that this would not mean Costa Ricans get shipped abroad automatically. A Costa Rican judge would still have to approve every single case, and that ruling would have to be final. On top of that, the act would have to be a crime in both countries. If something is illegal in the country asking for the person but legal in Costa Rica, the answer is still no. Lawyers call this double criminality, and it stays in place.

The Assembly’s year is split into two kinds of sessions. During special sessions, the president decides which bills get debated. During the regular sessions, which started in August, the deputies set their own agenda — and that is the only window in which a constitutional change can be introduced. So, the Executive handed over five ordinary bills on July 27, held this one back, and said it would come on today, August 3.

There is already a competing idea from inside the governing party. Deputy José Miguel Villalobos wants to go further. Instead of naming specific crimes, his version would allow extradition for any crime that carries more than four years in prison, as long as the other country also punishes it. His argument is not that the government is being too soft, but that a written list will always miss something. He said he needs signatures from other deputies first, and then he will decide whether to file his version on its own or as a replacement for the government’s.

Whatever version moves, none of this happens fast. Changing the Constitution is much harder than passing a normal law. The proposal has to be introduced in ordinary sessions, accepted for debate, studied in committee, and then approved by two-thirds of all deputies, which is 38 out of 57.

Then the whole thing has to be taken up again by the next Assembly, where it faces three more debates and the same two-thirds bar before it actually becomes part of the Constitution. The Constitutional Chamber also reviewed the last extradition change before it advanced, and the same is expected here. Legal experts put the realistic minimum at about two years. The 2025 change took longer than that.

It is worth being clear about what would not change. Judges still decide, case by case. The act still has to be a crime in both countries. Costa Rica does not have the death penalty or life imprisonment, and it will not send someone somewhere they could face either, so the requesting country has to guarantee that first. And this reform on its own would not update the 1971 extradition law. The Assembly had to pass a separate law in late 2025 to make that statute match the constitutional change, and it would need to do something similar again.

For anyone who became Costa Rican by naturalization rather than by birth you are treated the same. That has been true since 2025, and the new text does not change it. There is no separate rule, no lesser protection, and no extra exposure written into the Constitution.

In practice, though, someone who lived, worked or held assets in another country before becoming Costa Rican is more likely to have conduct that both countries treat as a crime, and the offenses being added are mostly cross-border by nature. Holding a second passport neither helps nor hurts. Costa Rica allows dual citizenship, and it does not affect how an extradition request is handled.

The 2025 change stopped being theoretical some time ago. Costa Rica carried out its first extradition of citizens in March, sending former security minister and ex-magistrate Celso Gamboa Sánchez and Edwin López Vega to the United States. By mid-June, officials counted 23 citizens by birth or naturalization who had been detained after extradition requests, and more U.S. requests have arrived since.

The old rule had also let foreign nationals who obtained Costa Rican papers claim the same shield as someone born here, which was a large part of why the ban was lifted in the first place. The Justice Ministry has separately tightened prison rules for inmates with active extradition cases.

For now, this is a proposal and nothing more. Whether it passes in the government’s version, in the broader version Villalobos wants, or not at all will be settled over the next two Assemblies.

World.title: Costa Rica Under Yellow Alert as Saturated Ground Raises Flood Risk
World.content:
If you are driving to Limón, Turrialba or the southern Pacific today, expect delays and check the road before you leave. A yellow alert is in effect today for Pococí, Guácimo, Siquirres, Matina and Turrialba after a tropical wave moved across overnight and a green alert covers a much wider stretch of the Caribbean, the Northern Zone and the south.

The green alert is for Limón and Talamanca on the Caribbean side, Sarapiquí, San Carlos, Río Cuarto, Los Chiles, Guatuso and Upala in the Northern Zone, and Pérez Zeledón, Buenos Aires, Osa, Golfito, Puerto Jiménez, Corredores and Coto Brus in the south. As a reminder. yellow means preparation and active monitoring, not evacuation. Green means stay aware and watch conditions where you are.

The reason the alert level went up has less to do with how much rain is coming than with how much has already fallen. Some watersheds are more than 90% saturated, which means the ground cannot absorb anything more. Rain that would normally soak in now runs straight off hillsides and into rivers that are already high. That is why a moderate downpour today can cause more damage than a heavier one would have caused two weeks ago.

Tropical Wave 28 crossed this morning and strengthened the band of storms sitting over the Pacific near Costa Rica. Rain arrived overnight near both coasts and across the Caribbean and Northern Zone lowlands. Through the afternoon, expect scattered moderate rain and thunderstorms along the Pacific coast and in the mountains west of the Central Valley, with more isolated showers over the northern and Caribbean plains. By evening the rain shifts toward the southern Pacific coast.

Totals should land between 20 and 40 millimeters (roughly 0.8 to 1.6 inches), with the heaviest accumulations reaching about 100 millimeters (roughly 4 inches) in the south. Isolated gusts near storm cells could hit 80 kilometers per hour (about 50 miles per hour), enough to bring down branches and power lines.

Parts of the Caribbean, unfortunately, did not wait for today’s system. Flooding over the weekend affected Matina, Siquirres, Talamanca and Turrialba, and rescue crews worked before dawn Sunday in Matina, where a river overflow at Finca Estrada left 22 people cut off. Emergency teams are also watching Hamburgo, Islona and Dos Bocas, and the Sixaola river in Talamanca has been running high.

As we have suggested in previous articles when tropical waves come, do not drive through standing water, because you cannot see whether the road under it has washed out, and moving water only 30 centimeters (about a foot) deep can push a car sideways. Do not try to cross a swollen river or creek on foot for the same reason. In towns, storm drains that are already full will back up quickly, so streets can flood faster than the rain seems to justify. If you hear thunder, get inside and stay away from windows and tall isolated trees until it passes.

One more thing worth mentioning here, emergency lines fill up fast during weather events, and every call that is not an emergency delays one that is. Call 911 if someone is in danger. For everything else, follow official updates rather than forwarded messages, which tend to recycle photos and closure reports from previous storms.

Alert levels can change during the day as rivers respond to rainfall upstream, so a canton that is green this morning may not stay that way. Check the current status before committing to a route through any of the affected areas.

World.title: Costa Rica Makes Forbes 2026 List of Best Places to Retire
World.content:
Costa Rica has again been named one of the world’s best places for Americans to retire, appearing in the 2026 edition of the Forbes ranking of overseas retirement destinations published July 31. The list identifies 96 retirement locations across 24 countries on five continents, twelve of them in Europe.

Compilers weighed relative cost of living, taxes, healthcare quality and cost, ease of returning to the United States to see relatives, crime and political instability, and the risk of social isolation in places where English is not widely spoken. They also assessed how difficult each country makes it to obtain permission to stay long term, and factored in climate change and natural hazard exposure.

Costa Rica is described as a place with beaches on two oceans, extraordinary ecological diversity within its tropical forests and a relaxed pace of life that continues to appeal to American retirees, particularly those drawn to the outdoors. Living costs are rated significantly below the U.S. average, crime is characterized as low and the political system as stable. The entry also names a drawback that shapes daily life across much of the country during the green season: flooding.

Healthcare in the larger cities is rated excellent and inexpensive, with the ranking noting that foreign residents who retire here can enroll in the Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social for roughly $150 a month. In practice, CCSS calculates contributions for foreign residents as a percentage of declared income, so what an individual actually pays varies. Spanish is described as helpful but not essential.

As far as residency is concerned, the ranking points to the pensionado category, a two-year renewable status requiring proof of $12,000 in annual income, and notes that Americans can remain in the country as tourists for six months while working toward longer-term permission. That threshold corresponds to the $1,000 monthly lifetime pension required under Costa Rica’s General Law on Migration and Foreigners, Ley 8764, administered by the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería. It is one of several residency routes open to foreign retirees and investors, and among the lowest income bars in the region.

The tax picture is also cited as an advantage. The United States and Costa Rica have no treaty preventing double taxation, but Costa Rica does not tax the foreign income of retirees — a function of the country’s territorial tax system rather than a benefit written specifically for pensioners.

Four locations are singled out: our capital, San José; the mountain area in the Central Valley including Atenas, named for its year-round climate; and Santa Cruz in Guanacaste. Miami and Houston are each about three hours away by nonstop flight. The Central Valley towns have long anchored the country’s foreign retiree population, in part because rents and daily costs there run well below the beach markets while remaining close to San José’s hospitals and the airport.

The ranking arrives against a measurable shift in where Americans spend their later years. As of the last official count at the end of 2024, 712,000 Americans were receiving Social Security benefits abroad, a 20 percent increase over thirteen years. Countries on the list are described as generally regarding U.S. retirees with sufficient assets or retirement income as an economic asset rather than an immigration problem — a pattern Costa Rica has benefited from repeatedly in recent years.

Costa Rica shares the list with several countries competing for the same demographic. Panama, Mexico, Belize, Colombia and Uruguay all appear, as do Albania, Argentina, Austria, Canada, Cyprus, France, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Malaysia, Malta, Mauritius, Montenegro, Portugal, Slovenia, Spain, Thailand and Vietnam. Mauritius and Vietnam are first-time entries.

Climate risk reshaped parts of the list this year. Recommendations for Bordeaux, France, and several locations in Spain including the Costa del Sol were dropped over wildfire and heat exposure, though less than one percent of the land mass in each country had burned. The Philippines and Indonesia were excluded altogether after ranking first and second — the worst — among 193 countries on the latest World Risk Report compiled under United Nations auspices.

Costa Rica has appeared on comparable rankings for years, and the pensionado category that anchors its position has existed in national law since 2009. What changes between editions is the surrounding field: which countries are competing, what income thresholds they set, and how much weight compilers now assign to flood, fire and storm risk.

World.title: CONCACAF Calls for Reckoning With Infantino’s FIFA Leadership
World.content:
North and Central American football’s governing body CONCACAF yesterday called for a “comprehensive reckoning with” Gianni Infantino’s leadership of FIFA after his aborted plan to allow private investment in the World Cup. “This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behavior,” CONCACAF said in a statement.

“A comprehensive reckoning with this presidency is imperative.” Last week, world governing body FIFA had announced plans to create a commercial subsidiary which would run its biggest events, including the World Cup and Club World Cup. This body would be open to minority private investment, under a plan which Infantino said would “turbocharge the development of the game globally” by raising up to $4.2 billion.

On Friday, facing a fierce global backlash, Infantino pulled the plug on the plan. CONCACAF, which includes all three co-hosts of the recently concluded 2026 World Cup — the United States, Canada and Mexico — as well as Caribbean associations, yesterday welcomed the decision to scrap the divisive proposal.

It joined European organization UEFA in criticizing Infantino’s actions and expressing doubt over his suitability to continue in the role. “This concern is not CONCACAF’s alone. It is shared across many confederations, Member Associations and those who serve and love the game,” said the statement.

In defending his initial proposal, Infantino had said that it could provide each of FIFA’s 211 member associations with a one-off payment of $20 million in early 2027 and increase their funding allocation for the 2027-2030 cycle from $8 million to $20 million. But the CONCACAF statement noted that FIFA already has “vast reserves,” and said that its members would push for those finances to be disbursed “for football development across our region, without compromising our shared future.”

Infantino’s plan had “advanced outside every established governance framework, without transparency, consultation or due process,” it said. “A proposal of this magnitude does not reach that stage by accident. It is a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first.”

World.title: Carlton McKoy and baby reportedly injured in shooting near San Ignacio Puma gas station
World.content:
Carlton McKoy and baby reportedly injured in shooting near San Ignacio Puma gas station

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A man and a baby were reportedly injured during a shooting near the Puma Gas Station in San Ignacio Town on Monday night.

Preliminary information identifies the adult victim as Carlton McKoy, who reportedly sustained gunshot wounds to the abdomen and leg. The baby was reportedly struck by gunfire during the incident and was later transferred for further medical treatment, possibly to Belmopan or Belize City.

Initial reports suggest the shooting may have occurred during an attempted robbery and that a security officer fired at the suspected robber. However, the exact circumstances surrounding the incident have not yet been confirmed by police.

The conditions of McKoy and the injured child remain unknown. Police are expected to release additional information as their investigation continues.

World.title: Firestarter: Maskall woman burns down boyfriend’s home after removing all her stuff; Charged for arson
World.content:
Firestarter: Maskall woman burns down boyfriend’s home after removing all her stuff; Charged for arson

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 21-year-old Maskall Village woman has been charged with arson following a fire that destroyed the home she shared with her boyfriend.

Vayda Ashanti August, an unemployed labourer, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, August 3, where she was arraigned on a single count of arson.

Police allege that on Saturday, August 1, August intentionally set fire to a 16-by-24-foot wooden and zinc house belonging to 33-year-old Jose David Recinos. The house and its contents were valued at approximately $35,000 and were completely destroyed.

According to the prosecution’s allegations, August and Recinos were separating, and a man had been hired to help her remove her belongings from the residence. After the items were loaded onto a pickup truck, August allegedly told the driver that she had set the house on fire.

The driver and other persons reportedly attempted to extinguish the blaze but were unsuccessful. August was later detained following a report made by Recinos.

No plea was taken because prosecutors are awaiting instructions from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions on whether the case will proceed summarily or on indictment.

August was granted bail of $10,000, along with two sureties of $5,000 each. She was ordered not to contact Recinos or members of his family, remain at least 100 yards away from places he lives, works or frequently visits, and report to the Maskall Police Station every Wednesday.

She must also reside with her mother and notify the court of any change of address. August met bail later that afternoon and is scheduled to return to court on September 23, 2026.

World.title: One detained, another sought after 18-year-old Ewart Hernandez shot dead on Vernon Street
World.content:
One detained, another sought after 18-year-old Ewart Hernandez shot dead on Vernon Street

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained one man and are searching for another in connection with the murder of 18-year-old Ewart Hernandez in Belize City.

The shooting occurred at approximately 1:15 p.m. on Sunday, August 2, 2026, while police officers were patrolling the area. The officers reportedly heard a gunshot and responded to Vernon Street, where they found Hernandez suffering from a gunshot wound.

Hernandez was rushed for medical treatment but later succumbed to his injury.

Police said surveillance footage showed Hernandez travelling along Vernon Street and stopping near its intersection with Partridge Street, where he remained seated on his motorcycle. Several minutes later, two men approached him, and one reportedly pulled out a firearm and fired a single shot, striking Hernandez.

A man matching the description of one of the suspects was apprehended shortly afterwards and remains in police custody. Investigators are searching for the second suspect.

Authorities said footage from police surveillance cameras across Belize City assisted investigators in identifying the suspects and directing subsequent police operations. Police confirmed that the detained suspect is known to law enforcement, while Hernandez was not known to police.

The shooting was initially reported near the St. Martin de Porres Swift Hall on Vernon Street. Police have not yet disclosed a possible motive for the murder though some reports allege he was robbed for a chain.

World.title: Man detained after chopping 62-year-old grandmother in Succotz during alleged ‘mental health crisis’
World.content:
Man detained after chopping 62-year-old grandmother in Succotz during alleged ‘mental health crisis’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained a 23-year-old man in connection with a chopping incident that left his 62-year-old grandmother seriously injured in San Jose Succotz Village.

The incident occurred at a residence in the village at about 7:30 p.m. on Saturday, August 1.

The injured woman was rushed for medical treatment and was listed in a stable condition at the time of the police press briefing. Police officers, assisted by community members, later apprehended the suspect and took him into custody.

Police said their preliminary investigation suggests that the man may have been experiencing a mental-health crisis. The woman was reportedly injured when she attempted to assist him.

Initial community reports described the injured woman as the suspect’s grandmother, although police officially referred to her only as a female relative.

The man remained detained as police continued their investigation. No criminal charges had been announced at the time of the briefing.

World.title: Police do not suspect foul play in death of ‘Kimmy Boo’
World.content:
Police do not suspect foul play in death of ‘Kimmy Boo’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police say they do not presently suspect foul play in the death of 22-year-old Kimane Rosita Ashanti Garbutt, whose decomposing body was found inside an upstairs room in Belize City on Sunday.

Garbutt, who was also publicly known as “Kimmy Boo,” was discovered at a building at the corner of Vernon Street and Amandala Drive at about 9:30 a.m. on August 2.

Police said Garbutt was last seen alive at approximately 7:00 a.m. the previous day, when she told a friend that she was not feeling well. The friend returned to check on her the following morning and entered the room after repeated calls went unanswered.

Garbutt’s motionless body was found in a seated position and had already begun to decompose.

According to information previously released to the media, Garbutt was in the third trimester of pregnancy, had suffered from epileptic seizures and had reportedly experienced pregnancy complications. She had visited the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital for a prenatal check-up approximately two weeks before her death.

Police said a post-mortem examination will determine the cause of death.

World.title: Orange Walk man Luciano Acosta drowns after canoe capsizes at Honey Camp Lagoon
World.content:
Orange Walk man Luciano Acosta drowns after canoe capsizes at Honey Camp Lagoon

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating the drowning of 44-year-old Luciano Acosta after a canoe overturned during an early-morning fishing trip at Honey Camp Lagoon in the Orange Walk District.

Acosta had gone to the lagoon with relatives and friends on Saturday, August 1. At about 3:00 a.m. the following morning, he and 41-year-old Eliseo Escalante reportedly boarded a canoe to go fishing.

The canoe later capsized. Escalante managed to swim to a mangrove patch, where he called for help and was subsequently rescued. Acosta was found several hours later, partially submerged near a mangrove patch in the lagoon.

Police do not suspect foul play and Acosta’s body awaits a post-mortem examination.

Honey Camp Ranch, where Acosta had reportedly offered his support for several years, remembered him as an authentic person who was always willing to share Belize with others.

World.title: Thirty-five young women empowered through the Girls in Governance Leadership and Art Empowerment Camp
World.content:
Thirty-five young women empowered through the Girls in Governance Leadership and Art Empowerment Camp

Thirty-five young women from across Belize strengthened their leadership and entrepreneurial skills through the Girls in Governance Leadership and Art Empowerment Camp, a six-day residential programme hosted by the Department of Youth Services (DYS) in collaboration with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) at the Kindred Spirit Campgrounds in Belmopan.

Participants took part in sessions on leadership, governance, public speaking, advocacy, digital literacy, media engagement, and entrepreneurship, while developing personal leadership plans to create positive change in their communities.

The camp also featured hands-on creative activities, including designing Belize-inspired tote bags, crafting jewelry, creating eco-art, and learning branding and marketing skills. The initiative reflects the shared commitment of DYS and UNDP to empowering young women through leadership, entrepreneurship, and civic engagement.

World.title: Guatemalan man, Rudy Toj, dies in apparent drowning in Belmopan creek
World.content:
Guatemalan man, Rudy Toj, dies in apparent drowning in Belmopan creek

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating the apparent drowning of a 38-year-old Guatemalan national whose body was found in a creek in Belmopan on Sunday morning.

The deceased was identified as Rudy Bernabe Toj, a resident of Otox-Ha Street in Belmopan.

Police were called to the creek in the San Martin area at about 7:30 a.m. on August 2, where officers found Toj’s motionless body. Efforts were made to resuscitate him, but they were unsuccessful.

Investigators also found a transparent bottle containing alcohol at the scene. Police said they believe Toj had consumed alcohol before entering the water, but have not determined whether it contributed to his death.

His body awaits a post-mortem examination as the investigation continues.

World.title: CLA weeds out high fees
World.content:
From left: Walter Melbourne, Cannabis Licensing Authority’s (CLA) director of licensing and applications; CLA board chair Dr Nadeen Spence; Chief Executive Officer Farrah Blake; and Simoy Brown, director of public relations and communications, address journalists at yesterday’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange.(Photo: Joseph Wellington)

A craving for traditional marijuana farmers to be included in the regulated industry locally has prompted the Cannabis Licensing Authority (CLA) to relax and reduce some entry requirements, including the cost of registration, for easier access to the system.

The registration fee for ganja farmers, which was US$3,000, has been slashed to US$150 under a Cultivator’s Transitional Special Permit Programme introduced by the CLA.

This provides a phased pathway for traditional cannabis farmers to transition into the regulated industry while working toward full licensing compliance.

Addressing this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange at the newspaper’s head office in St Andrew, senior members of the CLA, including board chair Dr Nadeen Spence and Chief Executive Officer Farrah Blake, were adamant that the new moves are intended to open the doors to the regulated industry for traditional ganja farmers, and were in no way an attempt to shut them down.

Spence told Observer editors and reporters that there are many traditional ganja farmers who yearn to be a part of the regulated industry and the CLA is ready and willing to assist them in doing so.

“Those who want to do business in the medical cannabis industry, we will give them the information to do so if they want,” Spence said.

“The CLA processes licences for those who would like to conduct business, conduct operations [under the Dangerous Drugs Act]. For those who want to be involved, we want to provide as much information and guidance as possible,” added Spence.

She pointed to an ongoing roadshow which forms part of the initiatives that the CLA has embarked on to attract small farmers.

This is designed to expand participation in the sector as well as to guide applicants and promote the medical cannabis special permit programmes, such as the community and transitional cultivators’ permit.

Meanwhile, Blake said the roadshows are a source of education for the public and an opportunity for officials of the CLA to meet face-to-face with people who want to enter the regulated industry.

“There is going to be, maybe, some apprehension about engaging us through these programmes. The islandwide road tour is to ensure that we have that face-to-face interaction. If there’s assistance needed to complete the forms, we’re there to do that. If there’s assistance needed to determine whether or not these farming programmes are for you, we can give that advice. We can also give advice about the existing licensing products that we have,” said Blake as she underscored that farmers who are not currently regulated will not be reported to law enforcement agencies.

“You have to understand that me asking you to come into the legal space is not to try to burn down your farms or anything like that. The law of the amended Dangerous Drugs Act provides for the religious side and it provides for the commercial side. That is where the CLA operates, within the commercial space. So we try to encourage the public to stay on the right side of the law, come into the legal framework, and operate there. These farming programmes are created to further engage traditional farmers who might not have wanted to participate as of 2015 to now. We’re not planning to report you. We’re not calling the police on you,” insisted Blake.

She was supported by Walter Melbourne, the CLA’s director of licensing and applications, who scoffed at claims that there is no room for small ganja farmers in the regulated industry.

“That is why we have the cultivators’ permit. Those persons who would not have the necessary skills and requirements, moneywise as well, you could come in, and we’ll accept you into the programme. There’s a US$150 application fee and there are no more [fees] once you’re qualified,” said Melbourne.

“It is actually creating a pathway for the small man,” added Melbourne as he indicated that the CLA is prepared to hold the hands of people who want to enter the formal system and guide them through the entire process.

For the people concerned about whether they will be able to continue to operate their farms while they transition through the programme, Melbourne said they would be given special permits once they meet the requirements, which, he pointed out, are no longer very strict.

“You would have to make an application to come into the system and [the programme] is for two years. It is meant to allow you to transition. We’ll hold your hand, show you what to do. We have a Cannabis Specialisation Unit within the CLA that will assist you in terms of growing techniques, everything that you need to assist you to ensure that it’s viable. We have the requisite resources within the authority to assist you. You just have to make the application. We will assist you in guiding you in setting up your home, to set up your farm, and all of that, and you make the transition.

“We’ll go through line by line with you. I’ve seen situations in which a person cannot read or write, and I’m not mentioning this to be discriminatory or anything, but to show that we are very inclusive, in the sense that if persons cannot read or write, we’ll hold your hand. People will actually fill out the form and show you where to sign. So you take in stuff to us, like what area of land are you going to use… do you have a lease agreement? Do you have a title? Land is not a sore issue, in the sense that if you don’t even have title to it, we will say, if you have been farming the land for some time, occupying the land, we’ll take declarations from persons who have known the land for several years, just to verify and just to authenticate the fact that you have been occupying the land,” added Melbourne, as he explained that the process to become registered could take up to five months.

World.title: Gateway to Africa
World.content:
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama (left) shakes hands with Prime Minister of Jamaica Dr Andrew Holness following their media briefing at the Office of the Prime Minister on Monday. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

JAMAICAN manufacturers and exporters could soon gain easier access to a market of 1.4 billion people worth nearly US$3 trillion after Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama announced on Monday that he intends to push for the Caribbean’s inclusion in Africa’s free trade area next year.

Mahama also said Ghana would fast-track parliamentary approval of the air services agreement to allow direct flights between its capital, Accra, and Montego Bay, a move expected to strengthen trade, tourism and investment between the two countries.

Speaking during a media briefing with Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness as part of his four-day state visit to Jamaica, Mahama said discussions between the two leaders had focused on moving the long-standing historical relationship between Ghana and Jamaica beyond shared heritage and towards deeper economic cooperation.

He said Ghana intends to use its chairmanship of the African Union (AU) next year to pursue closer trade ties between Africa and the Caribbean, arguing that stronger commercial partnerships must become the next phase of Pan-African cooperation.

“When I was speaking with Mr Prime Minister, I said that one of the things that I would champion when I become AU chair next year… is to expand the remit of the African continental free trade area to include the Caribbean. We set up the African continental free trade area that allows us to export goods duty-free and tariff-free into each other’s markets. That’s a 1.4 billion population market, and that also is a 1.3 trillion GDP economy, and so we can plug the Caribbean in so that we can exchange goods between Africa and the Caribbean duty-free, tariff-free,” he announced.

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which came into force in 2021, is the world’s largest free trade area by the number of participating countries and is designed to boost trade by reducing tariffs and other barriers among African nations. Mahama suggested extending that framework to the Caribbean would significantly broaden opportunities for businesses on both sides of the Atlantic.

He added that improved transport links would be critical to making those ambitions a reality, revealing that Ghana intends to move quickly to activate the air services agreement negotiated between the two countries.

“We have to activate the bilateral air services agreement between us, and it’s currently before our Parliament, and we’ll fast-track it so that it becomes operational, so that either national carriers between Jamaica and Ghana or third-party carriers can fly direct flights from Accra to Montego Bay,” he said.

Holness welcomed the commitment, saying direct air links would represent one of the most tangible outcomes of the state visit and could help unlock greater tourism, trade and investment between the two countries.

“Africa is the fastest-growing continent both in terms of demographics and in terms of their economies. It is an area which we have paid as a people great rhetoric, we’ve always been speaking about south-south cooperation. What I try to do is to find meaningful, tangible ways in which we can bring this cooperation to fulfilment. Clearly, Marcus Garvey set the foundation, connecting us intellectually, connecting us as a people. We now must take that and create… the economic emancipation of our people,” he said.

Holness noted that the state visit should not be viewed as merely symbolic, stressing that both governments are seeking practical outcomes capable of generating jobs, investment and long-term economic growth.

“We have focused primarily on, from a tourism perspective, trade and services, heavily on North American and European markets of late South American markets. But now we have to turn our attention to the African continent where there is a growing middle class who wants to travel, who wants to experience the world and who could be right at home and comfortable right here in Jamaica. So we see these visits as not just courtesies; these visits are important to set the foundation for the trade in goods and services that will come,” he said.

Beyond aviation, both leaders outlined plans to strengthen logistics and maritime cooperation, viewing their countries as strategic gateways to their respective regions.

Holness pointed to Jamaica’s continued investment in expanding the Port of Kingston, while noting Ghana is pursuing similar ambitions in West Africa. He said connecting the two logistics hubs could create more efficient trade routes for exporters and investors.

Mahama echoed that view, saying the Atlantic should become a conduit for commerce rather than a barrier separating the two regions.

World.title: Ras Ajai gunned down
World.content:
Ras Ajai (left) accepts his Grammy Certificate from Stephen Stewart for appearing on Buss A Bubble, a song from Live N Livin, Sean Paul’s 2022 Grammy Award-nominated album. Occasion was the August 2024 Grammy Certificate Ceremony at the ATL Automotive Audi Showroom in Kingston..

When British music publisher Kennedy Mensah and reggae artiste Ras Ajai recently spoke to each other the latter expressed a desire to record songs that honoured the music’s legacy. He never got that opportunity.

Ras Ajai (real name Brian Todd Boucher) was killed in Waterford, Portmore, St Catherine, on August 1.

The 43 year-old singjay/actor and another male victim were shot by gunmen in an area of that community known as Third World.

At press time, the police had reported no arrests being made in relation to the incident.

The other man remains in hospital.

“One of our last conversations, he was talking about wanting to do a strong reggae project, he described it as a real reggae project, because he believed the youths nowadays not dealing with the real reggae thing,” Mensah, who is based England, recalled. “He wanted to put out some serious messages, and also to capitalise on the notoriety he got from being in the One Love movie.”

Ras Ajai, who was from Waterford, lived in New York City and toured for several years with Sean Paul. He made his acting debut in Bob Marley: One Love, the 2024 biopic based on the reggae legend.

The dreadlocked artiste had a small role as Claudius Massop, the West Kingston enforcer who was Marley’s close friend. Massop was controversially killed by police in February 1979.

Known for songs like Well Misbehave and Vice Grip, Ras Ajai is also featured on Buss A Bubble, Sean Paul’s 2019 single. That track is from Live N Livin, Sean Paul’s album which was nominated for a 2022 Best Reggae Album.

In August 2024, Ras Ajai was presented with a Grammy Certificate for appearing on the album at Mensah’s Grammy Certificate Ceremony in Kingston.

Mensah said he first met Ras Ajai in 2019 during a music publishing workshop he conducted at Jamaica Promotions (Jampro) in Kingston. Shortly after, Ras Ajai became a client of Mensah’s Back 2 Da Future Limited.

“To say that the news of his passing came as a shock would be a total understatement. I can’t imagine how his family must be feeling,” said Mensah. “We’re going to miss Ras Ajai, but at least we have a body of music to remember him by.”

World.title: Infantino’s re-election bid hit by Welsh withdrawal
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (left) and US President Donald Trump hold the FIFA World Cup trophy moments before presenting it to 2026 World Champions Spain after the final at New York/New Jersey Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, on Sunday, July 19. (Photo: AFP)

PARIS, France (AFP) — Wales on Monday became the first national football association to publicly withdraw support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s re-election bid, piling pressure on the Swiss administrator after the collapse of his controversial plan to sell private investment stakes in the World Cup and other FIFA competitions.

The Football Association of Wales (FAW) said it would not support Infantino’s candidature in the FIFA presidential election in Rabat, Morocco, in March 2027.

“The Football Association of Wales hereby confirms its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Mr Gianni Infantino, for re-election as FIFA president for the 2027-2031 term,” the FAW said in a statement.

“The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgement have led us to a position where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football.

“Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.”

The English Football Association is also understood to have informed FIFA it no longer supports Infantino. It said on Saturday it fully backed UEFA’s position after European football’s governing body declared it had lost confidence in the FIFA president.

Concacaf has called for “a comprehensive reckoning” with Infantino’s leadership, while the Asian Football Confederation has urged greater transparency.

The backlash followed Infantino’s decision to abandon plans for the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), which would have brought private investment into FIFA’s flagship tournaments, including the men’s and women’s World Cups. The proposal, announced last week, was withdrawn within days after opposition from three continental confederations.

The collapse of the plan has left Infantino facing the biggest political challenge of his decade in charge of world football.

The 56-year-old, first elected FIFA president in 2016 and re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023, had appeared politically stronger than ever after overseeing expanded editions of the Club World Cup and men’s World Cup while increasing revenues distributed to FIFA’s 211 member associations.

But critics say the FFE debacle reinforced concerns that FIFA has become increasingly centralised under his leadership.

Former UEFA president Michel Platini, under whom Infantino served as secretary-general from 2009 to 2016, has been among his sharpest critics.

“Unfortunately Infantino has become more of an autocrat since the [COVID-19] pandemic,” Platini told

The Guardian in January.

“I think he lost the game. There is less democracy than in Blatter’s time.

“He was a good No 2, but is not a good No. 1.

“He worked very well at UEFA but he has one problem — he likes the rich and powerful people, the ones with money.

“It’s his character.”

Infantino’s close relationship with US President Donald Trump has also drawn scrutiny. The investment proposal involved a firm led by Joshua Kushner, brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

“Josh Kushner’s firm has a legitimate track record,” former World Cup bid strategist Terrence Burns told

AFP.

“But the association was always going to be read politically… We’ve understood in sponsorship for 40 years that a partner brings their whole context with them.”

Following the collapse of the investment proposal, Infantino pledged to restore unity within world football.

“Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together… in the spirit of shared interest in our game,” he said.

“And with the objective to continue growing football everywhere.”

Nominations for the FIFA presidential election close on November 18 ahead of the vote in Rabat next March.

World.title: DAY TO FORGET
World.content:
Abdullah Shafique (right) of Pakistan scores runs off Kemar Roach (left) of West Indies during the second day of their second Test match at Queen’s Park Oval in Port of Spain, Trinidad, and Tobago, on Monday. (Photo: AFP)

PORT OF SPAIN, Trinidad (CMC) — A superb batting display by Abdullah Shafique and Babar Azam has left Pakistan in firm control of the second Test against West Indies at the close of play on the second day here on Monday.

Shafique’s unbeaten 107 off 185 balls coupled with Captain Azam’s 86 not out off 126 balls powered the visitors to a formidable 266 for two in reply to the West Indies’ total of 344 at the Queen’s Park Oval.

The pair has so far added 168 runs for the third wicket to put Pakistan on course to post a mammoth first innings total and give their side a hefty lead as they trail by just 78 runs heading into Tuesday’s third day of play.

West Indies contributed to their own demise with their wayward bowling gifting Pakistan’s batsmen free runs, with wicket-taking deliveries few and far between.

The home side’s opening pace attack of Kemar Roach and Jayden Seales were surprisingly inconsistent, with Azan Awais hitting Roach for three consecutive boundaries in the third over of the innings.

Together, with partner Imam-ul-Haq, they put on 34 runs inside eight overs before Shamar Joseph produced a snorter off a good length that hit the top of his bat and ballooned to gully for Jomel Warrican to take an easy catch.

Awais continued to take advantage of the slack bowling on offer, hitting Joseph for four fours in the 12th over to move into the 40s, while Shafique wasted little time in joining in on the action by blasting Warrican for sixes in successive overs.

Awais eventually brought up his maiden Test half-century off 61 balls by driving Warrican down to long on for a single.

It was Warrican who broke their 64-run partnership, with the West Indies needing to review an lbw decision against Awais after he was initially given not out, to dismiss him for 55 and leave the score 98 for two.

Azam joined Shafique at the crease, and for the next three hours, they neutralised the home side’s passive bowling attack, which was without the services of first match hero Justin Greaves.

The skipper showed his aggressive intent early on by bludgeoning Seales for three fours in the 24th over.

Pakistan went to tea at 139 for two, while scoring at just over four runs an over, and the same continued after the break, with Shafique getting to his seventh Test half-century off 79 balls with an exquisite straight drive off Roach for four.

Azam followed in the same vein by notching his 33rd half-century as Pakistan tightened their grip on the contest at 184 for two.

Azam was lucky not to have been dismissed almost immediately after, but Joseph failed to hold on to a difficult one-handed catch on the long on boundary, with the ball going over the boundary ropes for six.

With the close of play looming, Shafique reached his sixth Test century by pulling Warrican to the midwicket boundary, his first time scoring three figures since 2024.

The duo then navigated the remaining overs of play to ensure Pakistan remained in complete control of the contest.

Earlier, resuming the day on 239 for five, the West Indies’ last five wickets added 104 runs, with spinner Sajid Khan responsible for three of them to fall.

Justin Greaves only added nine runs to his overnight score of 64 before driving a delivery from spinner Ali Usman straight into the hands of point.

Captain Roston Chase reached his 12th Test half-century and added 35 runs with Roach until he was bowled off his pads by pacer Ubaid Shah for 70 to leave the Windies 304 for seven.

Khan then wrapped up the tail by dismissing Joseph, Roach, and Seales to end with figures of 4-85, while Shah (2-66), Mohammad Ali (2-67), and Ali Usman (2-80) took two wickets apiece.

World.title: WATCH: Waves of excitement at Old Harbour Bay Regatta on Emancipation Day
World.content:
Crew members of 'Empress' pose with the coveted Yamaha engine prize after winning the Yamaha Engine Race at the 43rd annual Old Harbour Bay Regatta on Saturday, August 1, 2026.

Sutania Beckford beamed with joy after her boat crew guided ‘Empress’ to a thrilling victory in the Yamaha Engine Race which brought an exciting close to the 43rd annual Old Harbour Bay Regatta on Emancipation Day.

It was sweet triumph for the crowd favourites and their supporters after losing the marquee event in the six-race boat competition to rival ‘Father’s Day’ last year.

“Every year, people come just to see [Empress] because it’s like we are up against everybody,” Beckford said.

“However, Empress decided this time not to have any boyfriends, she was under proper supervision this time, so she came out victorious,” she added with a smile.

Each Emancipation Day, hundreds of residents and visitors converge at the Old Harbour Bay Fishing Village to participate in what Jason Fuller, the president of the Old Harbour Bay Community Development Association, calls “the premier boat racing competition in Jamaica”.

It was another massive turnout on Saturday, with numbers estimated to be in the thousands.

“They love it, they live for it every year,” Fuller said about the lure of the event. “This is their passion, this is their love. And we just try each and every year to ensure that we improve and make it a memorable one.”

In addition to the races, the residents also unite for food, entertainment, and other competitions – including fish scraping, cook-offs and beer drinking – at the regatta. Due to the event’s massive growth, the organisers introduced live streaming at last year’s edition to share the experience with persons who are unable to physically attend.

“Remember, it’s the largest fishing village in Jamaica. So almost everyone have some interaction with fishing, whether you’re a fisherman, a family of fishermen, or so on,” Fuller said. “So, that is one of the main reason why the regatta means so much to the community.”

Noting that a number of fisherfolk in the community were affected by Hurricane Melissa last October, Fuller said the regatta organisers partnered with sponsors this year to give away nets and other items to help affected persons get back on their feet.

“So, even though they were affected, we are trying our utmost best to make it a seamless transition to getting back to what they were before,” he said.

Social Development Commission’s parish manager for St Catherine, Shana-Lee Archibald hailed the event for the economic activity it generates for small businesses in the community.

“The regatta is a great event, it provides an opportunity for our small businesses to benefit and that’s one of the main reasons the SDC is a part of the activities,” Archibald said.

In the meantime, spectators commended the organisers of the regatta while expressing their satisfaction for the fun and entertainment provided.

“Good energy, good vibes, super lit,” said spectator from Canada who goes by the name “Breezy”.

“I just like the view, the people, the music, it’s very nice,” he said.

– Julian Richardson

World.title: Stronger than ganja!
World.content:
Consultant child and adolescent psychiatrist Dr Ganesh Shetty says child guidance clinics are now seeing more children addicted to digital devices than to marijuana. He has sounded an alarm over what he describes as a pattern of “disconnection and misconnection, alienation and addiction” amongst Jamaican youngsters.

“These algorithms are created by behavioural specialists, and they drag you into something more interesting, something more wonderful, so that it will suck you in to addiction. I have more tablet addicts coming to my child guidance clinics than weed addicts nowadays,” Dr Shetty disclosed as he warned minors of the danger courted daily.

There are 23 of these clinics in hospitals and health centres throughout Jamaica, providing mental health and counselling services for clients up to 18 years old. Key services include behavioural assessments, emotional support, and treatment for conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and depression.

It is unclear if the troubling trend has emerged at all of them.

Dr Shetty, who is also acting director, adolescent mental health, in the Ministry of Health, made the disclosure on digital device addiction during last week’s press conference to present findings of the National Study on Social Media Use and the Protection of Children.

He outlined the toll addiction takes.

“We have teenagers who are so disconnected [from] everybody and everything. And this is what happens when you’re disconnected, and misconnected, and addicted: You don’t sleep; you don’t eat; you’re miserable. Next day, nobody can talk to you, including your mom. And sometimes, when you see a lot of shooting and fighting and cutting off head and cutting off fingers on your screen, you get disconnected [from] that human suffering. So somebody gets hit in school [and you are more] interested in taking a video of it and putting it online so it can go viral — not going and assisting that person,” he pointed out.

Dr Shetty noted that the attraction to screens has its genesis in seemingly harmless choices made by parents and guardians during their children’s early years. He cited the example of a mother who gives her two-year-old an iPad when out in public to prevent the child from “running up and down”. The woman is proud of her baby who appears well-behaved and does not cause “discomfort to others and mother”.

The mental health professional then described a scenario in which the mother has two more children at home, absent fathers, and she uses digital devices to fill the gap as she does household chores such as cooking.

“So she has to have the older two watch some TV and the younger one to deal with the tablet. What happens? The child gets disconnected from the human beings around her/him, and gets connected with the machine and, even at this age, can get addicted to the machine,” Dr Shetty outlined.

He said a child’s affinity for his electronic device only grows, becoming a competitor for the time spent on every other aspect of life.

“It can affect you, affect your energy, affect your focus, affect your memory, affect your school grades, affect what you want to become. You can’t become [a success] because you don’t have grades to go to college, but you have just grades enough to go to supermarket and push cart,” he warned.

Dr Shetty is heartened that there is recognition that a holistic approach is needed to tackle the areas of concern outlined in the study, which is said to be “one of the most comprehensive national assessments ever undertaken” on social media use by minors in Jamaica.

“I’m glad that most folks you interviewed think it has to be done together. Government cannot do it alone. Community cannot do it alone. Family cannot do it alone. Young persons have to be involved in it. It is a family and community effort,” he said.

According to the study, nine out of every 10 respondents, or 90.2 per cent, support government regulation of minors’ social media use, while 2.9 per cent expressed opposition. Nearly 84 per cent believe Jamaica should establish a clear national policy framework governing minors’ use of social media.

World.title: Can Europe contain the Ceuta fallout?
World.content:
Home affairs ministers are meeting this morning as the fallout of the Ceuta crisis continues to roil Europe.



Last week’s sudden influx of migrants into the Spanish exclave — most of whom have since returned — sparked heated exchanges between European leaders. On the show, hosts Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart preview whether today’s emergency meeting can cool tensions, and what measures the Commission may propose to address concerns across the bloc.

Next, a drought in Hungary and Romania could grind nuclear power plants to a halt since the River Danube has fallen too low to cool their reactors. Budapest and Bucharest are on high alert over the risk of an energy crisis in the coming days.

Plus: The Belgium push to encourage young people to

Manchester’s Heron House building is the site of a new No.10 North, dubbed the “situation room for growth” by the PM. Burnham has vowed to work from the building regularly, alongside other Cabinet ministers.

World.title: Greece’s Mitsotakis: EU needs new tools to fight back against weaponized migration
World.content:
Recent events at Europe’s borders, most notably in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, are the latest reminder that migration is no longer just a humanitarian issue or management challenge. In some cases, it has become a tool of geopolitical coercion.

The EU has made important progress on this issue with its Pact on Migration and Asylum. It has introduced mechanisms to manage migratory pressure, including flexibility in its procedures and solidarity among member countries. But these tools are designed for situations that remain, at their core, manageable. They do not adequately address scenarios in which migration is weaponized, or where flows are engineered, amplified or facilitated in a way that creates a de facto hybrid challenge.

To be sure, we don’t yet know what caused the situation that unfolded in Ceuta last week. But scenarios like these are not unprecedented.

Greece faced a similar situation at its land border with Turkey in Evros in 2020, as did Lithuania, Poland and Latvia at their borders with Belarus in 2021. What we are witnessing in these cases is not a gradual increase in arrivals but the sudden, massive and often coordinated movements of people — sometimes in the tens of thousands within just a few days — that overwhelm national capacities and test the EU’s resilience as a whole.

In such extreme circumstances, the immediate and full application of standard asylum and reception systems for all arrivals is not simply difficult — it is often impossible. Systems risk paralysis, public trust erodes and the very functioning of Schengen is put under strain.

Europe needs to acknowledge this gap and act decisively.

World.title: EU ministers to back Spain as Ceuta crisis pushes migration up the agenda
World.content:
The groundwork for Tuesday’s meeting was set on Monday when EU ambassadors held talks that lasted around two and a half hours. The Spanish envoy gave Madrid’s account of the Ceuta crisis, during which more than 70 people died, and reprimanded some capitals for spreading disinformation, according to one of the diplomats. The ambassador was asked for verification of Madrid’s figures on returned migrants and for the situation to be closely monitored, two other diplomats said.

Concerns were also raised that Spanish government policies may have been used by people-smugglers and gangs to encourage the events in Ceuta.

“There’s a concern that … the legalization of a million irregular migrants, that it’s been possible [for people-smugglers] to use that to give the impression that the door was open,” said one diplomat from a country that has been critical of Spain.

Italy called for the EU to immediately establish migrant deportation hubs in non-EU countries, one of the diplomats said. The plans follow the approval of a law granting EU capitals the power to set up centers in non-EU countries for processing migrants who have been denied the right to stay in the bloc — so-called return hubs.

But the Spanish ambassador criticized Italy for amplifying false claims about the migrant regularization program, such as Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani’s suggestion on social media that it automatically grants EU citizenship. The program provides legal residency to eligible migrants but does not confer Spanish nationality.

Rallying to support Spain

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen set the tone of conciliation on Monday by writing to Sánchez to praise Spain and Morocco for their handling of the crisis and calling for a united European response. She said the episode showed the need for stronger controls at the EU’s external borders, closer cooperation with partner countries, better early-warning systems, action against smuggling networks and more effective returns.

World.title: Europe wants to kick its Palantir habit
World.content:
“Let's be honest, Palantir’s product is very good and addictive, it's pretty much like the sugar in Coca-Cola,” said French digital sovereignty advocate, Philippe Latombe. “Palantir can treat massive amounts of data with great precision and with their experience, they had time to improve their algorithms with many clients and adapt them to many use cases.”

Still, the drive to break free from Palantir is sweeping around the continent, from Madrid, where the government of Pedro Sánchez has instructed state-backed companies to block Palantir from future public procurement contracts, to France’s domestic intelligence services (DGSI) selecting French company ChapsVision over Palantir. In Britain, the next test may come in February 2027, when the new Labour government of Andy Burnham will face a choice of whether to cut off Palantir’s £330 million National Health Service Federated Data Platform contract.

Last month’s decision by the French and German intelligence agencies to choose ChapsVision was a double-blow for Palantir’s leadership. CEO Alex Karp showed little patience for the sudden turn away from his company’s wares, declaring that he wasn’t worried about European competitors. “We have a model of what doesn’t work," he quipped last week on Fox Business. "It’s called Europe.”

Palantir CEO Alex Karp visits "The Claman Countdown" at Fox Business Network Studios. | John Lamparski/Getty Images

Olivier Dellenbach, ChapsVision’s chief executive, told POLITICO that his company has benefited from what he calls a “visceral rejection of Palantir” in Europe.

But he also cautioned that he did not want ChapsVision reduced to an anti-Palantir way out. Digital sovereignty, he argues, will remain an empty phrase unless governments turn it into industrial policy. “We need more public procurement,” Dellenbach said.

Belgium, Germany, Luxembourg, Romania, the Netherlands and Canada have already shown interest in the French Army’s Artemis AI, according to Patrick Moreau, one of the architects of the solution built by French aerospace and defense company Thales.

World.title: What tools does the EU have to fight wildfires? Are they enough?
World.content:
Europe is facing another summer of devastating wildfires. Data from the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS) on July 30 shows that more than 434.976 hectares have burned since the start of 2026. So far, 1.407 fires have been detected, releasing an estimated 17.98 million tonnes of CO₂.

 

"These fires are out of capacity," said a European Commission official, describing how wildfires were spreading faster than firefighting efforts could match.

The EU has spent the last two years building what it calls a more serious, integrated wildfire strategy with new funding, a new fleet, a new Cyprus hub, and since March 2026, a new philosophy that puts prevention ahead of suppression. So, what exactly does the EU have, and is it holding up under this summer’s pressure?

The toolkit

At the centre of the system is the EU Civil Protection Mechanism, a solidarity framework that lets an overwhelmed country ask other member states for help. It does not activate automatically: a state must request assistance, usually once it determines a fire has outgrown its capacity.

Running that process around the clock is the Emergency Response Coordination Centre (ERCC) in Brussels, which matches offers of aircraft, crews and equipment to whichever country needs them, and helps co-finance the transport.

Backing that up is rescEU, the EU’s strategic reserve of firefighting planes and helicopters, held for when national and pooled resources run short. Alongside it is the European Civil Protection Pool, made up of national assets governments have pre-committed for EU-wide use. Layered on top are Copernicus, the satellite mapping service producing real-time maps of burn zones and infrastructure at risk, and EFFIS, the European Forest Fire Information System, which forecasts fire danger up to ten days ahead and tracks active fires every few hours.

New for 2026 is a firefighting hub in Cyprus, able to pre-position six aircraft, plus a dedicated Wildfire Support Team reinforcing the ERCC from June to September.

What’s been sent this summer

For the 2026 season, the Commission put 22 firefighting planes, 5 helicopters, 777 firefighters from 14 countries, and 21 certified teams on standby across 12 countries. As fires in Iberia and France escalated, France received seven planes and four helicopters, drawing crews and aircraft from Czechia, Croatia, Germany, Portugal, Slovakia, Sweden, and Türkiye.

Spain received six planes and three ground teams, with help arriving from Greece, Italy, Portugal and Türkiye. Five Canadian planes were split between the two. Commissioner Hadja Lahbib said the mechanism is “under pressure” but insisted “it is working.”

A strategy still on paper

In March, the Commission presented a communication on integrated wildfire risk management, reframing the EU’s approach around prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery as one continuous cycle rather than a seasonal scramble for planes. It acknowledged that Europe had spent years treating symptoms instead of causes, fighting ever-bigger fires rather than stopping the landscape from becoming so flammable.

Four months on, little of that has translated into new rules. Environment Commissioner Jessika Roswall told agriculture ministers in late May that the Commission does “not plan any new initiatives on forest management” and has no new indicators or guidelines in the pipeline.

The one binding-adjacent document to emerge, a recommendation on integrated wildfire risk management adopted on 29 June, is non-binding. Forest management remains a national competence. A blocking minority, traditionally Sweden and Finland, often joined by France, has resisted giving Brussels more say, having helped stall the Nature Restoration Law in 2024 and pushed back on the proposed Forest Monitoring Law.

“We cannot just blame the fire situation on climate change”

Alexander Held, a forester at the European Forest Institute’s Pan-European Forest Risk Facility, has watched the pattern shift over 25 years in the field. “Now we have fires from Turkey over Greece to Spain to Portugal to France,” he said, describing the collapse of the old split fire season into something closer to simultaneous, year-round risk across the continent.

“We see fires now up in Iceland, we see fires in Greenland, we see fire in the Arctic Rim,” he added, evidence, he said, that “the pyrogeography is definitely changing.”

But climate change is the enabler, not the whole story. “We cannot just blame the fire situation on climate change,” Held said, arguing that land management decisions, abandoned farmland, pine and eucalyptus monocultures, and forests with broken-up canopies, do “our part of making the landscape more flammable.”

Even the newer EU instruments, he said, tilt toward hardware over resilience: “despite all the declarations, we don’t see the coordinated investment in the broader field of learning to live with fire,” because “it’s much easier still to invest in the response side” than in prevention.

Held points to Portugal as the counter-example, a country that “shifted its strategy from fire suppression to really fire management and investing 50percent of the budget in land management and prevention.”

His own wish, he said, would be a euro spent on resilience for every euro spent on suppression: “I would wish that we get a 50percent leverage, any euro that is spent on suppression is going into this 5R framework.”

Crucially, he warned against newly fire-prone countries assuming more trucks and planes is the answer, when even well-resourced states are losing control of major fires: “if other countries with a lot more resources and experience and capacity can’t control [these fires], how do we conclude, oh, let’s do the same and then we can control it?”

The EU is prepared, but stretched

Commission spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen frames the shift in similar terms, if from inside the institution. “It is very clear that climate change is making each summer hotter and harsher and more dangerous,” she said, noting that “Europe is the fastest warming continent in the world” and that “more than one million hectares were burned” across the EU to wildfires in 2025 alone.

“We cannot focus only on literally putting out fires,” Itkonen said. “Preparedness for us is really, really important.” She pointed to the EU’s forthcoming portal and guidance on integrated risk management, due by early 2027, reinforcement of EFFIS, and the ongoing purchase of a permanent rescEU fleet, 12 new firefighting planes and five helicopters, though deliveries won’t be finished until 2030.

On the funding, she cited a wider climate push behind the numbers: 35percent of the EU’s next long-term budget earmarked for climate and environment, including “almost 19 billion euros from cohesion funds for adaptation.” The Commission’s plan is clear: “the goal is not to fight more fires. The goal is to have a good prevention policy and good coordinated action across the European Union.”

Is it enough?

Even by the Commission’s own account, the system is being tested by scale, not just fire behaviour. Officials have said the 2026 season began earlier than last year’s, with the first activation of the Civil Protection Mechanism at the end of April; by July, fires had burned hundreds of hectares.

Every plane and helicopter in the current fleet remains nationally owned or committed elsewhere when several countries burn at once, and rescEU’s permanent fleet won’t be complete until 2030. Interoperability gaps between national equipment and command systems, an ageing firefighting workforce in several member states, and EU sanctions still grounding Russian helicopters in Spain all narrow the margin further.

The tools themselves: the Civil Protection Mechanism, the ERCC, rescEU, Copernicus, EFFIS, pre-positioned crews, are real, tested, and expanding. The EU’s bet isn’t whether it can find another aircraft, but whether it will fund the slower, less visible work of making its landscapes harder to burn before the next fire season starts. "We know the roadmap," he said, "but it's a long way to go," says Held.

World.title: Oil rebounds as markets trade mixed following Wall Street rally
World.content:
In addition to earnings reports this week, investors were also still weighing the impact from last week's joint US-Japan currency intervention, analysts said.

 

Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 slipped 0.3% to 63,585.58, as the US dollar inched up to 157.51 Japanese yen from 157.18 yen. The euro cost $1.1511, little changed from $1.1514. The dollar was trading at 160-yen levels before regulators stepped in to boost the yen's value after it fell to nearly 40-year lows.

Some analysts said the effectiveness of such an intervention remains uncertain as it doesn't address the fundamental economic reasons behind the currency fluctuations, including inflation, interest rates and the relative strengths of the economies.

“A US-backed operation carries far more signaling weight than Tokyo acting alone, and the pledge of further action will give speculators pause. But any US contribution will probably be constrained by size,” a report by BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions, said.

Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at global financial services firm Ebury, noted the latest effort could have some impact because it appears to signal a real change in monetary policy rather than just a one-time defensive move.

“This is an historic and meaningful development for the yen, which materially improves confidence in our mildly bullish call for the currency,” he said.

Markets unsettled

South Korea's Kospi sank 1.3% to 6,174.72. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 1.2% to 9,129.00. Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 0.5% to 25,881.99, while the Shanghai Composite gained 0.2% to 3,802.61.

Markets remain unsettled by swings for stocks of companies that make computer chips. They’ve been veering up and down for weeks on worries about whether their surging revenues because of the artificial-intelligence boom are sustainable.

Dow hits all-time high

On Wall Street, share prices rallied Monday after easing oil prices helped calm worries over inflation. The S&P 500 jumped 1.5% and is just 0.1% below its record set earlier this summer.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, which measures a narrower slice of the US stock market, climbed 693 points or 1.3% to an all-time high, while the Nasdaq composite leaped 2.1%.

Oil prices rebound

In energy trading in Asia early Tuesday, benchmark US crude gained 84 cents to $81.18 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, jumped $1.15 to $84.92 a barrel.

A day earlier, oil prices dropped more than 5% after US President Donald Trump said over the weekend that he had decided to hold off on new strikes against Iran at the urging of allies in the region.

Brent’s price careened between $72 and $102 last month as worries rose and fell over the war in Iran and when oil tankers would be allowed to freely exit the Persian Gulf again to deliver crude to customers worldwide.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury sank to 4.68% from 4.75% late Friday. It remains well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran.

World.title: Forest fire spreads in southern Netherlands nature reserve, authorities say
World.content:
Firefighters are rushing to contain a forest blaze in the southeast of the Netherlands that spread overnight to engulf 100 hectares on Tuesday, authorities said.

 

It was the latest in a string of wildfires to hit western Europe, following deadly heatwaves that have dried up riverbeds and vegetation, extreme weather events scientists have linked to human-made climate change.

The fire started around Monday afternoon in a nature reserve near the village of Oostrum in Limburg province, close to the border with Germany.

The blaze spread to 100 hectares as of early Tuesday and was still not under control, provincial authorities said on their website.

The winds kept changing direction and sped up the fire's spread, a regional safety spokesperson told the ANP news agency.

A helicopter drops water on a wildfire in the southern Netherlands, 3 August, 2026 Screenshot from AP video 4676428

Around 300 emergency workers took part in containing the blaze overnight and firefighting helicopters were set to resume operations on Tuesday morning, authorities said.

A nearby campsite was evacuated and trains passing through the area were suspended.

"Because of the drought, fire can spread quickly in nature reserves," provincial authorities said, without specifying the cause of the fire.

European countries are facing a major drought, marked by dried-up rivers, water restrictions and devastating forest fires, following an unprecedented heat wave in June.

Human-fuelled climate change has accelerated moisture loss from soil, lakes and rivers, heightening the risk of extreme droughts, scientists from World Weather Attribution warned last month.
