World.title: Can the EU's GenAI ambitions survive contact with reality?
World.content:
The EU has recently announced three new AI projects — Floods and droughts, Eunomia.AI and EuropAI — that aim to support the uptake of Generative AI in public administrations across the EU.

 

The total funding for the projects comes to €36.8 million, of which €18.4 million is provided directly by the EU. The final outcomes of these projects are expected by 2029-2030.

While testing and scaling GenAI solutions across EU member states does indeed require flexibility, the future influx of funding for GenAI and ApplyAI solutions in the EU must come with strict oversight and increased participation by European private-sector players with real-world experience building GenAI solutions.

In the past, bureaucracy and Kafkaesque paperwork often prevented fast-moving startups and scaleups from participating in both EU and national public tenders and funding programs.

However, the oversight of where and how the EU funding should be directed will increasingly be necessary to prevent a new wave of “AI-washing” — echoing the “innovation-washing” of the past, where EU funding sometimes did not translate into measurable impact.

Floods and droughts project

The “Floods and droughts” consortium is led by Italy and co-developed by stakeholders from France, Spain and Greece.

The project’s total value is €8.8 million, with €4.4 millions provided by the EU. The project is expected to end by 30 June 2030.

The consortium aims to provide public administrations with Gen-AI-enabled tools that improve anticipation, crisis management and citizen communication related to increasingly common climate disasters such as floods and droughts.

Eunomia AI project

The “Eunomia AI” consortium is led by Spain and joined by 13 more EEA countries: Austria, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Portugal, Latvia, Germany, the Netherlands, Poland, Italy, Hungary, Norway and Malta.

The project’s total value is €13.9 million, with €6.9 million provided by the EU. The project is expected to end by 30 June 2029, with the first pilot projects expected in one and a half years.

The goals of the project are twofold: first, accelerate the adoption of trustworthy GenAI in European public administrations by deploying it in 25 public administrations and at least 15 public services. Second, reinforce the European tech sovereignty by using and fine-tuning the EU’s open-source models.

The project description states that this will be achieved by procuring and hosting “centralized, high-performance GenAI infrastructure” at the University of Granada, with an option to create federated local nodes.

EuropAI project

The third project, “EuropAI,” is led by the Netherlands and includes Denmark, Belgium, and Luxembourg. The project’s total cost sits at €13.9 million, with €6.9 million provided by EU funding. The estimated project date is on 30 June 2029.

The goals of this consortium are to accelerate the adoption of sovereign and trustworthy GenAI solutions across European governments by creating a framework for EU member state governments to co-create, test, and share GenAI solutions in three strategic domains: legislative & administrative simplification, urban analysis and spatial planning, and digital assistance for citizens across web and mobile.

The consortium describes its own project through a lens of a kitchen.

“European public administrations currently rely on imported 'AI fast food' from non-EU providers, like ChatGPT, Copilot or Gemini — expensive, opaque solutions misaligned with European sovereignty and compliance requirements".

The plan, EuropAI's team says, is to offer member states a trusted "community kitchen where Member States co-create, test, and share GenAI solutions".

The system's backbone, comparable to a professional kitchen's equipment, is built on Denmark's OS2ai platform, which already serves more than 28,000 employees, and the Netherlands' GovChat-NL.

On top of that sit ready-made tools that have already been piloted and validated, described as "pre-cooked meals ready to serve," along with reusable building blocks such as European-made AI models, blueprints that let other countries replicate what works, compliance checks that act as "nutrition labels," and an app marketplace serving as "an organised pantry".

This story was originally published on EU Tech Loop and has been shared on Euronews as part of a syndication agreement.

World.title: These are the world’s greatest luxury hotels, according to Robb Report
World.content:
A boutique stay in one of Nepal’s most remote areas has just been named the greatest luxury hotel in the world.

 

The annual list from Robb Report, which first started in 2023, ranks the top 10 properties around the globe before organising the remaining 40 by region.

This year, the highest ranked hotel is Shinta Mani Mustang in the Kali Gandaki River Valley, a 29-key property with a five-night minimum stay.

Wellness is a key focus at the retreat, with each guest attending an individual consultation with a Tibetan medicine doctor to create a tailor-made programme that makes use of Himalayan plants and herbs as well as traditional practices.

No visit to Nepal would be complete without a spot of hiking, and so naturally your stay includes wilderness trekking with routes customised to your ability levels and experience as well as the conditions on the day.

You’ll be able to fully immerse yourself in Nepalese culture, too, with trips to local villages as part of the itinerary.

The setting alone is reason enough to visit, with suites looking out to the 7,000m-high peaks of the Nilgiri mountain range.

Robb Report creates its list by consulting its 24 travel masters who were asked to select five newer properties they recommend, as well as past favourites, explaining why each deserves its spot on the list.

This year, five of the top 10 are in Europe, with a further 10 properties joining the top 50.

The 29-key Shinta Mani Mustang is found in one of Nepal's most remote regions Sherpa Hospitality Group

The greatest luxury hotels in Europe

A former hunting lodge in the Scottish Highlands claimed the top spot on the continent, coming in third overall.

For much of the year, Hope Lodge in Sutherland, which has seven bedrooms, is available for exclusive use, but you can also book individual rooms in the summer months.

The lodge is set among a 100,000 acre estate, which you can explore with the help of expert guides. Stays include access to the hotel’s adventure centre and kit room, which has wetsuits, paddleboards, bikes and more.

Writing about the lodge, Robb Report said: “Think of this as a Scottish safari lodge, with guides as connected to the natural surroundings as many trackers would be.”

An all-inclusive retreat, food is sourced from the lodge’s own estate as well as local suppliers.

Florence’s Collegio alla Querce, which was named the best new hotel in the world by Esquire earlier this year, ranked sixth overall.

Housed within a building that started life as a villa in the 16th century before serving as a boarding school, the 83-key hotel has views over the city and the Tuscan countryside.

Claridge’s, described as the “Mayfair mainstay that’s become synonymous with luxury hospitality in London”, ranked seventh, quickly followed by Le Bristol Paris, “the grande dame of the Right Bank” in eighth place.

Casa Bonavita in Malta completed the top 10, with the 18th-century building having been thoughtfully transformed into a 17-room hotel that opened its doors earlier this year.

World.title: Venezuela earthquake death toll crosses 6,000
World.content:
The updated death toll comes weeks after the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude quakes hit on June 24, causing massive damage to people and property.

The twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela in late June killed 6,125 people, the latest figures revealed by top lawmaker Jorge Rodriguez on Monday showed.

The updated numbers come weeks after the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude quakes hit on June 24, unleashing massive damage on people and property, and triggering national emergencies. Unofficial estimates say between 17,000 and 29,500 people are still unaccounted for.

The previous death toll was 5,546.

What was the scale of the damage?

The quake led to nearly 200 buildings collapsing, mostly in the coastal state of La Guaira, which was hit the worst.

Rodríguez said that clean-up operations continued, clearing almost 350,000 tons of debris, which is about 16.5% of the 2.1 million tons of total wreckage estimated by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).

Authorities classified over 16,200 structures as unsafe, pushing many to leave. Thousands of people are now living in makeshift shelters in La Guaira and Caracas.

Several structures were deemed unsafe in the aftermath of the earthquake Image: Jimmy Villalta/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

On Friday, lawmakers in the country unanimously approved a law that makes it easier to rent properties, a measure aimed at helping displaced victims. It repeals an anti-rental legislation passed by former leftist administrations.

Venezuela's Acting President ​Delcy Rodriguez came to power after US forces kidnapped her predecessor Nicolas Maduro in January and took him to New York, where he is facing trial. She has defended the government amid criticism ​that officials did not do enough to help ⁠quake victims, including people trapped in the rubble.

World.title: Cuba: Further blackouts disrupt energy restoration attempts
World.content:
Authorities say unfavorable weather in the Caribbean has hampered efforts to restore power to Cuba's national grid amid repeated blackouts. Many Cubans now have power only for a few hours a day.

Cuba's efforts to restore electricity after a series of blackouts were hampered again on Monday when a second nationwide power cut in a day, the sixth this year, struck its national grid.

Power began returning to parts of Havana and several provinces in central and western Cuba during Monday and, by midday, authorities said about half of the capital had electricity again.

However, the state electricity provider later warned that unfavorable weather had again interrupted the restoration process.

Cuba blackouts: What have authorities said?

"In the process of reestablishing the [National Electric System], existing weather events caused disruptions to the grid, directly affecting the generator units that were online," the provider said in a statement posted to social media on Monday afternoon, without specifying the extent of damage or how many areas were affected.

"We continue to work intensively to revert the situation and achieve the system reset as soon as possible."

By early evening, authorities were reporting some progress, saying four generating units at Energas Jaruco were operating and several transmission substations around Havana had ​been re-energized.

Cuba faces most severe energy crisis in decades To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Cuba: Life amid blackouts

Repeated blackouts ⁠since the start of the year have ​disrupted businesses, public services and life in general across Cuba, a Caribbean ​island of roughly 10 million people.

Most Cubans now have power only for a few hours a day at best, making normal life nearly impossible.

The government, which is already battling shortages of food, fuel ​and medicine and a long economic downturn, blames decades of United States sanctions and embargoes which limit access ​to fuel, financing and ⁠spare parts needed to maintain its power system.

The Trump administration has this year tightened sanctions and enacted an oil embargo, further choking the Caribbean country.

Washington claims the outages reflect failures of ⁠the country's state-run economic model.

Edited by: Rana Taha

World.title: US: 25 states sue over Trump's new tariffs
World.content:
The coalition of largely Democratic-led states is challenging the Trump administration's argument that tariffs will address imports produced by alleged "forced labor" abroad. The White House insists the move is legal.

Twenty-five US states sued President Donald Trump's administration Monday over its latest tariffs, saying they were a pretext for replacing import taxes struck down by the Supreme Court in February.

The United States imposed double-digit tariffs on 59 countries plus the European Union last month, accusing them of not doing enough to crack down on imports produced by forced labor.

The new tariffs took effect just as the clock ran out on temporary tariffs President Trump had turned to after the Supreme Court defeat.

What did the 25 states say in their lawsuit against Trump tariffs?

"After losing at the Supreme Court, the administration is once again trying to illegally raise taxes on families and businesses with a new round of tariffs," said New York Attorney General Letitia James, launching the lawsuit.

"Despite losing every step of the way, Trump is trying yet again to inflict more on working families and homegrown businesses," added Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield.

Joining New York and Oregon in the legal action were the Democratic-led states of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Maryland, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin – plus Republican-led Nevada and Vermont.

"There is no rational fit between the purported problem of forced labor in international supply chains and the blanket global tariffs," the coalition of states argued in their court filing.

What do Trump's tariffs really have to do with forced labor? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

White House insists Trump tariffs are legal

Since taking office for his second term, Trump has argued that US trading partners have been taking advantage of the world's largest economy, and has sought to use tariffs as leverage to strike new trade deals.

His administration has upended global trade by imposing wide-ranging tariffs – often at eye-watering levels – against Washington's friends and foes alike.

The latest tariffs, invoked under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, range from 10% to 12.5% and hit countries that account for 99% of American imports.

"The Tariff Action is arbitrary, capricious and contrary to law," the lawsuit said, but the White House hit back, insisting that the government move was legal.

"The United States is using its lawful authority to obtain the elimination of unreasonable acts, policies, and practices that burden US commerce," said White House spokesman Kush Desai.

"A foreign country's failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor is unreasonable and burdens US commerce, including American workers, and must be addressed."

World.title: Study shows why younger generations may be more cancer-prone
World.content:
Researchers are observing certain age-related types of cancer more frequently in younger people. A new study suggests this could be because younger generations are aging faster than their parents or grandparents.

Susanna was just 28 years old when she was diagnosed with bowel cancer. Andre developed lung cancer when he was only 34. Both of them have turned to social media to talk about their fight against the disease. Neither of them are medical outliers — not anymore.

The German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) has reported a sharp increase in gastrointestinal cancer cases for patients between the ages of 20 and 39. In the US, researchers have observed a similar development, with an even higher disease ratio than in Germany. Younger people are also increasingly being diagnosed with other types of cancers, including those that affect patients' bone marrow or uterus.

Cancer is usually regarded as an age-related disease. According to the German Cancer Aid non-profit, the average age for men and women with cancer is around 69. Cancer cells form when certain sections of the genetic sequence mutate and can no longer be repaired. The older we get, the less reliable our repair system becomes.

Making cancer cell therapy affordable To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Gap between chronologal and biological gap increasing

A study by researchers at Washington University School of Medicine, US, has now found a link that could help explain why an increasing number of people under 50 are developing early-onset cancer. The reason, they suggest, is that younger generations are displaying a wider gap between their biological and their chronological ages. In short, they are aging faster.

While the chronological age counts how many years have passed since a person's birth, their biological age describes how much their body has aged, based on the cellular damage accumulated. Individual organs and tissues can age at varying speeds.

In other words, the same person's liver, heart and brain could each have different biological ages, all of which could differ still from the person's actual age.

The recent study has now for the first time established a link between the increasing gap between biological and chronological ages in younger generations on the one hand, and the risk of early-onset cancer on the other, Ron Jachimowicz explains. He's an attending physician and hematologist at the University Hospital Cologne, as well as head of the Max Planck Research Group for Biology of Aging.

"Don't forget, this is a correlative study," Jachomowicz cautions.

Correlation refers to two things appearing in concert, so it looks like they are related. It does not prove causation, which we speak of when one factor causes another.

While results can provide certain indications that seem quite plausible, researchers were already well aware of the fact "that there is an association between biological age and the risk of developing cancer," Jachomowicz says.

Here's what you need to know about breast cancer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

DNA, bloodmarkers and telomeres: How to determine one's biological age

It's not easy to determine a person's biological age. Calculating it requires a number of parameters — there is no single, precise test. Instead, epigenetic tests are used to determine chemical alterations of DNA sequences, evaluating certain blood values and measuring the length of so-called telomeres — that is, the repetitive DNA sequence located at the end of chromosomes that function as protective caps.

There are also physiological tests, to monitor various body and organ functions, as well as cognitive evaluations.

Researchers in the study at hand applied a combination of these various measurement techniques to analyze the data of more than 150,000 individuals drawn from the UK Biobank, a British biometric dataset.

They found that people born between 1965 and 1974 had a significantly higher gap between their chronological and biological ages than people born between 1950 and 1954. The younger the cohort examined, the wider that gap appeared to grow.

An investigation involving more than 10,000 US individuals revealed an even higher deviation for participants born between 1990 and 1999, compared to a cohort born between 1965 and 1969.

"In Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom (UK) and the US, people born in the 1990s face at least fourfold higher risk of early-onset colorectal cancer compared with those in the 1960s," the authors write in the study.

Prostate cancer: The shift in early detection To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can I improve my biological age?

We used to assume that a healthy lifestyle could make up 75% to 90% of one's biological age. Now we know that's not true, Jachimowicz explains.

"We can influence about 50% of it," he says, "while the other 50% are genetically predetermined."

To help slow the aging process, he recommends "typical lifestyle interventions," such as working out regularly, eating a balanced diet, getting enough sleep, and avoiding drugs and alcohol.

And the value of social contacts should not be underestimated, he adds.

It's not easy to say why, on a biological level, younger generations are aging faster than their parents and grandparents. But there are a few hypotheses.

"Younger people are being exposed to earlier and longer obesity," says Tanwei Yuan, an epidemiologist in the Department of Clinical Epidemiology and Aging Research of the DKFZ in Heidelberg.

Other contributing factors are a sedentary lifestyle, and poor sleep quality due to extended periods of time in front of a screen, Yuan adds. She says the current study delivers valuable insights that confirm hypotheses long held by cancer researchers.

She also stresses the value of a healthy lifestyle to help reduce the risk of early-onset cancer.

"If you feel unwell, go to a doctor and ask for the screening," Yuan recommends.

Could microrobots be used to zap cancer cells? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yuan knows what she's talking about. The 32-year-old researcher says she had felt unwell for quite some time before being diagnosed with intestinal polyps last year. While these can start out benign, if left untreated, polyps can become cancerous. That's why it's important to listen closely to your body and take measures early, she says.

Can my doctor determine my biological age?

In a word: no, says Jachimowicz.

Determining an individual's biological age is the "subject of current scientific research, but in no way a practical routine or part of everyday clinical work."

However, he believes it should be, especially when it comes to initiating early cancer interventions. He believes this current study is particularly valuable because it highlights this path forward for future studies.

"It's still far off in the future," he says, "but it's very exciting."

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Dry Danube River threatens nuclear power in Romania, Hungary
World.content:
Hungary's Paks nuclear power plant was operating at about 10% of capacity because of a lack of cooling riverwater. In Romania, the military blew up a rock outcrop in a bid to improve water flow to the Cernavoda plant.

Several central and eastern European countries are facing power shortages and impacts on industry amid prolonged hot and dry weather and record low levels on the Danube River and other waterways.

Hungary narrowly averted switching off its lone nuclear plant, but had still powered it down to a fraction of capacity. In Romania, the navy demolished a rocky outcrop exposed in the Danube's riverbed, trying to improve the water flow.

And in Serbia, hydroelectric power output was severely impacted by the dry conditions.

Continued hot and dry weather is forecast during the week, providing little sign of relief.

The Cernavoda nuclear plant draws its cooling water from the Danube Image: Andreea Alexandru/AP Photo/picture alliance

How did Romania try to feed the Cernavoda power plant?

Romania's military detonated a rocky outcrop exposed by the low water levels on a branch of the Danube, seeking to improve the flow of cooling water to the Cernavoda nuclear plant, which typically supplies about one-fifth of the country's power.

The plant draws all of its cooling water from the Danube.

Soldiers detonated a rock some 50 kilometers (roughly 30 miles) upstream. The debris would be taken to a strategic spot and sunk to help raise the water level.

Defense Minister Radu Miruta said the operation was a success, and also said the military had been waiting for a chance to access and demolish the rocks for decades.

Romania's navy was in action on the river on Monday Image: Andreea Alexandru/AP Photo/picture alliance

If the partial diversion of the water fails, Miruta said, the plant would likely have to shut down entirely by Thursday.

Caretaker Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan said that carmakers Dacia and Ford had agreed to suspend production in Romania until August 19, following a crisis meeting with representatives of the energy-intensive industry. He said that other companies would be taking similar steps.

What was the situation at Hungary's Paks power plant?

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said it was possible to avoid the unprecedented total shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant on Monday that was originally announced last week.

But the four-reactor station that typically generates almost half of Hungary's electricity production and around a third of its consumption was running at little more than 10% capacity on Monday.

The four-reactor Paks plant is a key contributor to Hungary's energy output Image: David Balogh/Xinhua/IMAGO

Hungary had asked industrial users to curb consumption and households to make voluntary savings. Electric-powered freight trains were also stopped on Monday to reduce the load on the grid.

Magyar thanked people for their restraint on Monday evening.

"We have entered the critical period. The network is stable, consumption is currently well below planned levels, thanks to self-restraint. The last Paks turbine is operational. I will report back shortly from the (grid operator) MAVIR control room," he said.

Magyar also said slightly earlier on Monday that "water management forecasts for the coming days have become slightly more optimistic."

How power plant closure impacts Hungary's new government To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How was Serbia affected?

In Serbia, the vast Iron Gate hydroelectric plant on the Danube was operating at only around one-fifth capacity on Monday.

Prime Miniser Djuro Macut convened an emergency meeting on Monday to discuss the energy problems.

He appealed to residents to "minimize the use of big consumers of electricity in their homes, such as air conditioners," having described the situation as "serious an demanding" late on Sunday.

Shallower stretches and Danube tributaries have been reduced to a trickle in the heat Image: Andreea Alexandru/AP Photo/picture alliance

Far upstream in Bavaria, the Danube's levels were also affecting freight transport.

New German Transport Minister Steffen Bilger said the historic low levels on the Danube, and particularly the Rhine to the west — Europe's busiest inland freight waterway — were providing a first challenge for his tenure.

"It is indeed a very tense situation with the low waters," Bilger told Reuters TV on Monday, saying he would chair a crisis meeting on Thursday. "We are used to repeated low water situations, but this is really a very early point in the calendar year for problems of the kind we're currently experiencing."

Typically European rivers reach their lowest levels slightly later in the summer — it's entirely possible that several more weeks of predominantly hot and dry weather are yet to come.

Danube water levels far upstream in Bavaria are also well below even their seasonal expectations Image: Manfred Segerer/IMAGO

World.title: Ceuta: EU calls borders a 'shared European responsibility'
World.content:
The European Commission has offered Morocco more support at the border to Ceuta and Melilla, and called for "united action" from the bloc on border security. Its interior ministers will discuss the issue on Tuesday.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has told Spain's prime minister that border security is a "shared European responsibility" and suggested Brussels could provide more assistance to Morocco.

This comes as Spain tries to return the last of tens of thousands of people who swam around or otherwise breached the border to the North African exclave of Ceuta last week.

Officials installed an additional 500-meter barrier near the border post after thousands swam or waded around this entrance point Image: Jorge Guerrero/AFP

European Union interior ministers will convene for an emergency video meeting on Tueday to discuss potential responses. The scenes had led to friction betwen EU members and to Italy and France implementing temporary border controls, even though it's not possible to travel from Ceuta to the mainland without providing identification.

What did von der Leyen say in her letter to Spain's prime minister?

Von der Leyen wrote to Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday, which was soon seen by several news agencies, calling for "united action" on border security within the bloc.

"From this incident it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points," she wrote.

"The protection of all our external borders is a shared European responsibility," von der Leyen said, calling for vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed.

She commended Sanchez on his "swift handling" of the situation, with the vast majority of the roughly 50,000 people having already returned across the border to Morocco.

Ceuta's top government official Juan Jesus Vivas estimated that between 3,000 and 5,000 people remained in the city, with the Spanish governemnt's delegate offering a slightly lower estimate.

Von der Leyen also praised Morocco as an important security partner Image: Jon Nazca/REUTERS

Von der Leyen also raised the prospect of intensified cooperation with and assistance for Morocco if necessary when it came to the Spanish coastal exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla.

"Morocco is an important strategic partner, particularly in our efforts to combat migrant smuggling and illegal migration," von der Leyen wrote. "In cooperation with Spain, especially on anything related to Ceuta and Melilla, we could enhance border management early-warning systems and improve our technical and financial support to Morocco.

Alone in Ceuta, 15-year-old Moroccan teen faces uncertainty To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

EU interior ministers' video conference set for Tuesday

The sudden large-scale rush across Ceuta's border starting on Thursday triggered sharp tensions among the EU's members states, with France announcing temporary border checks.

Migration-averse governments or ministers in Italy, Denmark and Finland even called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-travel area, while right-wing opposition politicians around the bloc were often even more vocal.

Madrid responeded critically to what it called a "selfish" response from some partners, and called for emergency talks among European interior minister to chart a way forward.

Von der Leyen said Tuesday's talks would be a "first step," promising the issue would also feature in October's EU leaders' summit.

What led to the rush into Ceuta, after months of reduced migration?

The EU has significantly tightened its migration rules in recent months, in steps that have led to a marked reduction in irregular migration into the bloc more generally.

It's also agreed on the option of sending failed asylum seekers to partner third countries deemed safe outside its borders, calling these destinations "return hubs." So far, though, no such deals have been set up even though legislation enabling them has been ushered in.

Migration expert Gerald Knaus, the director of the European Stability Initiative think tank, told DW it was clear that last week's developments were not based on "anything structural," given no meaningful changes either in Morocco's social situation or in Spain's migration policy.

Instead he said there "was a lot of false information" online wrongly spreading rumors like "Spain was opening its borders" and "there was an opportunity to get through."

He said the lower numbers of people swimming around the border checks earlier in the week fueled the fire and led to the vastly increased numbers by Thursday.

What did migration analyst Knaus say about the wider political response?

Knaus said the current situation was in no way comparable with the 2015 when thousands were arriving on a daily basis, many fleeing civil war in Syria.

"In this crisis, there were very, very few asylum seekers. Most of them were young Moroccan men. So, no, this is not a sudden increase in structural pressure from a big displacement crisis," he said.

But Knaus said that the political reaction throughout Europe and the way it generated similar panic and far-right calls to close the Schengen zone demonstrated that the difference in scale and the event being an outlier rather than a pattern didn't really matter.

"What we see is that politically, even two days of an event in North Africa create fear in Finland and Denmark and Germany," Knaus said. "And so clearly, all countries in Europe have an interest in helping the countries in the Mediterranean find a policy. And the policy has to be signaling clearly: Don't do this. Don't climb across the fence. Don't take to the boats. Don't swim across the sea. Because when you do, we will treat you humanely, but we will return you and if necessary, to a safe third country."

Knaus said that this message, if conveyed and shown to be true, would stop dangerous sea crossings almost completely and overnight. And he said that the new EU rules could make it possible to achieve.

However, he said he did not hold out much hope for the events in Ceuta leading to concerted action or cooperation among EU members.

"What is most likely is that there will be some grandstanding — that different governments will accuse each other. Spain will respond and will say it is not to blame and there will be bad feelings and no solution," Knaus predicted.

Spain's Ceuta grapples with aftermath of border chaos To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Growing impact of extreme heat on informal workers in Asia's cities
World.content:
When temperatures soar across Asia's cities, informal workers face a choice: risk their health or lose their income. For many, the effects don't end when the workday is over.

Brijpal Singh spends long hours working construction under the blazing sun in Noida, a sprawling industrial satellite city in India's National Capital Region. Even as temperatures soar past 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit), work on the building site rarely stops.

By the end of each shift, the 51-year-old says his heart is pounding, and he's usually dizzy, dehydrated and physically drained from hours in the heat. Yet taking a day off is a luxury he cannot afford.

Missing work would mean losing his daily wage of 500 to 600 rupees ($6 to $7, €5.20 to €6.10). The money supports his wife and three children living in a village in Uttar Pradesh, a two-day journey away .

"There are days when I don't feel like working," said Singh. "But if I miss a day, who will take care of my children and pay for their expenses?"

After a day in relentless heat on a construction site, Singh tries to find relief in front of a fan Image: Danish Pandit/DW

Some 5 million people work in the Delhi region's informal economy, accounting for roughly 80% of the total workforce. And as climate change drives up temperatures, many paid by the day like Singh are faced with an impossible trade-off between providing for their families and protecting their health.

Extreme heat harms health, productivity and earnings

The past decade has been India's warmest on record, bringing more frequent, intense, and prolonged heat waves. At the same time, heat is reducing productivity and increasing illnesses, with one study finding rising temperatures could be costing informal workers the equivalent of 2% of their country's GDP annually. That's nearly $80 billion (€69 billion).

"Wage losses are only going to worsen as temperatures continue to rise," said Ameena Kidwai, lead researcher at People's Courage International, a nonprofit aiming to strengthen informal workers' rights. "Workers are now putting in many more hours than they did before to complete the same amount of work."

The US-based organization surveyed informal workers in five Asian cities. Kidwai said some of those surveyed reported that tasks once completed in eight hours now take 10 to 12 hours during the hottest months, as they slow down to cope with dangerous conditions.

With heat becoming a major occupational hazard, workers described the harm to their health, ranging from respiratory and gastrointestinal illnesses to stroke and kidney disease.

"As a result, workers also have to spend more on over-the-counter medicines and visits to clinics or hospitals," Kidwai said.

Out of the work frying pan and into the home furnace

A lack of ability to recover is a defining feature of urban heat for informal workers — from construction laborers and street vendors to delivery riders — say researchers.

Like Singh, many are migrants who leave their families behind to earn a living in fast-growing cities, said Patricia Samantha Narvaez, a program manager at the Philippine development organization IDEALS.

"You would expect home to be a place of relief," said Narvaez. "But many live in densely packed neighborhoods with poor ventilation, little green space and heat-absorbing concrete."

That's the case for Singh, who returns to a single room with poor ventilation after work. During the hot months from April to June, it becomes a furnace, and frequent power cuts make it difficult to cool down before the next day's shift.

"During the hot days, I can't eat well," Singh said. "I often drink oral rehydration solution and go to bed without eating."

Narvaez surveyed informal workers in Quezon City for a report on the impacts of extreme heat. The city is just northeast of Manila, the capital of the Philippines, a country in which some 42% of the employed population are informal workers.

"Some participants described Quezon City as a 'concrete jungle' because even at night it remains unbearably hot," said Narvaez.

Fifty-year-old Aida Tano has experienced such conditions firsthand. Tano worked in a garment factory in Quezon City for nearly two decades, where soaring temperatures, heat-generating machinery and poor ventilaton turned the production floor into an oven. With no air conditioning, four workers shared one electric fan.

Aida Tano, like many informal workers, bears the brunt of extreme heat both at her job and at home Image: People's Courage International

"There was no escape from the heat," Tano said. "We complained, but management told us that if we couldn't endure it, we could leave."

Narvaez says it's not unusual for factory owners to restrict measures that help workers cope with the heat even for trivial reasons such as not wanting fans to break down. At Tano's workplace, she had to pay for her own drinking water, and even climbing stairs to leave on her break became too exhausting in the heat.

The factory has since closed, but after a long day in extreme heat, Tano, who now does odd jobs like sewing and cleaning, would come back to a house with no AC. She still relies on electric fans and keeping windows covered to block the sun, both of which do little to cool her home.

Working women bear the brunt of extreme heat

The economic impacts of climate change hit women hardest, largely because they account for a majority of the world's poor, according to the United Nations.

Women in the informal economy also shoulder a disproportionately large burden because they combine paid work with unpaid caregiving responsibilities, said Ameena Kidwai of People's Courage International.

"They're managing their jobs while also running their households," Kidwai said. "When children or older family members fall sick during a heat wave, the caregiving duties falls largely on women."

Shanti Devi, a 36-year-old daily wage laborer in Noida, has been her family's sole breadwinner since her husband was injured in a workplace accident several years ago.

"Now I have to manage the house, care for my children and also try to earn a living," said Devi.

During heat waves, school closures and a shift to online classes often force Devi to stay home with her four children instead of going to work. Each day of lost wages adds to the already struggling family's financial strain.

"I took the day off because it is too hot to work, and my children are home because their school is closed for the summer," Devi said. "I have to cook for them. When school is open, they eat their meals there."

If Shanti Devi misses work to care for her children, she loses out on a much-needed pay check Image: Danish Pandi/DW

Frequent power outages and overheated homes, also leave many women up through the night caring for family members in the heat before returning to work the next day. Disrupted sleep and lack of rest come with increased health risks, such as heart disease and diabetes, meaning women are often more vulnerable than men in heat waves.

Researchers say these overlapping pressures expose a gap in many cities' efforts to adapt to a heating planet. While India has introduced heat action plans, and Quezon City is developing its own measures, protections for informal workers remain limited and unevenly enforced.

As temperatures rise because of human-caused climate change, experts say measures focus largely on short-term responses and often overlook the realities of informal workers' lives.

"Climate change will only deepen existing inequalities because those with the fewest resources are often the most exposed to extreme heat," Narvaez said. "Ultimately, resilient cities cannot be built on exhausted and unprotected workers."

Danish Pandit in Delhi, India, contributed to this report.

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

World.title: “En el rap, destaca el que tiene más ingenio. Lo que hacemos tiene un verdadero peso cultural”
World.content:
Arkano, el adolescente que descubrió su identidad gracias al rap. Conversaciones sobre la educación que queremos | Pensemos el mañana (Episodio 2)

Arkano, rapero y referente del ‘freestyle’ en España, se sienta a conversar con Bohemia, una joven promesa de la improvisación, sobre cómo el error forma parte del aprendizaje, cómo gestionar las críticas y cómo la educación colabora en crear mejores artistas urbanos

Guillermo Rodríguez 'Arkano' Artista de rap Su trayectoria reúne algunos de los grandes hitos del freestyle desde que, con 15 años, se proclamó campeón de España de la Red Bull Batalla de los Gallos de 2009. Incluso batió un récord Guinness al improvisar durante 24 horas y 34 minutos seguidos. Paralelamente, impulsa y participa en iniciativas sobre salud mental y colabora en campañas contra el acoso escolar Isabel Arrabal 'Bohemia' Estudiante de 3º de ESO Y ‘freestyler’ A sus 15 años, compagina los estudios en el IES Averroes (Córdoba) con sus primeras competiciones de freestyle. Empezó a improvisar con 14 años, tras descubrir el rap en YouTube, y forma parte de una nueva generación de jóvenes que ha encontrado en la cultura urbana un lugar donde desarrollar su confianza

Dice Arkano (Alicante, 32 años) que el rap le transformó, que incluso le salvó la vida. A los 15 años, cuando aún lo conocían más como Guillermo Rodríguez y todavía cursaba la ESO, ganó en España la Red Bull Batalla de los Gallos, la competición de improvisación más importante del país. “Yo era un chaval muy tímido, no tenía habilidades sociales, lo pasé bastante mal en la época del instituto y descubrir el rap fue como encontrar una voz propia”, cuenta. La cultura urbana le alumbró, le infundió más confianza.

“El 'freestyle' se basa en lanzarse al vacío, no podemos aspirar a que todo sea perfecto. Tenemos que estar preparados para el error”

Isabel Arrabal, conocida como Bohemia, tiene la misma edad que tenía Arkano cuando se coronó como una joven promesa. No es su única coincidencia; esta cordobesa también ha ganado seguridad en sí misma después de atreverse a rapear. En Pensemos el mañana, el proyecto de Fundación Unicaja y Grupo Prisa sobre la educación del futuro, reflexionan sobre cómo han podido desarrollarse gracias a sus inquietudes artísticas y a esos entornos sociales fuera de las aulas, no convencionales.

"El rap me ayudó mucho a relacionarme con mis compañeros, a tener más seguridad en lo que hago, porque antes era muy tímida. Me ha ayudado a confiar más en mí”

Bohemia y Arkano charlan, además, sobre lograr que el miedo a equivocarse no les inmovilice, la relación entre educación y rap (y la importancia de tener “un lenguaje más rico”, como precisa Arkano) o la gestión de críticas y redes sociales. Aunque sea una asignatura pendiente para algunos adolescentes, Bohemia ha aprendido a manejar esos mensajes anónimos y ofensivos: “A mucha gente le puede llegar a afectar, y el consejo que les daría es que piensen en quiénes son ellos realmente”.

Pensemos la educación del futuro ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja, busca fomentar el conocimiento, los valores de la educación, un aprendizaje sostenible y responsable y dar respuestas a los grandes desafíos de la educación del futuro. El proyecto pivota sobre seis ejes: 1 Aprendizaje y sentido vital 2 Bienestar y salud mental 3 Futuro y empleabilidad 4 Sostenibilidad y sentido colectivo 5 Tecnología y ética 6 Carácter y ciudadanía ¿Qué está ocurriendo en estos tiempos de cambios profundos y transversales? ¿Cuáles son los grandes retos para afrontar la transformación que viene? ¿Qué educación necesitamos? Diferentes personalidades de todos los ámbitos nos ayudarán a responder a estas y otras preguntas destinadas a impulsar cambios, dinamizar ideas y apoyar propuestas con impacto pedagógico y social. ‘Pensemos el mañana’ es un proyecto inspirador para las futuras generaciones llamadas a conquistar nuevas cotas del saber en un mundo complejo y cambiante.

World.title: Las calles de Gràcia se preparan para la fiesta mayor con espacios para familias y medidas contra el calor
World.content:
Agosto acaba de empezar y la expectación entre los vecinos de Gràcia de Barcelona ya se centra en el inicio de la fiesta mayor del barrio, una de las más tradicionales de toda Barcelona. Se celebrarán del 15 al 21 de agosto, con 23 calles, plazas adornadas y con la novedad de un espacio específico para familias y adolescentes. Tras los récords de calor registrados en Cataluña desde el inicio del verano, nuevas medidas para hacer frente a las altas temperaturas fueron necesarias para acoger la celebración. Sin embargo, la fiesta, conocida por reforzar el espíritu vecinal, ha sufrido este lunes un ataque inesperado a una de las entidades. La comisión de la calle La Perla, integrada por un grupo de vecinos del barrio, ha denunciado en sus redes sociales el sabotaje de la persiana de su local, que apareció sellada con silicona e impidió su apertura y funcionamiento.

El periodista e historiador Vicenç Sanclemente será el pregonero de esta edición, mientras que el cartel, obra del diseñador Pol Lupiáñez, conocido como Kota, recupera la imagen de los bailes populares en las calles decoradas como homenaje a los orígenes vecinales de la celebración.

El cartel de las fiestas mayores de la Vila de Gràcia 2026. Alba Ibáñez / ACN

Entre las principales novedades de esta edición será la transformación de la plaza Joanic en un espacio pensado casi exclusivamente para niños, adolescentes y familias. Durante el día acogerá cuentacuentos, talleres, espectáculos infantiles, juegos tradicionales y un espacio de lectura. Por la noche la idea es convertirse en una “zona tranquila para cenas familiares y programará actividades dirigidas al público adolescente, como cine al aire libre, concursos musicales”. Para evitar las franjas de máxima insolación, gran parte de las actividades matinales finalizarán antes de las horas de máximo calor y las de la tarde comenzarán más tarde.

Sabotaje a la calle Perla

La entidad de vecinos en la calle Perla ha explicado que el incidente se produjo después de una jornada dedicada a las tareas de decoración de la calle que, según la entidad, transcurrió “en un ambiente tranquilo y sin ninguna actividad festiva nocturna”. La comisión, que reúne a un grupo de amigos y se considera pequeña ante las otras organizaciones, ha subrayado que ningún vecino trasladó durante la jornada quejas o molestias y rechaza que lo ocurrido pueda justificarse como una reacción a incidentes de la noche anterior. Sin embargo, la comisión considera que se trata de “una acción deliberada” y la interpreta como “un ataque directo” al trabajo voluntario que realiza durante todo el año para organizar la Fiesta Mayor de Gràcia.

Para los miembros de la comisión, el sabotaje es parte de un contexto de creciente cuestionamiento del modelo de la Fiesta Mayor de Gràcia. Según han relatado, la entidad “comparte preocupaciones relacionadas con la suciedad, los botellones, los orines en la vía pública, el ruido fuera de horario y otras conductas incívicas”. No obstante, han rechazado propuestas como la reducción de los horarios de las actividades o la expulsión de las comisiones de las calles porque consideran que estas medidas comprometerían la viabilidad de la fiesta mayor. “Si lo que se quiere es una fiesta popular mejor, nos encontraremos dispuestos a trabajar para conseguirla”, han señalado desde la comisión, que pide que el debate sobre el futuro de la celebración se desarrolle desde el diálogo y no desde acciones de sabotaje.

World.title: Pistas para un viaje de verano a Portugal: de las playas del Algarve a los azulejos de Lisboa
World.content:
Ciudades y pueblos llenos de encanto, pistas para comer bien y barato y algunos trucos para descubrir el país

Año tras año, Portugal es un destino de vacaciones recurrente. Pero decir Portugal puede tener muchos significados: están las playas del Algarve que acogen a los amantes del surf, los pueblos del centro del país llenos de encanto y calles empedradas o los paisajes que dejan el Duero y el Tajo a su paso por el país vecino. Además del magnetismo de Lisboa y Oporto, dos ciudades llenas de vida y de historia.

Esta es una guía de destinos para quienes este verano viajen a Portugal.

Además, dos pistas gastronómicas para saber dónde comer y qué pedir en Lisboa y Oporto. Así como una visita cultural imprescindible en la capital lusa.

Y la experiencia viajera en primera persona de Paco Nadal, dispuesto a regresar una y otra vez al país.

World.title: Candidatos a secretario general de la ONU prometen reformar el organismo para que recupere protagonismo
World.content:
La campaña para la elección del próximo secretario general de Naciones Unidas ya está en marcha. De mantenerse la rotación de sus máximos representantes, a partir de 2027 sería el turno de América Latina y esta región es la que ha postulado a más candidatos: cinco de los siete en total que están en carrera. Este lunes, los aspirantes latinoamericanos a suceder al portugués António Guterres al frente del organismo internacional participaron en un evento organizado en Montevideo en el que subrayaron que la ONU necesita recuperar capacidad de acción y liderazgo en un mundo que enfrenta el mayor número de conflictos armados en décadas. Coincidieron en la necesidad de reformar la ONU para evitar que se profundice la pérdida de confianza y protagonismo.

La costarricense Rebeca Grynspan y la ecuatoriana María Fernanda Espinosa participaron in situ del diálogo público impulsado por el Gobierno uruguayo que buscaba dar a conocer las prioridades de quienes aspiran a dirigir el organismo. La guyanesa Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett intervino de forma remota, mientras que la chilena Michele Bachelet y el argentino Rafael Grossi se hicieron presentes a través de mensajes enviados con antelación. Estuvieron ausentes los candidatos africanos, el senegalés Macky Sall y el ugandés Olara Otunnu.

Para Grysnpan, secretaria general de la UNCTAD (Conferencia de las Naciones Unidas sobre Comercio y Desarrollo), defender la ONU es “tener la valentía de reformarla”. A 80 años de su creación, considera que el organismo se ha vuelto conservador y debe corregir el rumbo y ofrecer resultados para recuperar la confianza perdida. “Tiene que asumir riesgos”, resumió. “Cuando yo voy alrededor del mundo lo que la gente me pregunta es dónde está Naciones Unidas. No nos ven en los escenarios de conflicto”, lamentó Grynspan, quien reclamó que la la paz y la seguridad deben volver a ser uno de los ejes prioritarios del organismo.

La exvicepresidenta segunda de Costa Rica es una de las candidatas más firmes a la secretaría general, que siempre ha estado en manos de un hombre. Durante su intervención, Grynspan quiso poner luz también sobre gestiones exitosas de la ONU y sus agencias y puso como ejemplo las negociaciones con Rusia y Ucrania para poder recuperar el comercio de granos tras la invasión lanzada por Moscú y evitar una crisis alimentaria. La representante costarricense insistió en que para poder mantener el rol mediador, el secretario general necesita “imparcialidad y legitimidad”.

Crimen organizado y cambio climático

Rodrigues-Birkett, antigua ministra de Asuntos Exteriores de Guyana, es otra de las candidatas que parten con más apoyos. Este lunes se comprometió a impulsar “reformas continuas” en la ONU para ganar eficiencia y ser más cercana a la gente. La candidata guyanesa destacó que más allá de los conflictos armados hay desafíos que también requieren decisiones globales para ser resueltos, como el crimen organizado trasnacional y el cambio climático.

Espinosa defendió el rol de América Latina en este momento, por tratarse de “una zona de paz libre de armas nucleares en un momento de gran debilitamiento del tratado de no proliferación de armas nucleares”. “Es el momento de América Latina y de una mujer latinoamericana”, dijo a la audiencia que escuchaba el debate tanto de forma presencial como virtual.

El candidato que más sabe sobre armas nucleares es el argentino Rafael Grossi, director general del Organismo Internacional de Energía Atómica. A través de un mensaje grabado, Grossi recuperó la figura del único secretario general latinoamericano hasta la fecha, Javier Pérez de Cuéllar (1982-1991), para reivindicar su actuación concreta en la resolución de conflictos como la guerra entre Irán e Irak, el conflicto en Afganistán y la desmilitarización de Angola, entre otros. Para Grossi, esa capacidad de acción que tenía el organismo, ahora “se ha perdido”. El canciller argentino, Pablo Quirno, defendió su candidatura al sostener que Grossi ha estado “presente en algunos de los escenarios más sensibles del mundo, manteniendo abiertos canales de diálogo cuando otros se cerraban”.

Bachelet no pudo viajar por una afección y envió una carta en la que destacó que la ONU está ante una oportunidad que definió como histórica: “Que sea una mujer latinoamericana quien encabece la organización”. La candidatura de la expresidenta chilena nació con mucha fuerza por el apoyo tripartito con el que gozaba: Chile, México y Brasil. Sin embargo, perdió el de su propio país cuando asumió el ultra José Antonio Kast el pasado marzo y ha perdido posiciones. La exmandataria apuntó que quien sea elegido debe gobernar con “independencia, imparcialidad, criterio y valentía” ya que estará sometido a presiones de gobiernos, potencias y distintos intereses.

Guterres tiene mandato hasta final de año y el proceso de elección de su sucesor puede alargarse durante meses. La fase clave del proceso son las llamadas votaciones de color, en las que se diferencia si votan Estados Unidos, Francia, el Reino Unido, Rusia o China, los cinco miembros con derecho a veto del Consejo de Seguridad. Estos son los que deciden quién está fuera y quién dentro de la carrera.

World.title: Hunza G, los bañadores de los mil colores, la talla única y el tejido prodigioso
World.content:
Georgiana Huddart ha insuflado vida a la firma de moda de baño Hunza G, hasta convertirla en la más deseada del plantea. Este verano estrena colaboración con Burberry

En el arsenal de moda de esta temporada estival hay unos cuantos imprescindibles: unas sandalias de goma de Ancient Greek, un collar de conchas de Juju Vera, un vestido de Dôen, un capazo de Loewe, un par de gafas ovaladas de Oliver Peoples x Khaite… y un traje de baño de Hunza G. Y, además, si es uno de los que acaba de lanzar con Burberry, que el verano pasado firmó el revival del año cuando combinó el biquini de triángulo con el clásico estampado de cuadros de la casa británica, la combinación se lleva el premio gordo.

“Es un sueño hecho realidad”, dice Georgiana Huddart (Londres, 40 años), a propósito de la colaboración que surgió de una conversación de sobremesa con Jonathan Kimal, director de marketing de la centenaria enseña inglesa Burberry. “Creo que nadie se la esperaba, pero tiene todo el sentido”, sostiene la cofundadora y directora creativa de Hunza G. “Dos firmas británicas, ambas con un gran legado, una apuesta firme por la innovación y referentes en sus categorías. Puede que no tengamos tanta trayectoria en el tiempo, pero fuimos los creadores originales del tejido crinkle y los primeros en aplicarlo a la moda de baño”, apuntala.

Georgiana Huddart, que en 2015 relanzó la firma Hunza añadiendo la G de su inicial al nombre. “Hemos cambiado las reglas del juego”. Manuel Vázquez

La colección ya se ha coronado superventas. Con unos ingresos que superan los 41 millones de euros anuales y una previsión de crecimiento imparable espoleada por su expansión internacional —de Bongénie en Suiza a la boutique del hotel Six ­Senses en Ibiza— y la entrada en nuevas categorías de producto —­como los accesorios para el pelo y la colección de camisetas que acaba de lanzar con la artista Joe Sweeney—, Hunza G es a la ropa de baño lo que Alo Yoga a las mallas de deporte y Le Creuset a las cocottes. El tipo de éxito comercial que deriva en metonimia.

Todo empezó en una feria industrial en los ochenta, cuando, buscando una alternativa asequible a los tejidos hiperceñidos de Alaïa, Peter Meadows —un veterano de la industria textil— dio con la famosa tela arrugada y pensó que sería perfecto para hacer trajes de baño. En 1984 lanzó la marca y la bautizó Hunza por el valle paquistaní cuyos habitantes, dicen, son unos de los más felices del mundo. No tardó en convertirse en nombre de culto. Por ejemplo, con el icónico vestido azul y blanco que Julia Roberts llevaba en Pretty Woman. Hasta que los noventa trajeron el minimalismo y, para cuando llegó el cambio de milenio, la fantasía neón de la firma cayó en el vacío. Silencio absoluto.

Confeccionados en telares especiales, un solo bañador de Hunza G requiere más de nueve millones de puntadas. Manuel Vázquez

Si Georgiana Huddart la conocía era porque le recordaba al bañador rosa que su madre llevaba cada verano. Quiso la casualidad que un día, cuando trabajaba como asistente para la editora Camilla Nickerson en Vogue, se encontrara con un barullo de piezas vintage en una tienda de Berlín. “Me las llevé todas”, recuerda hoy. Cada vez que se ponía una, a la ristra de cumplidos le seguían las preguntas sobre dónde podían comprarse. Empezó a plantearse producir ella misma aquel tejido prodigioso. Sin suerte.

En 2015 conectó con Peter ­Meadows. Por aquel entonces el empresario, que rondaba los 60 años, estaba jubilado, pero aún conservaba un puñado de muestras del tejido original. “Le dije que tenía un plan para revivir la marca, manteniendo el legado pero actualizándolo”, recuerda Huddart. “Le gustó la idea”. En poco más de una semana habían trazado un plan. Contactaron con el proveedor original, añadieron la G de Georgiana a la marca, abrieron una cuenta de Instagram y empezaron a producir: sin despliegue de marketing, ni embajadoras ni rondas de capital multimillonarias. Solo un buen producto y una idea muy clara: “Crear una marca que se adaptase a todo tipo de mujeres y cuerpos”. Caló. “Creo que incluso a Peter le sorprendió la demanda que llegó a tener, y lo rápido que sucedió”, dice la empresaria.

Objeto de culto en los ochenta, el pasado y el archivo aún son fuentes de inspiración. Manuel Vázquez

“Nos han copiado muchísimo. No solo el tejido, sino también la forma en que hemos entendido y desarrollado esta categoría durante los últimos 10 años”, confiesa la británica. Manuel Vázquez

Lo que hilvana el éxito de Hunza G es el tejido. Una mezcla de poliamida y elastano que funciona como una fórmula secreta que muchos intentan imitarla pero nadie consigue hacerla igual. Para confeccionar el Original Crinkle™ hace falta conocer la técnica al dedillo y contar con unos telares especializados que producen las prendas sin costuras mediante una construcción tubular. “Cuando empecé a escribir a distribuidores y fabricantes para hacerla, la respuesta era siempre la misma: era demasiado complicado”, recuerda Huddart. Tuvieron que recurrir al taller que surtía a ­Meadows en los ochenta para que desentrañase el proceso. Empieza con una combinación de hilos muy precisa, luego llega el momento de tejer. Cada máquina tiene varios miles de agujas que deben ajustarse, calibrarse y reemplazarse a mano. Funciona de forma ininterrumpida y produce 6.600 millones de puntadas al día. Un solo bañador requiere más de nueve millones. Cada metro de tejido se examina con lupa y a contraluz para asegurar la uniformidad de la puntada, el gramaje y el entramado antes de cortarse y teñirse. “Si hay un defecto, todo se desmorona”, apunta Huddart.

Empezaron con un ordenador y tres amigos. Hoy son medio centenar de empleados, con una red comercial internacional e ingresos de 30 millones de libras. Manuel Vázquez

Su proveedor está en Austria y solo produce para ellos. Los tintes se trabajan en Alemania, en una fábrica donde el 85% de la energía viene de fuentes renovables y el agua que resulta del proceso se trata y depura hasta tener la calidad de la de un río.

“La clave está en el elemento tubular”, señala Georgiana Huddart. El proceso de encontrar a alguien capaz de recrear ese tejido no solo visual, sino estructuralmente, fue muy complejo. “Lo cual también me hizo darme cuenta de que era algo realmente único, algo muy especial que no cualquiera podía replicar con facilidad”. En el momento en el que se corta y se cose por el lateral —como suelen hacer las marcas que intentan imitarlos— se pierde la magia. Tiene que ser un único pedazo de tela, sin costuras. “No es solo una cuestión visual”, reivindica. Es el resultado de décadas de innovación hasta llegar a concebir un tejido que permite diseñar con un concepto de talla única, adaptándose a todo tipo de cuerpos.

Heredera del hedonismo ochentero, el color es clave en los diseños de la casa. Cedida por Hunza G

“Es curioso ver pasar a la gente del escepticismo a la lealtad absoluta”, dice la empresaria. Comprensible: en la percha, un traje de baño de Hunza G no tiene ni un palmo de ancho. La proyección de embutirse en un pedazo de tela diminuto no es tentadora. “Hasta que se lo prueban y se dan cuenta de lo bien que sienta, y lo bien que se sienten. No está pensado solo para adaptarse a tu silueta, sino también para cambiar con tu cuerpo y, al mismo tiempo, recuperar siempre su forma original. Conseguir ese nivel de maleabilidad requiere muchísimo trabajo técnico. De hecho, hemos rediseñado el tejido varias veces. La calidad que tenemos ahora es diferente a la de los ochenta”.

Trabajan con el mismo proveedor que hace el textil de muchos hospitales en Europa y la tela de los altavoces de Google. “Son pioneros”. Con ellos también han creado un género con material FPU 50 para una colección que, curiosamente, a menudo se cuela entre su superventas. “Es un tejido diferente, italiano, y no es de talla única. Pero comparte los mismos pilares que el crinkle: es técnico, favorece, se adapta y responde al cuerpo, y te hace sentir segura”.

El elemento tubular de su tejido, Original Crinkle™, es la clave. Y lo que lo hace tan difícil de copiar. Manuel Vázquez

“La idea siempre ha sido ayudar a que las mujeres se sientan increíbles en un momento en el que pueden sentirse más vulnerables”, cuenta Huddart. Manuel Vázquez

En una enseña que —además de patrones que sirven a distintos cuerpos y diseños que saben ir desde la oleada de lujo discreto al maximalismo más hedonista, pasando por los guiños pin up— se cimenta en las bondades de sus tejidos, la innovación juega un rol clave. Lo que no implica dejar de lado el pasado. Pero tampoco instalarse en la nostalgia facilona. La relación de Hunza G con el legado es particular. “Es divertido recuperar un diseño del archivo de vez en cuando y reeditar el vestido de Pretty Woman en Halloween —­porque en Estados Unidos todo el mundo quiere disfrazarse de Vivian Ward—. Pero hoy la firma tiene una dimensión diferente”. Otra narrativa. “Nunca tuve en la cabeza esa estética de Australia y modelos atléticas e intercambiables. Ese jamás fue el concepto”.

En su lugar forjó la imagen de la enseña con las fotos que sus clientas subían a las redes luciendo las piezas de la firma. Ya fuese una madre con sus hijos, una mujer embarazada o Rihanna. Incluso cuando se podía permitir orquestar una campaña, en vez de fotografiar sus bañadores de talla única en seis modelos de la 34, lo hacía en seis mujeres con cuerpos diferentes. Y caló. “Creo que conectó con una emoción profunda en las mujeres: el deseo de sentirse bien. No creo que ser excluyente sea el futuro. No es divertido, comercialmente no es una buena idea y, simplemente, no creo que refleje el momento en el que estamos. Ya lo sentía así en 2015, antes de que la diversidad fuese parte de la conversación. Para nosotros nunca ha sido una cuestión performativa, y creo que, en lo que a moda de baño se refiere, cambiamos el juego”.

World.title: Las mejores playas en los alrededores de Santander
World.content:
Los Tranquilos. La preciosa y relajada playa de Los Tranquilos –por algo su nombre– es, en realidad, la prolongación del arenal que a lo largo de seis kilómetros se extiende desde el Puntal, que penetra en plena bahía de Santander, hasta la localidad de Loredo después de pasar por el paraíso surfista de Somo. Los Tanquilos se encuentra, pues, al final de esta increíble franja de arena que permite el baño, bien en las calmadas aguas de la bahía o, hacia el otro lado, entre las agitadas olas del mar abierto, donde se ubica Los Tanquilos. La mejor manera de venir es también en una de las embarcaciones que comunican Santander con Somo y desde allí en un agradable paseo por la orilla. En un ecosistema dunar, las vistas a la inmensidad azul del Cantábrico y la isla de Santa Marina son un regalo añadido que quienes visitan esta playa por primera vez no podían imaginar.

KevinAlexanderGeorge (Getty Images)

World.title: Agua caliente gratis sin electricidad: las 5 duchas solares más vendidas para usar en exterior
World.content:
Se trata de duchas para la terraza muy fáciles de instalar y con recarga solar

Sus bases son antideslizantes, la temperatura regulable e incluyen grifos más pequeños para lavarse los pies

Las duchas solares para el exterior del hogar son una alternativa ecológica y sostenible, pues permiten ahorrar energía y en la factura de la luz al reducir el consumo de electricidad. Además, son muy fáciles de instalar y la mayoría de los modelos simplemente necesitan conectarse a la manguera del jardín.

Y no solo son prácticas para ducharse al aire libre o antes y después de darse un baño en la piscina, las duchas solares también son útiles para otras actividades. Como puede ser para lavar equipos deportivos, tablas de paddle surf o enjuagar objetos sucios en el jardín. También destacan por su durabilidad, puesto que están diseñadas para resistir las condiciones exteriores, como las que se recogen en esta selección que se pueden comprar en Amazon.

Sin duda alguna, son una opción perfecta para equipar el jardín este verano y pueden complementarse con otras opciones ‘top’ para ganar en comodidad como la tumbona portátil de la que te hablamos hace poco.

Ducha solar para jardines o piscinas, más de 3.000 valoraciones

Elegante y sencilla ducha solar de 216 centímetros de altura y equipada con un termómetro para controlar cómo se está regulando el agua (depósito de 35 litros). El cabezal de la alcachofa es redondo y giratorio (puede orientarse de manera personalizada). Incluye un grifo para los pies y tacos de acero con tornillo para fijarla al suelo fácilmente.

Ducha solar para jardines o piscinas con conexión para la manguera del jardín

Ducha solar para jardín y piscina

Esta ducha solar destaca por su diseño moderno y tiene un tamaño de 217 x 20 x 19 centímetros. El agua de la ducha puede regularse y calentarse hasta los 60 grados y su depósito es de 40 litros (se conecta a la manguera del jardín).

Ducha solar para jardín y piscina. © Amazon

Ducha exterior para el jardín, con altura regulable

Comodidad asegurada con esta ducha para exterior: la intensidad del agua y la altura de la fuente (hasta cuatro metros) se controla con el pie, gracias a una rueda instalada en el propio plato de ducha, y tiene un diseño portátil, por lo que se puede utilizar en el jardín y también es perfecta para campings. Se conecta fácilmente a la manguera del jardín y la base es antideslizante.

Ducha exterior para jardín y terraza con plato de madera y altura regulable

Ducha de jardín y piscina con más de 5.000 valoraciones, varios colores

Esta ducha solar también puede transportarse fácilmente, gracias a su diseño compacto y su ligereza (7 kilogramos). La orientación de la alcachofa puede regularse y esta puede extraerse, para manejarla con más comodidad. La altura del pie de esta ducha exterior también puede ajustarse hasta 2 metros.

Ducha de jardín y piscina. © Amazon

Ducha solar para piscina sin conexión eléctrica

Está fabricada con un plástico resistente a los rayos UV e incluye una cubierta que la protege de factores externos. Cuenta con un diseño moderno que encaja perfectamente con cualquier estilo de decoración. Tiene un tamaño pensado para que cualquier persona la pueda utilizar y su depósito ofrece una capacidad de 35 litros.

“La llevamos usando 2 años y no nos ha dado ningún problema. El agua sale a buena temperatura”, cuenta uno de los usuarios de Amazon. La ficha del producto supera las 2.000 reseñas y tiene una nota media de 4,1 sobre 5.

Ducha solar para piscina sin conexión eléctrica. © Amazon

Preguntas frecuentes sobre las duchas solares

¿Cómo funcionan?

El agua almacenada en el depósito se calienta gracias a la energía solar y sale caliente al abrir el grifo o el mezclador.

¿Cuánto tarda en calentarse el agua?

Todo depende de la intensidad del sol, la capacidad del depósito y la temperatura ambiente, pero puede tomar entre dos y cuatro horas.

¿Qué temperatura puede alcanzar el agua?

Entre 40 y 60 °C.
