World.title: Shell sells Dutch solar farms in retreat from renewables
World.content:
Shell is selling every solar farm it owns in the Netherlands. The five sites, plus a combined wind and solar park at Pottendijk near Emmen, are going to the French oil company TotalEnergies.

The deal covers all of Shell’s wind and solar projects on land across Europe (its offshore windfarms are not included) and the company will not disclose what it is being paid.

The Dutch sites can produce up to 254 megawatts between them, enough to power tens of thousands of homes. They are at Moerdijk, Heerenveen, Emmen, and Sas van Gent and Koegorspolder near Terneuzen.

Some were built on land Shell had already used for oil and gas, and the company used them as proof it was changing. The Emmen farm stands on the site of an old gas treatment plant, part of a project Shell said could be an example for the rest of the country.

The sale needs approval from regulators and is expected to be completed at the end of 2026.

Retreating from transition

Wael Sawan, Shell’s chief executive, has shifted spending back towards oil and gas and away from low-carbon projects. TotalEnergies has moved the other way, buying renewable assets across Europe.

The Hague district court ordered Shell in 2021 to cut its emissions by 45% by 2030. The company dropped Royal Dutch from its name and moved its headquarters to London the following year, and won its appeal in November 2024.

Milieudefensie has taken that case to the Supreme Court and launched a second action last year over the company’s 700 oil and gas projects that are still in development.

Shell is not leaving Dutch renewable energy altogether. It keeps its stakes in North Sea wind farms, its Holland Hydrogen 1 plant at Rotterdam and its carbon capture work.

World.title: Doctors want more hospitals to offer late-term abortions
World.content:
The Dutch association of gynaecologists, the NVOG, and the healthcare inspectorate IGJ want more hospitals to carry out late-term abortions – between 22 and 24 weeks – saying access to the care is not currently assured for all women.

Abortion is legal in the Netherlands up to 24 weeks. Terminations up to 22 weeks usually take place in abortion clinics, while those between 22 and 24 weeks are carried out in hospitals, of which only a small number currently do so.

Sanne Gordijn, head of obstetrics at the UMCG in Groningen, one of the few hospitals already providing the care, said some women were travelling to Spain, Britain or parts of the United States because they could not get a termination here.

She told broadcaster NOS that a late abortion is emotionally difficult for staff and never becomes routine, which is why the work needs to be shared out. The risk of medical complications after 22 weeks is why the procedure takes place in hospital.

Amsterdam’s OLVG has said it has been asked to take part but that reports it has already begun doing so are incorrect.

Gordijn said the grounds for a termination are usually a combination of factors, that the pregnant woman’s need comes first, and that no distinction is made between medical and non-medical grounds.

The UMCG said staff and medical social workers discuss the situation with women, including alternatives such as adoption, and that psychological support is available. Just over 39,000 abortions were carried out in the Netherlands in 2024, of which 331 were between 22 and 24 weeks.

Abortion clinics have reported a rise in attacks and intimidation in recent years, and MPs voted last year to bring forward a review of the abortion law, on a motion from NSC and the ChristenUnie.

World.title: Three terror suspects kept in custody as inquiries continue
World.content:
Three teenagers who were arrested in dawn raids last week on suspicion of planning terrorist attacks have had their detention extended while police inquiries continue.

A 19-year-old man named as Muhammad K. was detained at his home in Eindhoven last Wednesday, at the same time as a 16-year-old youth from Rotterdam and a 17-year-old from De Rijp, a village near Alkmaar.

K. was sentenced to 112 days in prison and banned from travelling out of the Netherlands two years ago after a court convicted him of plotting attacks on nightclubs and police stations in Belgium. No attacks actually took place.

The other two suspects were among a group of 14 people aged between 14 and 30 who were arrested in April last year for allegedly inciting others to carry out terrorist attacks, using the social media platform TikTok.

The public prosecution service said the arrests were carried out by the special interventions service (DSI), acting on information from the intelligence agency AIVD. It added that no weapons were found during the raids and there were no signs that a specific attack was being planned or a target had been identified.

A magistrate in Rotterdam agreed last Friday to detain the trio in custody for a further 14 days.

World.title: PostNL delivers fewer parcels as Asian web orders decline
World.content:
The Dutch postal service PostNL delivered fewer letters and parcels in the first six months of this year, mainly due to a slump in orders from websites based in Asia.

The number of packages from abroad declined by 15% compared to the first half of 2025, the company’s latest quarterly figures show.

PostNL’s domestic deliveries declined in volume by 4.2%, reflecting the fact that consumers placed fewer orders. The total number of letters and cards sent was down by 8%, continuing a long-term trend.

However, PostNL’s turnover in the first six months was almost identical – €1,589 million, €1 million less than in 2025 – as the average cost per delivery increased by 4%.

Three-day deliveries

The trend is likely to continue as PostNL began imposing a €3 surcharge for all packages sent from outside the EU from July 1.

PostNL is also likely to benefit from a change in the law ending its obligation to deliver post within 24 hours. PostNL’s maximum delivery window was extended to two days on July 12 and will become three days next year, allowing it to charge extra for next-day deliveries.

CEO Pim Berendsen said he was satisfied with the results, but PostNL still needed to push through major reforms such as three-day deliveries to secure its future.

“Thanks to the disciplined rollout of our new strategy, we have achieved robust results and seen a strong improvement in our cashflow. At the sale time, we see external challenges are on the rise.”

World.title: Jumbo’s quinoa now comes from Groningen, not Peru
World.content:
More than two dozen farmers in the Netherlands are growing quinoa, a South American seed that copes with salt far better than the crops usually planted on coastal land.

Salt is a worsening problem around the Dutch coast, with too little fresh water flowing to hold back the sea, and salt also seeps up from the ground in dry conditions.

This destroys potato and onion yields, but quinoa can survive much more easily, being able to withstand up to 12 grams of salt per litre of water. Potatoes begin to struggle at one gram.

Robert Van Loom, a researcher at Wageningen University, began breeding quinoa for Dutch conditions in the 1990s. He crossed an Ecuadorian variety, which could not handle the long Dutch summer days, with a Chilean one that was too bitter to sell. That cross became the basis for growing quinoa across Europe.

Renze Rispens, a farmer in Vierhuizen in Groningen, grows crops close to the sea dyke, on ground that has always carried a lot of salt. He read about quinoa in a trade magazine and planted it last year. Even in this summer’s drought, he said, the crop is standing well.

Most growers have contracts with GreenFood50, set up to sell Dutch-grown quinoa. Founder Marc Arts said its farmers now work about 200 hectares, producing 600 tonnes a year. A few others grow it independently.

Jumbo has switched its own-brand quinoa entirely to organic Dutch supply, under a three-year contract covering 12 farmers. Dutch quinoa costs more to buy in than imported, sustainability manager Marjolein Verkerk said, but she expects that to level out. The chain sells hundreds of thousands of packs a year.

Quinoa grew up around Lake Titicaca in the Andes, which was once a saltwater lake. That is where the salt tolerance comes from.

World.title: Wildfire breaks out in Limburg, train services halted
World.content:
A large wildfire is burning in the Rosmolen nature reserve at Oostrum in northern Limburg, and has stopped trains on the line between Nijmegen and Venray.

The fire broke out at 11.45am. The Limburg-Noord safety region said it had scaled up its response because of the drought and asked people to stay away from the area and leave room for emergency services. Large numbers of crews and vehicles are at the scene.

Fire brigades from several provinces and regions have been sent in, regional broadcaster L1 reported. Crews are trying to stop the fire crossing the nearby railway line.

The blaze is burning in the treetops, which allows it to spread quickly and makes it difficult to put out.

Rail operator NS expects the line between Nijmegen and Venray to stay closed until 6pm.

The Netherlands is in an official water shortage after weeks without significant rain. Last week the fire service called in help from Germany, France and Belgium to tackle wildfires elsewhere in the country.

World.title: Bonaire’s coral reef is disappearing, researchers warn
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The coral reef around Bonaire has fallen to about 5% of the seabed, down from more than 60% fifty years ago, researchers told broadcaster NOS on Monday.

The figures come from fieldwork on the Dutch Caribbean island that has not yet been published and which the researchers describe as a first analysis. A Wageningen Marine Research report published last year put average coral cover on Bonaire at under 10% and said algae now dominate the reefs.

The reef is central to a climate case Greenpeace Nederland brought against the Dutch state. Research behind that case found the coral helps shield Bonaire from flooding and that part of the island will be lost as sea levels rise.

The Hague district court ruled in January that Dutch climate policy breached the human rights of Bonaire’s residents and treated them unequally with people in the European Netherlands.

It gave ministers six months to quantify how much greenhouse gas the country can still emit, 18 months to turn that into binding targets, and until 2030 to produce a climate adaptation plan for the island.

The cabinet is appealing but remains bound by the judgment.

Coral researcher Erik Meesters of Wageningen University and Research said warming seawater was the main cause, worsened by a severe El Niño, and that higher temperatures also made coral more prone to disease.

Fast-growing species are surviving, he said, but the large reef-building corals that can reach ten metres are disappearing.

Bonaire’s economy depends heavily on diving tourism. The organisation Reef Renewal said it has planted 20,000 pieces of new coral around the island, while acknowledging the scale is not enough to solve the problem.

World.title: Ferries cancelled as rivers drop to record low levels in drought
World.content:
Several ferries across the Waal and IJssel rivers in Gelderland have been cancelled after the major Dutch rivers dropped to historically low levels in July.

The service across the Pannerdensch Kanaal, near where the Rhine flows into the Waal, between Doornenburg and Pannerden was stopped on Monday morning. The ferry operator said on its website it had taken the decision “to guarantee safety”.

The Rheden ferry, which takes pedestrians and cyclists across the IJssel at Rhederlaag, ran its last service on Monday evening.

Helmsman Richard van Oijen told Omroep Gelderland it was an unprecedented step. “We’ve been out of service in the past, but it was always because of high water.

“This is the first time I can remember not being able to run because of low water.”

Uitwaarde, which runs 10 connecting ferries in Gelderland, has suspended three of its routes across the Waal and Linge rivers because of low water.

The Rhine last week dropped to 6.46m, its lowest level, above sea level at Lobith, the point where the river enters the Netherlands from Germany. This week it is expected to fall another 11 centimetres.

River barges

The flow in the river is down to around one-third of its regular level for July, causing problems for cargo barges and river cruises. Several cruise operators have had to cancel or shorten trips upriver because the water is too low.

Restrictions have also been imposed on river barges, while nearer the river mouth sluice gates have been closed or limited to a few openings a day to prevent sea water getting into the drinking water supply.

The canal locks at Eefde, which up to 20,000 ships pass through a year between the IJssel river and the Twentekanaal, were closed for the first time last Friday, closing off traffic to Almelo, Hengelo and Enschede.

Deventer closed its harbour to shipping for the first time in eight years last week after the IJssel dropped below safe levels.

Polish swimmer Bartłomiej Kubkowski has become the first person in history to swim across the Baltic Sea between Sweden and Poland, covering a distance of just over 160 kilometres (99 miles). On Sunday evening, an exhausted Kubkowski clambered onto the beach in the town of Dziwnów on Poland’s northern Baltic coast, around 56 hours after he had set off from Kaseberga in Sweden on Friday. The achievement marks a personal triumph for Kubkowski, for whom this was the fifth attempt to complete the route. His effort this year has raised over 715,000 zloty (€166,000) for children’s cancer treatment so far, with donations to his fundraiser still coming in. View this post on Instagram A post shared by PURELY ATHLETICS (@purelyathletics) During the crossing, Kubkowski was unable to sleep and, although a support boat accompanied him and provided food and drink, he was not allowed to touch the vessel itself. His journey of around 160km was not far off the longest-ever continuous, unassisted open-water swim ratified by the Marathon Swimmers Federation, which was the 168.3 km swum by American Sarah Thomas in 2017 in Lake Champlain, between the US states of New York and Vermont. Kubkowski has been attempting to swim the route between Sweden and Poland since 2022, getting progressively closer to achieving the goal. Last year, he came within 11km of the Polish coast before extreme exhaustion and deteriorating weather forced him to give up, reported Eurosport. However, Kubkowski, a former competitive swimmer who now devotes himself to ultraswimming, did last year manage to break the world record for the longest distance swum in a swimming pool over 24 hours, after he managed to cover 103.6 km (64.5 miles). Another Polish swimmer, Karolina Szczepaniak, is also currently attempting to swim from Sweden to Poland along a slightly different route to Kubkowski’s. At the time of writing, she is around 110km into the 172km journey, and has raised almost 400,000 zloty for charity. Szczepaniak, a former Olympic swimmer, also attempted the feat last year, but was forced to give up after 57 hours amid worsening weather. However, the 146.7km she swam set a new record for the longest distance covered by a female swimmer in the Baltic Sea and a Polish record for open-water swimming by a woman. The company has offered 32 zloty per share, valuing Żabka at 32.6 billion zloty (€7.56 billion). World.title: The split in Poland’s opposition could help them unseat Tusk’s government [Opinion]
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles If Mateusz Morawiecki cuts his final ties with PiS and forms a new party, it may help broaden the opposition’s appeal by offering voters a more moderate, centre-right option. While the strings have not yet been fully cut, Poland’s main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), is splitting in two. A group of 40 MPs led by former Prime Minister (and PiS deputy leader) Mateusz Morawiecki have now formed a separate parliamentary caucus of their own, after last week refusing to sign a pledge of loyalty and quit the association they had formed – as had been demanded by PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński. Former Polish PM @MorawieckiM says 41 lawmakers aligned with him will form their own parliamentary caucus, deepening a split in conservative opposition party @pisorgpl. The proposed group would become the third-largest bloc in Poland's Sejmhttps://t.co/coOdpS7pia — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 The move means that Morawiecki’s caucus, known as Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), is now the third largest in parliament, while PiS, which is down to 147 MPs, has lost its status as the biggest. For now, most of Morawiecki’s followers officially remain members of the PiS party, a situation that will only change if they either resign or are thrown out following a disciplinary process that could take weeks. But unless either or both sides make major concessions, it seems only a matter of time before Development Plus becomes a separate party. A lot of international reporting has suggested that these developments will harm Poland’s right-wing opposition and boost the re-election chances of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s more liberal coalition at next year’s parliamentary elections. In fact, PiS’s split could well help the opposition win a majority. Over the last year, PiS has found itself in an increasingly difficult position. Its support in the polls has fallen below 25%, the party’s lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, combined support for two far-right opposition groups – Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) – has risen to over 20%, threatening PiS’s longstanding dominance on the right. In response, Kaczyński has pushed his party in a more rightward direction, picking a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s prime ministerial candidate in March. That signalled that PiS was aiming to compete head to head with the far right on many issues, taking tougher positions on Ukraine, the EU, migration and climate policy. In many cases, that meant disowning the legacy of the PiS government led by Morawiecki from 2017 to 2023. It also meant that the party was ceding the centre ground, something Morawiecki, who represents the more moderate, technocratic side of PiS, was particularly concerned about (alongside his own waning influence). When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal. This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 Should Morawiecki now, as expected, launch his own centre-right party, focused on economic development, it would appeal to moderate conservatives who are opposed to the Tusk government but put off by the far right and PiS’s own hardline turn. Inevitably, some of the support for Development Plus would come at the expense of PiS – but not all of it, and possibly not even most of it. An example of something similar happening can be seen elsewhere among the opposition. Until last year, KKP was part of Confederation. However, its leader, Grzegorz Braun, was expelled after announcing a run for the presidency against Confederation’s official candidate, Sławomir Mentzen. In June 2025, KKP formed its own parliamentary caucus. Since then, support for Confederation has remained stable at around 13-14%, while KKP has risen to over 9% in the polls. So, by splitting, the two groups actually increased the size of their potential electorate, with KKP successfully appealing to an even more radical pool of voters than Confederation. It is possible that Morawiecki could do the same in the opposite direction – his new party winning over moderate conservatives while PiS continues to appeal to its most loyal supporters as well as competing with the far right. There certainly seems to be fertile ground for such a party. Regular polling by the state research agency CBOS shows that the proportion of Poles with a negative view of Tusk’s government rose to its joint-highest level this month, at 48%, while only 29% have a positive view. The last time that positive views outnumbered negative ones was in February 2024, the second full month of the current ruling coalition’s time in power. Among those who voted for Tusk and his allies in 2023, dissatisfaction is strongest among moderate conservatives. Both Tusk’s centrist KO and one of his coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), are polling only slightly below the proportion of votes they received in that year (30.7% and 8.6%, respectively). However, the most conservative part of the coalition, the centre-right Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance, has fallen from 14.4% of the vote in 2023 to only around 4-5% today for the two parties that constituted it, Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) and the Polish People’s Party (PSL) (which last year decided to go their separate ways). An IBRiS poll for Polsat News in April this year found that, whereas 84% of KO voters and 57.1% of Left voters have a positive view of Tusk’s government, that figure falls to 42.5% for Third Way voters, a majority of whom (51.6%) have a negative opinion. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 Moderate conservatives’ disillusionment with the government, combined with PiS’s shift away from the centre ground, gives a clear opportunity for Morawiecki. And Tusk’s coalition itself showed in 2023 the advantages for the opposition in offering a broader set of options. While some – in KO in particular – had pushed for centrist and left-wing parties to stand jointly on a single list at that year’s elections, instead they campaigned as three main blocs. That gave voters opposed to the PiS government a genuine choice, and likely played a big part in the record turnout that helped bring Tusk’s coalition to power. It is similarly possible now that a four-branched opposition, ranging from Morawiecki on the centre right, through PiS and Confederation, to Braun on the radical right, could together win a parliamentary majority. Polls currently show those four groups with combined support of around 50% (though polling regarding support for Morawiecki’s prospective party should for now be treated with caution). Jestem dumny z tego, co wspólnie zrobiliśmy dla Polski. I wiem jedno – nasza misja wciąż trwa💪🇵🇱#RozwojPlus pic.twitter.com/xOnxKDoroS — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 31, 2026 However, even if they do win a majority, it is far from certain what would happen then. In 2023, the three opposition blocs were, although standing separately, clearly aligned with one another and focused on removing PiS from power. When they together won a parliamentary majority, it was absolutely clear they would form a coalition government. By contrast, today’s opposition is deeply divided. Confederation and KKP regularly attack PiS. It is not at all clear that Confederation would be willing to form a coalition government with PiS, while Kaczyński has explicitly ruled out working with the pro-Russian, anti-American Braun. Meanwhile, Morawiecki’s split has followed months of bitter infighting within PiS, which has often been carried out in public. The manner in which he and his allies are now departing the party means that relations with PiS are likely to remain difficult. The national-conservative opposition PiS party's newly named candidate for prime minister has made overtures to the far-right Confederation. But he also ruled out Grzegorz Braun, an even more radical far-right figure, serving in a PiS-led government https://t.co/i3zOZJWdUN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 9, 2026 It would therefore be hard for the opposition to form a government, even if they do win a majority. In this situation, the role of President Karol Nawrocki may be vital. Though elected with the support of PiS last year, he was technically an independent and maintained good relations with Confederation and even, to some extent, Braun (who endorsed Nawrocki after being eliminated in the first round). When Morawiecki this week announced the “ten pillars” of Development Plus’s programme, he made clear his loyalty to Nawrocki: the second of those pillars is “respect for the president”. Nie ma silnej Polski bez wielkich ambicji. Nie ma wielkich ambicji bez ludzi, którzy je zdefiniują i będą gotowi wziąć odpowiedzialność za ich realizację. Bezpieczeństwo. Rozwój. Suwerenność. Ambicja. Tożsamość. Patriotyzm. To nie hasła wyborcze, ale fundamenty państwa, które… pic.twitter.com/G0YBbfhLye — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 28, 2026 Many on the right hope that Nawrocki can play a role next year in helping the opposition present a more united front during the election campaign. It is also the president who decides who gets the opportunity to try to form a government after the elections. That role would be of particular significance if, as is very possible, Tusk’s KO emerges as the biggest individual party but the opposition together may be able to form a parliamentary majority. Given that we are still over 14 months away from the elections, and Morawiecki has not even yet officially split from PiS, it is still far too early to make confident predictions. However, while Morawiecki’s likely departure is clearly a personal blow to Kaczyński – and a sign of the 77-year-old’s waning influence over not only the Polish right but even his own party – it may conversely provide a boost to the opposition as a whole. Poland has banned children from using smartphones and other electronic devices in primary schools and preschools in a bid to improve their wellbeing and safety. The new legislation, signed into law by President Karol Nawrocki on Thursday, will take effect at the start of the school year on 1 September, but schools will have until the end of 2026 to adjust. Prezydent podpisał nowelizację, która zakazuje korzystania z telefonów komórkowych w przedszkolach i szkołach. (PAP)#PAPInformacje pic.twitter.com/CK7YFU7sru — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 30, 2026 Under the new rules, pupils in primary schools and preschools will be prohibited from using smartphones and other electronic devices allowing communication or audio and video recording for the entire school day, including breaks and lessons held outside of school grounds. Schools will be allowed, but not required, to create designated places where pupils’ devices can be stored in a safe way and with respect for their privacy. The law, however, allows for some exceptions. When pupils need a device because of illness, disability or other special needs, school headteachers can permit their use. Phones could also be used in emergencies where there is a direct threat to life, health or property. Furthermore, pupils will be permitted to use mobile phones if a teacher deems them necessary for educational purposes and gives approval. The law also allows secondary schools to introduce bans on smartphone use if they choose, but does not make this compulsory, with such schools retaining autonomy to set their own rules through their statutes. The draft law banning phones from primary schools was first approved by the government in June. It then went to the Sejm, the lower and more powerful chamber of Poland’s parliament, which introduced amendments, including extending the measures to preschools. The Sejm then approved the bill in a rare near-unanimous vote, with only some MPs from the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) voting against it. Subsequently, the Senate passed the bill without amendments, sending it to Nawrocki, who could have signed it, vetoed it, or sent it to Poland’s constitutional court for review. Poland’s government has approved a ban on mobile phones in primary schools as well as tougher age-verification requirements for online pornography. Both measures still require parliamentary and presidential approval before becoming law https://t.co/y4Ycf46FQD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2026 The president ultimately decided to sign the law, with his office noting that the measures aim to “create safer learning conditions” and support the “healthy and responsible” use of digital technologies by pupils. Poland’s education minister Barbara Nowacka said last month that the law would “improve teachers’ power, autonomy and agency, as well as order and digital wellbeing in schools”. She added that, although many schools already have such bans in place, teachers had asked for legal backing to help enforce them. For more on the measures, see our earlier report from when the bill was approved almost unanimously by parliament, with only the far right voting against it https://t.co/9Mx0SfkE5V — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 According to a survey conducted in April by the Polish state research institute CBOS for the Polish Press Agency (PAP), 85% of Poles support a ban on the use of smartphones in primary schools. Poland has been recently stepping up efforts to protect young people from various digital threats. The topic has been a rare area of consensus between the government and Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record number of bills. Earlier this month, Nawrocki signed a law banning online content depicting illegal acts or other forms of abusive and degrading behaviour – known in Polish as “patostreaming”. Another measure approved by the government that is now being considered by parliament is the introduction of stricter age-verification requirements for accessing online pornography. In January, the digital affairs ministry also announced that it hoped to introduce measures blocking children from access to social media. Poland hopes this year to introduce measures preventing children from accessing social media, says the country's digital affairs ministry. It is working on tools that would require platforms to verify the age of users https://t.co/G7qeEl2q9x — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 5, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Polish authorities have confirmed that the object that violated Polish airspace and crashed in eastern Poland was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload. The missile entered Poland during a period of intensive overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine, travelling around 100 km over Polish territory before exploding in a field in the Lublin region on Thursday morning. The object was “a potentially very dangerous missile,” Tomczyk added. Asked whether the incident could have been a deliberate move by Moscow, he said that no possibilities could be ruled out. “We don’t know, and if we do find out, it will mainly be through intelligence. I’m sure the coming weeks will provide us with more answers,” the deputy minister said. Tomczyk said Poland was working closely with Ukraine, adding that 20 of the roughly 70 missiles fired by Russia overnight from Wednesday to Thursday were at one point heading towards Poland. “It is also worth noting that the vast majority of these missiles were shot down by Ukraine over Ukrainian territory, which clearly bore the full brunt of the attack,” he said. He added that a Ukrainian pilot had tracked the missile that later fell on Polish territory but was unable to intercept it. “He turned back 20 seconds before reaching the border,” Tomczyk said, adding that the pilot “could not have flown into” Polish airspace. An object crashed into a field 100 km from Poland’s border with Ukraine overnight after a major Russian attack. The Territorial Defence Force combed through an area of approximately 3 km² and found numerous rocket debris, including propulsion components,” the Lublin prosecutor’s office said. He is banned from re-entering Poland and the Schengen area for five years. The 34-year-old was charged with promoting Nazism, an offence carrying a maximum sentence of three years in prison, and desecration of a memorial site. “A place that symbolises one of the greatest tragedies in human history requires special respect, and insulting it does not go without consequences,” said the border guard. @PolskaPolicja zatrzymała ob. Komendant #PlacówkaSGwKrakowie wydał wobec cudzoziemca decyzję o zobowiązaniu do powrotu oraz 5-letni zakaz wjazdu do 🇵🇱 i państw strefy Schengen. pic.twitter.com/kzfw1Kzw8w — Straż Graniczna (@Straz_Graniczna) July 30, 2026 Police in Oświęcim, the town where the museum is located, said in mid-July that they had detained a man after being notified by museum guards of a possible offence. A police probe found that the man, who had been living and working in the Wielkopolska province, had “posed for a photo making the Nazi salute” at the museum while visiting it. Prosecutors were informed of the case, police said, adding that the man was subsequently charged with two crimes: public promotion of Nazism and the desecration of a memorial site. He admitted to the offences and voluntarily submitted to his punishment, which consisted of a 2,000 zloty (€464) fine along with a decision for his verdict to be made public, they added. He was then handed over to Poland’s border guard, which decided to deport him and ban him from entering Poland and other Schengen countries for five years. The border guard said that the decision was “immediately enforceable”, and was based on “considerations of security and public order as well as the interests of the Republic of Poland.” It also noted that a court decided to place the man in a facility for foreigners in the city of Przemyśl, where he will await deportation. Auschwitz was first set up by Nazi Germany in occupied Poland in 1940 during World War Two as a camp to house Polish “political” prisoners, before later becoming primarily a site for the murder of Jews. At least 1.3 million victims were transported there, with at least 1.1 million of them killed at the camp. Around one million of those victims were Jews. The second largest group of victims – around 70,000 people – were ethnic Poles. Poland’s government has appointed a marketing and branding expert to develop a unified strategy for promoting the country abroad, saying the move will help boost tourism, support Polish products and attract foreign investment. Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, a professor at Wrocław University of Economics, noted that her appointment signals “a shift” from simple promotional activities to “managing the reputation of our great country”. The move comes as Poland seeks to capitalise on its economic success, including growth in tourism and continued investments. But the government says that current promotion efforts lack a single strategy and are fragmented. Czas na markę Polska! Witamy na pokładzie prof. Barbarę Mróz – Gorgoń 🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/PPX2eWTRSm — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 29, 2026 Last year, Poland’s sport and tourism ministry appointed Mróz-Gorgoń, who also advises companies and institutions on branding strategy and founded a think tank dedicated to promoting Poland, to an interministerial team tasked with developing a comprehensive new branding strategy for Poland. The government said, however, that efforts to promote Poland were so far fragmented and lacked a single strategy, which is why it created the post of commissioner for promotion of the Poland brand. In her new position, Mróz-Gorgoń will be tasked with preparing a strategy to build a national brand and help implement it, coordinate activities to help grow tourism, support investments, and improve Poland’s position on the world stage. “We will create one programme resulting in the joint promotion of our country’s brand,” said Tusk. According to the government, this will come at no further cost, but ensure that existing funds will be spent in a more “coherent and effective way”. Mróz-Gorgoń, meanwhile, noted that “the Poland brand is not the property of the government. It is created by entrepreneurs, artists, athletes, local governments and millions of Poles at home and abroad”. Developing this brand “means more investment, recognition of our brands and products abroad, and it also provides greater strength in international relations,” she continued. A suspected Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed in eastern Poland, around 100 km from the Ukrainian border, prompting the deployment of police counter-terrorism officers and other security services to the site. World.title: More Than Half of Czech Households Could Be Overpaying for Electricity
World.content:
A large number of Czech households may be paying more for electricity than necessary because they are using a distribution tariff that does not match their actual consumption.

A new analysis estimates that switching to a more suitable tariff could save households more than CZK 1.3 billion a year in total.

The analysis was conducted by energy company bezDodavatele.

The company examined electricity consumption at 1,132 household consumption points using the two most common household distribution tariffs, D01d and D02d.

According to data from the Energy Regulatory Office (ERÚ), D01d and D02d are used by around 65 percent of the approximately 6.5 million household consumption points in the Czech Republic.



The analysis found that changing the distribution tariff could reduce electricity costs for more than half of the households examined.

Many households never reconsider their tariff

One reason is that households often keep the same tariff for years without checking whether it still suits their electricity consumption.

A tariff that made sense when a household first connected to the electricity grid may no longer be the cheapest option after its consumption patterns have changed. Many consumers, however, do not regularly review the distribution tariff listed on their electricity bill.

According to the analysis, 53 percent of the households examined could have benefited from a different tariff. Their average potential saving was CZK 728 per year.

For some households, the difference was considerably larger, with potential savings reaching several thousand crowns annually.

Prague households show the highest potential

The analysis found differences between the country’s main electricity distribution areas.

In Prague, where electricity is distributed by PRE, changing the tariff could have been beneficial for 68 percent of the households included in the study. That was the highest proportion recorded among the three distribution zones.

In the EG.D distribution area, which covers much of southern Bohemia and Moravia as well as parts of the Vysočina, Zlín and Olomouc regions, the figure was 51.5 percent.

The lowest share was recorded in the ČEZ distribution area, where 46.3 percent of the households analyzed could potentially benefit from a different tariff.

The picture changes slightly when looking at the size of the potential savings. Although Prague had the highest proportion of households that could benefit from a tariff change, the largest average annual saving was recorded in the ČEZ Distribuce area, at CZK 833 per household.

World.title: Prague Welcomes STARLUX Airlines With New Taipei Connection
World.content:
Taiwanese carrier STARLUX Airlines has launched its first European route, connecting Taipei with Prague.

The airline’s first flight arrived at Václav Havel Airport Prague on Saturday morning after a journey of more than 14 hours. The service is initially being operated with an Airbus A350-900.

STARLUX plans to operate the Prague-Taipei route three times a week at first, with a fourth weekly service scheduled to be added from October.

For passengers traveling beyond Taiwan, the route also offers connections through Taipei to more than 25 destinations across Asia. These include cities in Japan and South Korea, as well as destinations in Southeast Asia, Hong Kong and Macau, according to Simon Liu, STARLUX Airlines’ director of strategy.

The new route makes Prague the airline’s first European destination. STARLUX launched operations only in 2020, two years after the company was founded, but has since positioned itself as a premium international carrier. Skytrax has awarded the airline a five-star rating.



A first-class cabin aimed at luxury travelers

STARLUX is introducing its Prague route with all four of its travel classes: Economy, Premium Economy, Business and First Class.

The First Class cabin has just four seats and comes with a price to match its exclusivity. Return fares can start at around $12,000, or roughly CZK 280,000, although prices vary depending on travel dates and other factors.

The experience begins before passengers reach the aircraft. First Class travelers departing from Prague can use an airport pickup service included with their ticket. In Taipei, the journey can continue with a limousine transfer from the airport to the passenger’s final destination.

Passengers also receive dedicated check-in facilities, priority airport processing and access to a private suite in the airline’s lounge.

On board, each First Class passenger has a private cabin with additional space and privacy, along with an enhanced dining and service offering.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by STARLUX Airlines (@starluxairlines)

Special AIRSORAYAMA aircraft coming to Prague

The aircraft serving Prague will also change later this year.

STARLUX plans to introduce its two specially designed AIRSORAYAMA Airbus A350-1000 aircraft on the Prague route. The planes were created in collaboration with Japanese artist Hajime Sorayama and feature metallic silver and gold liveries.

The airline has confirmed that the A350-1000 will replace the A350-900 on the Prague route from September. The two AIRSORAYAMA aircraft are scheduled to enter regular service on routes including Prague from October 1, when the airline also plans to introduce themed in-flight amenities.

The aircraft were created in partnership with Sorayama, whose work is known for its highly polished metallic representations of robots and the human form.

For Prague passengers, the arrival of the AIRSORAYAMA aircraft will add an unusual visual element to the new long-haul connection. The silver and gold A350-1000s are among STARLUX’s most distinctive aircraft and form part of the airline’s wider effort to combine aviation with contemporary design.

World.title: Inside the Mind: A Conversation with Neuropsychologist Helena Reina Calzado
World.content:
For many people, years of struggling with concentration, memory, or organisation are dismissed as personality traits or everyday stress.

It is often only when life becomes more demanding that they begin to wonder whether something else is going on.

That is where Helena Reina Calzado comes in.

A clinical psychologist and neuropsychologist based in Prague, Helena works with English- and Spanish-speaking patients, providing neuropsychological assessment and cognitive intervention for children, adolescents, and adults experiencing difficulties with attention, memory, executive functioning, and other cognitive abilities.



“Neuropsychology studies the relationship between the brain and behaviour,” Helena explains.

“We look at how someone thinks, processes information, pays attention, and solves problems, and then use that understanding to guide assessment and treatment.”

Neuropsychological assessment focuses on cognitive functioning. The process typically begins with a detailed clinical interview, followed by standardised tests tailored to the person’s specific concerns. When appropriate, neuropsychological intervention aims to improve everyday

cognitive functioning and help patients adapt to daily challenges.

One of the most common reasons people seek her help is a long history of unexplained difficulties that have never been fully understood.

“I often see adults who have spent years developing strategies to cope with attention or learning difficulties without realising there may be an underlying neurodevelopmental condition,” she says.

Conditions such as ADHD or specific learning disorders can go unnoticed well into adulthood, particularly among people who have learned to compensate for their challenges. Many continue functioning successfully until increased stress, career demands, or major life changes make those coping strategies harder to maintain.

“People often come for an assessment because something has changed,” Helena explains. “The strategies that worked for years suddenly aren’t enough, and they want to understand why.”

While awareness of mental health has grown significantly in recent years, Helena believes neuropsychology remains relatively unfamiliar to many people.

“People are much more open to talking about mental health than they were a decade ago,” she says. “But neuropsychology is still less well known. The more accurate information people have, the easier it becomes to challenge misconceptions.”

Outside the consulting room, she also finds moments of perspective in Prague. “Sometimes you forget how beautiful it is,” she says with a smile. “Then you go up to a rooftop, look around, and think, ‘Wow.'”

World.title: Martini Opens Its First Central European Terrazza in Prague
World.content:
Prague has become home to the first Martini Terrazza in Central Europe, with the Italian drinks brand opening a new rooftop venue at the Máj Národní department store.

The summer terrace is located on the Fly Vista rooftop, offering cocktails, food and views across the Prague skyline. The concept is designed around the Italian aperitivo tradition and is intended as a seasonal meeting place during the summer months.

Martini Terrazza venues have previously appeared in other European cities and holiday destinations. The Prague location brings the same format to the Czech capital, combining the brand’s drinks with music, themed evenings and social events.



The drinks menu includes several Martini-based cocktails, including Martini Bianco Spritz, Martini Fiero & Tonic and the Americano. Visitors can also order non-alcoholic Martini Spritz options, alongside a selection of food designed to accompany the drinks.

The terrace is scheduled to remain open throughout the summer season.

Martini has been associated with the Italian aperitivo tradition for more than 160 years. In the Czech Republic, the brand is distributed by Coca-Cola HBC Czech Republic and Slovakia.

“Prague has become the home of the first Martini Terrazza in Central Europe,” said Kateřina Valoušková, Martini Brand Manager at Coca-Cola HBC Czech Republic and Slovakia. She said the concept reflects Martini’s long-standing connection with the Italian aperitivo and social occasions.

World.title: World-Famous DJ Tiësto Returns to Prague on August 23
World.content:
Dutch DJ and producer Tiësto is returning to Prague on August 23, with a performance scheduled at DupleX Prague.

One of the most recognizable names in electronic music, Tiësto has been a major figure in the international dance scene for more than two decades. His Prague appearance will bring him back to the city for another night at the popular rooftop club in the centre of Prague.

The event is expected to feature a mix of Tiësto’s well-known tracks and newer material, alongside the production and atmosphere that have become a regular part of his live shows.

Tiësto, whose real name is Tijs Verwest, began his career in the Dutch club scene before becoming internationally known through his work in trance music.



Over the years, his sound has developed considerably, moving towards house, EDM and more mainstream dance music.

He has since performed at some of the world’s largest festivals and venues and worked with a wide range of artists. His music has also reached audiences well beyond the traditional electronic music scene, helping establish him as one of the genre’s most commercially successful artists.

Tickets are on sale through the official DupleX website.

New album

Tiësto is working on a new album that will see him return to his trance roots.

The Dutch DJ said he had recently “got re-inspired by trance music” and was gradually bringing the genre back into his sound. He said he hopes to finish the album soon.

The project follows “Bring Me To Life,” released last November as the first taste of what Tiësto said his 2026 album could sound like.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by D U P L E X P R A G U E (@duplexprague)

World.title: Spaniard Santi Denia Named Coach of the Czech Republic National Team
World.content:
Spanish coach Santi Denia took over the Czech Republic national team on Friday to become the first foreigner in the post.

The Czech soccer association said the 52-year-old signed a two-year contract with an option to be extended by another two years.

Czech football association head David Trunda introduced Denia at a news conference in Prague.

“We greatly appreciate that an expert with such a credit and immense experience at the international level is joining the Czech national team,” Trunda said.



“I’m happy to be here and I’m extremely motivated, because I consider it a great opportunity to lead the Czech national team,” Denia said. “Czech football has a magnificent history and I honestly regard it as a great honor to be here.”

Denia replaced Miroslav Koubek who resigned after the team’s early exit from the World Cup.

Denia was a center-back in Atletico Madrid (1994-2005) and has two games on the national team to his credit.

As coach, he led Spain to gold at the 2024 Paris Olympics. He also claimed the European titles with Spain´s under-17 (2017) and under-19 teams (2019).

He was most recently in charge of Al-Shahania, a club in Qatar.

His first major task in the post will be to face tough opponents in League A of the Nations League. The Czechs open the competition by hosting Croatia on Sept. 26 in a group which also includes England and World Cup champions Spain.

World.title: Czech PM Calls for Closing Schengen to Spain due to Migration Crisis in Ceuta
World.content:
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš called for temporarily excluding Spain from Schengen due to the migration crisis in Ceuta, where about 49,000 migrants entered uncontrollably from Morocco.

Italy has already suspended Schengen rules in connection with Spain.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš called for closing the Schengen zone to Spain after a sharp escalation of the migration crisis in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta.

According to Babiš, the situation in Ceuta is “absolutely scandalous,” and the cause of the crisis was the overly lenient migration policy of the Spanish authorities.



According to the publication, since Thursday, about 49,000 migrants have entered Ceuta uncontrollably from the territory of Morocco. At least 19 people have died trying to cross the maritime border.

Foreign Minister Petr Macinka (Motorists) described the situation as a serious challenge for the entire Schengen Area but stopped short of calling for Spain’s exclusion, saying he wanted to hear Madrid’s position before drawing conclusions.

What is the Schengen Agreement?

The Schengen Area allows people to travel between 29 European countries without routine passport checks at internal borders.

While border controls are normally abolished, member states can temporarily reinstate them if they believe there is a serious threat to public order or internal security.

Italy does not share a land border with Spain, so the decision to reintroduce border controls for a month will impact people travelling by plane or boat between the two countries.

Where is Ceuta?

Ceuta is an autonomous Spanish city on the northern coast of Africa that borders Morocco.

Spain also controls the nearby city of Melilla. Together, the two enclaves form the European Union’s only land borders with Africa.

Roughly the size of inner Sydney, Ceuta has a population of just over 83,000, according to Spain’s Instituto Nacional de Estadistica. It is home to Christian and Muslim communities, including Spanish and Moroccan residents and cross-border workers.

World.title: Prague’s Online Heat Map Shows Where to Find Water and Shade
World.content:
As another spell of extreme summer heat approaches the Czech Republic, Prague has published an online map showing where residents can cool down, find drinking water or spend time near water.

Temperatures in the capital could reach 38°C, with the hottest conditions expected toward the end of the week.

This map is designed to help people find relief across the city and includes public drinking fountains, misting systems, fountains, wells and locations suitable for swimming or relaxing beside the water.

The project was prepared by the City of Prague in cooperation with the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR Prague) and the municipal technology company Operátor ICT.



The initiative is part of the city’s broader efforts to prepare for more frequent periods of extreme heat. Prague says it is increasingly focusing on measures that can reduce the effects of rising temperatures over the longer term, rather than relying only on temporary interventions.

More trees, water and shade planned

Prague is also looking to incorporate more greenery and water into public spaces as part of new development projects.

The city is supporting measures including new fountains and other water features, green roofs, rainwater collection tanks, climbing plants, permeable surfaces and additional tree planting. The expansion of parks is also among the measures being considered.

Temperatures could approach 40°C

The current heatwave is expected to reach its peak on Friday, when temperatures could climb as high as 39°C in parts of the Czech Republic.

Friday night could also remain exceptionally warm, with overnight temperatures staying above 20°C in some areas.

A temporary change is expected on Saturday, particularly in parts of the country where showers and thunderstorms could bring some relief. The cooler conditions, however, are not expected to last.

At the beginning of next week, temperatures are forecast to rise again, with daytime highs between 32°C and 37°C.

World.title: Péter Magyar scraps Orbán’s giant office deal and demands about €1 million back from Orbán-linked businessman
World.content:
The Tisza government is scrapping the Orbán government’s 300 billion forint office deal in the Zugló district of Budapest, PM Péter Magyar said on Facebook on Monday.

Péter Magyar found irregularities concerning the Zugló office building contract

“The Tisza government is withdrawing from the purchase of the Zugló office complex and will demand the return of the more than 300 billion forints in public funds already paid by the [previous] Orbán government,” Péter Magyar said. He added that during the legal and financial review, the Hungarian National Asset Manager (MNV) found numerous breaches of contract, with nearly half of the closing conditions unmet.

The Zugló local council’s pre-emption right on the properties remained in place, even though the contract required this burden to be removed before closing. “That is why we are now withdrawing from the contract,” Magyar said. Magyar said the energy crisis clearly demonstrated the consequences of a government delaying for years investments that truly served the country’s security and the interests of its people, while spending hundreds of billions of forints “enriching business circles, relatives, and friends” close to it.

The construction of the office buildings which Péter Magyar does not intend to buy. Photo: Facebook/Hadházy Ákos

Public money should have been spent on Paks upgrade

“The safety of the Paks nuclear plant could have been significantly strengthened with a timely investment of a few tens of billions of forints. The energy crisis we now face could have been avoided,” he said. The Orbán government chose to spend 700 billion forints of public funds on “building and purchasing new, overpriced office buildings instead of investing in energy security or health care”, he said.

“A government’s true priorities are always revealed by how it spends our public money. The Tisza government chooses the security of the Hungarian people, functioning public services, and infrastructure resilient to crises and challenges.”

“The more than 300 billion forints (cca EUR 820,000) in public funds already paid by the Orbán government is enough to replace all the suburban trains, build hundreds of wind farms, or construct significant energy storage capacity,” he said. “This unnecessary multi-billion office investment was, in reality, a symbol of Fidesz governance,” he added.

“We will not move into the legacy of the Orbán system“

Magyar said the “panic-stricken” NER (system of national cooperation under the previous government) was doing “everything to hold on to the money” they had accrued during Fidesz’s time in power, and were in for a “potentially lengthy legal battle”. “We will not move into the legacy of the Orbán system. Not into the Carmelite Palace, not into the Tiborcz-circle office buildings. And we will reclaim what can be reclaimed. We will spend the Hungarian people’s money on things that truly serve the country’s security: functional hospitals, reliable railways, strong public services, and an energy system prepared for the challenges of the future.”

The Zugló office complex is a real estate development in the area behind Bosnyák Square. Originally intended as a new district centre, the mega-investment was built by the Bayer Construct Group. According to the 2021 November residential forum presentation, the Zugló City Centre was designed as a mixed-use development, including green spaces, public areas, offices, a commercial street, and residential buildings. The project was planned in four phases.

Geothermal heating of Zugló city centre could deliver fatal blow to Budapest’s thermal baths

In 2021, the government declared the Zugló City Centre project a nationally strategic investment, and six additional decrees later defined the construction rules, urban design requirements, public space development, and land use, exempting the project from local regulations.

The completed project, which has since been completed, now covers nearly 7 hectares behind Bosnyak Square. It includes seven large office buildings and the Zenit Corso shopping centre, which opened in autumn 2025. The state purchased the completed buildings for 244 billion forints to create a new government quarter.

Water-use restrictions and other extraordinary measures introduced in Hungary to avert crisis

World.title: Péter Magyar on possible stricter energy use interventions and conservation efforts
World.content:
If current energy conservation efforts can be maintained, stricter intervention will not be necessary, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Monday evening at the MAVIR electricity grid control centre after a meeting of the Defence Council.

Péter Magyar: grid load below projections

In a video posted on Facebook, he said the grid load is around 6,300MW, well below projections. Currently consumption is more than 500MW lower than forecasts prepared earlier by experts, the Hungarian news agency wrote. “We hope to maintain this advantage during the remaining critical hours today and in the coming days,” he said.

Water levels at Paks are currently stagnant, and “we are right on the edge”. In the coming hours, it will be decided whether output can be maintained at the last turbine, he said, adding it was an encouraging sign that the Danube’s water levels had stabilised in Budapest and had even risen by 1cm today.

“I am in constant contact with the leadership of the Paks nuclear plant. I receive reports even at night, and I will provide immediate updates to the country in the event of any significant change,” the prime minister said.

PM Péter Magyar and interim President Ágnes Forsthoffer. Photo: MTI

Wealthiest Hungarian’s companies remain silent

Magyar urged companies to continue energy conservation, noting however that some firms had not yet participated in voluntary efforts to reduce consumption. He mentioned the KALL Ingredients factory, which is linked to Lőrinc Mészáros’s business interests, that “received tens of billions of forints in state subsidies and favourable loans” under the former government. So far, the company has not responded to requests to voluntarily reduce its 13MW consumption, he said.

The prime minister added that forecasts suggested that Wednesday could be one of the most difficult days, as the heat may raise building and asphalt temperatures to levels that could increase energy consumption. “A lot will depend on the conscious behaviour that Hungarian companies and people have demonstrated in recent days,” Magyar said.

He urged companies to fully maintain their voluntary consumption reductions between 5pm and 10pm for the entire week and asked the public to continue monitoring their energy use during this period in the coming days.

Water-use restrictions and other extraordinary measures introduced in Hungary to avert crisis

Public should not listen to fake news

Magyar also said that authorities are continuously monitoring Danube water levels, rainfall reports in the Danube basin, and the balance of energy consumption.

The prime minister asked the public to rely only on reliable sources and not to share unfounded or false news and misinformation. He thanked Hungarian companies and people for their responsible approach.

“We will manage. Together, we will defend Hungary and emerge stronger from this difficult period,” the prime minister declared.

We are facing five make-or-break days, Péter Magyar says, as he calls for unity amid a barrage of criticism

World.title: Chaos continues at Budapest Airport? Taxi drivers incensed as airport insists there is nothing to see here
World.content:
Following the increase in taxi fares in Budapest from 1 August, passengers paying more were, by Monday morning, in no great position to arrive at the Budapest Airport on time, as everything ground to a halt. Horns blared; expletives flew.

From today, the system in the airport car park has also been overhauled, meaning it is no longer possible to drive in free of charge as many times as one likes.

Taxi drivers to pay for almost every entry

The new airport payment system went live on Monday at Liszt Ferenc International Airport, but early reports suggest it caused serious disruption, Totalcar reports. Even at dawn, taxis were queuing in long lines, and the congestion did not fully clear later on. Everyone seemed equally displeased: passengers lost time and money, drivers sat in the jam, and all the while they could even be charged for the privilege.

From 3 August, the previous five-minute free passage window has effectively disappeared for Budapest taxis. They may still enter the airport car parks free of charge once a day for five minutes, but every further entry must be paid for.

Taxi drivers could enter and leave the airport limitless before. Photo: depositphotos.com

On the first day of the change, a major tailback had already formed at daybreak. A TikTok video shared by Totalcar showed taxis lined up in a long queue, while posts on Reddit said traffic was heavy anyway because of the early low-cost flights. Owing to the congestion, many drivers even exceeded the 30-minute limit, pushing the exit fee up to 6,600 forints. The drivers thanked the airport with a chorus of horns.

One commenter said the chaos was not confined to the early hours: by midday, matters were scarcely better. Airport staff eventually lifted the barrier after a 10-minute wait and let everyone out without payment.

Drivers complain, but Budapest Airport will not bend

For taxi drivers, the chaos came at an especially sensitive moment, as Budapest taxi fares also rose from 1 August: the base fare increased to 1,300 forints, the kilometre rate to 521 forints, and the per-minute charge to 130 forints. Airport transfers also carry an 800-forint surcharge, so passengers are hardly unreasonable to expect to get there on time.

Budapest taxi fares rise from today – airport pickups also become more expensive

The Budapest Taxi Association had previously warned that the system could create chaos, and that passengers might even have to walk as far as 1,100 metres to the terminal entrance. Zoltán Metál, president of the National Taxi Association, said drivers were notified of the change only two weeks earlier, and that no prior consultation had taken place.

Budapest Airport, by contrast, insists it has not introduced a new fee, but merely ended the previous special treatment for Budapest taxis. In its view, the aim is for all passenger transport operators to use airport infrastructure on the same terms.

‘Temporary’ disruption, says airport

The airport operator said congestion is in any case common during the summer peak season, particularly at dawn and between 10am and 11am. It said Monday’s new payment system merely intensified that situation temporarily and to a minimal extent.

Serious traffic congestion today morning at Budapest Airport. Photo: PrtScr/TikTok/sargadriver

Budapest Airport says several payment methods are available, and recommends the Bónusz Card for taxi drivers, with balances deducted automatically after each entry. It also said that anyone who could prove they had incurred extra costs because of the congestion, and who reported this on the spot, had their exit fee reduced to 800 forints, while the first day’s exit charge was waived.

The airport has since indicated that it is prepared to fine-tune the system in light of experience.

World.title: Hungarian police officers save Ukrainian boy’s life on M1 motorway
World.content:
Hungarian police officers saved the life of a three-year-old Ukrainian boy who fell critically ill on the M1 motorway between Budapest and Vienna.

Parents of the Ukrainian boy appeared helpless

According to Budapest police, two officers rescued the child thanks to their swift and professional intervention.

The boy suddenly became unwell, and his family managed only to stop on the hard shoulder before getting out of the car. When the officers arrived, the child was not breathing.

The incident happened on the evening of July 30 and turned what should have been an ordinary journey into a nightmare for the Ukrainian family. The parents emerged from the car holding their son in their arms, but he showed no signs of life, his face and lips had turned blue, and they appeared helpless when Roland Agócs and Tamás Domszky arrived.

If you missed: French tourist’s life saved by lifeguards of the famous Gellért Bath in Budapest

Calm, professional response

“There was no time for questions. There was no time to hesitate,” the police said in a Facebook post.

Mr Domszky called an ambulance while Mr Agócs began life-saving measures. He performed chest compressions and several rounds of the Heimlich manoeuvre. Moments later — an age for those present — the boy began breathing again.

Paramedics took over the care of Maksym and took him to the Bókay Paediatric Clinic in Budapest.

The Budapest police expressed their gratitude to their colleagues, praising their calm, professional response, which saved the boy’s life.

Hungarian police officer saves life on his day off

World.title: The Danube-Tisza-Danube canal network may dry out causing severe crisis
World.content:
The Danube has fallen to a historic low in Serbia, triggering a severe crisis in Vojvodina’s water management system, with the Danube–Tisza–Danube canal network — crucial to the region’s water supply and agriculture — now under threat of drying up.

Danube-River Tisza channel may dry out

A state of emergency was declared last week in several towns across Vojvodina, including Sombor, Kula and Vrbas. The provincial government has set aside 270 million dinars, or about 837 million forints, for emergency measures, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

The water management system is facing one of the most serious hydrological situations of the past century, Dragan Glamočić, the agriculture, forestry and water management minister, said during a visit to the Danube pumping station at Bezdan.

He said the level of the Danube had dropped below the station’s original design threshold, making urgent action necessary.

Historic water level lows

According to the company Vode Vojvodine, the pumping station at Bezdan, which supplies water to northern Bačka, stopped operating on 29 July. The station at Gomboš (Bogojevo), which serves southern Bačka, is still able to draw water for now, but has a reserve of only about 20 centimetres, he explained. He added that operations at the pumping station in Grocka, near Belgrade, have also been temporarily suspended.

Water-use restrictions and other extraordinary measures introduced in Hungary to avert crisis

The national public health institute has warned of increased river pollution because of the exceptionally low water level, and has advised people not to eat fish from the Danube while the river remains at such a low ebb.

Severe drought in Budapest. Photo: Anadolu/Robert Nemeti

On Monday, the water level at Bezdan, near the Hungarian and Croatian borders, was measured at minus 163 centimetres, the lowest level since 1909. The previous negative record was minus 143 centimetres relative to the zero point on the gauge. Forecasts suggest the Danube could fall to minus 170 centimetres by Friday.

World.title: Water-use restrictions and other extraordinary measures introduced in Hungary to avert crisis
World.content:
Several Hungarian cities have introduced water-use restrictions today in a bid to avert potential shortages, while others have brought in emergency civil-protection and public-support measures to help residents ride out the next four to five days of historic heat. Budapest’s mayor has also spoken out, and further measures are expected across the country in the days ahead.

Water-use restrictions imposed in several Hungarian cities amid heat and energy strain

Water restrictions have been introduced in two Hungarian cities on Monday, as local authorities moved to respond to the intensifying strain on supply amid the country’s heat and energy crisis. Debrecen and Pécs have both declared first-level water restrictions. Under Hungarian law, such measures are decided not by the central government but by municipal authorities.

The restrictions ban the watering of green spaces and public areas using drinking water, hoses or sprinkling devices, as well as the filling of swimming pools. The cleaning and cooling of concrete, asphalt and decorative stone surfaces is also prohibited, along with car washing and the operation of fountains and ornamental wells. Water changes at private and public beaches, baths and wellness hotel pools must likewise be rescheduled in agreement with the water utility, according to MTI.

Taking HungaroMet’s forecast data into account, the chief medical officer has issued a third-level heat alert for the whole country until midnight on Tuesday, though the warning is expected to be extended depending on the weather outlook.

Budapest spared restrictions, but told to save water

There is currently no water shortage in Budapest, and therefore no water restriction in force, the mayor said in the capital on Monday. Gergely Karácsony added that Budapest Waterworks is still able to supply all users, though tap water will be used for watering only young trees and shrubs.

Mayor Gergely Karácsony today morning. Photo: MTI

The city introduced energy-saving measures in public transport yesterday, meaning trams and metro services are running one to two minutes longer than usual, while buses are replacing trolleybuses during certain periods. Mr Karácsony said essential public services would be maintained, including street lighting, MTI reported.

If you missed: The full damage is only visible at record-low water levels – why is the Danube still being polluted? – photos

Free bathing in one city, new wells in another

In Szolnok, municipal beaches will be free for local residents from Monday to Friday between 5pm and 8pm because of the heat, the city’s mayor announced on Facebook, following an initiative by András Cser-Palkovics, the mayor of Székesfehérvár. The free period may be extended depending on the weather, MTI said.

The Szolnok bath. Photo: Facebook/Györfi Mihály

Meanwhile, the mayor of Kaposvár announced the construction of two new water production wells on Monday in an effort to improve the security of the city’s water supply. Balázs Boda, technical director of the municipally owned Kaposvári Víz- és Csatornamű Kft. (KAVÍZ), said work would also continue on the installation of a system designed to detect burst pipes in advance. The sensors pick up leaks, allowing engineers to repair faults in good time and reduce network losses. Once the 450-sensor warning system is operational, losses are expected to fall below 10 per cent, which would mean an additional 1,000 cubic metres of water a day, mayor Károly Szita said.

Veszprém said young trees and shrubs are also being watered with high-nitrate water, which is not a problem for plants but is unfit for human consumption.

Water and energy crisis: even one of Orbán’s former strongmen admits their failure

World.title: We are facing five make-or-break days, Péter Magyar says, as he calls for unity amid a barrage of criticism
World.content:
Hungary’s prime minister, Péter Magyar, and Ágnes Forsthoffer, the speaker temporarily exercising the powers of the president, held talks with parliamentary group leaders on how to handle the energy crisis triggered by the extreme heat and the Danube’s record-low water level. In the crisis, the acting president and the prime minister said the country needs national unity, co-operation and decisions based on expertise, rather than party-political squabbling.

Péter Magyar: critical days, another heat record

Péter Magyar said the next five days could be the most critical, with another heat record potentially being broken. At present only one of the eight turbines at the Paks nuclear plant is operating, and even that is expected to last only another day or two. A full shutdown may become necessary because of the low water level of the Danube, though the prime minister stressed that nuclear safety is not in danger, that the required cooling water is available, and that no disruption to public supply is expected.

The government is preparing to bring reserve power stations online as needed, including blocks at the Litér and Mátra plants. It is also counting on voluntary consumption cuts by several hundred companies, which could save as much as 500 megawatts. If that proves insufficient, compulsory reductions in consumption or the shutdown of certain major users could also be considered.

PM Péter Magyar and Ágnes Forsthoffer. Photo: MTI

Sharp criticism and blame

The cost of the Paks shutdown is initially estimated at around 50 billion forints, but Péter Magyar said the public should not have to pay for it. In the short term, he said, alternative energy sources are needed; in the longer term, the risk of similar situations must be reduced through energy storage, wind farms and additional power-generation capacity.

The prime minister said the current situation has been caused by a historic lack of rainfall and extreme heat, and that the spread of disinformation is therefore particularly harmful. He asked opposition group leaders to help stop it. He cited the drought of 1983 as an example: some influencers claimed the country had ridden it out easily, but, according to the prime minister, Paks was barely operating at the time and, more importantly, the Danube’s water level was more than a metre higher. The group leaders also agreed on the need for a new water strategy. Péter Magyar said the crisis had also exposed the failure to complete earlier projects, such as the pumping system and Paks II, and criticised previous Orbán governments.

He added that all European rivers are struggling with low water levels, so this is not a uniquely Hungarian problem.

Péter Magyar also reiterated that nuclear safety is in no way at risk, that Paks’s engineers have the situation under control, that water for emergency cooling is available, and that there are multiple layers of redundancy. On the power plant, he said a short-term solution must be found so that if the same situation arises next year, it does not end the same way, but instead there should be B and C plans, MTI reported.

The government is not currently planning restrictions on households. No decision has yet been taken on the weekend working day, and if the weather cools from Friday, electricity demand is expected to ease, meaning intervention may not be needed.

If you missed – Water and energy crisis: even one of Orbán’s former strongmen admits their failure

Opposition voices

After the talks at the Sándor Palace, János Bóka of Fidesz said at a press conference that the prime minister had announced no concrete measures with deadlines, had made no initiative and had proposed no action. “The responsibility for governing lies solely with the Hungarian government,” he said.

Bence Rétvári said after the meeting with parliamentary group leaders, the prime minister and Ágnes Forsthoffer that they had come because the invitation spoke of national unity, which every Hungarian has a right to expect in difficult times, but Péter Magyar spent two hours doing nothing but insulting them in the language used in parliament.

László Toroczkai of Mi Hazánk said the atmosphere of the meeting was “basically peaceful”, apart from a few moments. He stressed that his party is the only political force with no responsibility for the crisis, since it has never been in government. He said Hungary must prepare for both excessively low and excessively high water levels on domestic rivers in the future. Commenting on assistance offered to Hungary by Slovak prime minister Robert Fico, he said there is still a “sea” at the Gabčíkovo waterworks, which he said raises questions.
