World.title: Sportsbet, TAB deny allegations reps offered escort and drugs to gambler
World.content:
Betting companies have denied explosive claims they offered customers access to illicit drugs and escorts to encourage continued gambling.

The allegations were aired during a Senate inquiry into the federal government's proposed gambling reforms, where Alliance for Gambling Reform chief advocate Reverend Tim Costello spoke about a young man he said received funding for travel, escorts and drugs from Sportsbet and TAB.

The man is now in prison after being charged over the alleged theft of $12.3 million.

Representing Sportsbet, Jules Norton Selzer said the company had found "zero evidence" to support the "deplorable" allegations raised by Rev Costello and said the company would "gladly" investigate the matter if further information was provided.

TAB also rejected the claims, saying the inducements described "do not in any way form part of TAB's customer offering" and that the company maintains "zero tolerance" for such behaviour.

Luke Bateman told the inquiry on Monday he was offered access to illicit drugs by a gambling company rep. (ABC News: Dave Sciasci)

Former NRL player Luke Bateman appeared before the inquiry on Monday, and said betting company representatives offered to source him illicit drugs while he was struggling with a severe gambling addiction.

Mr Bateman did not identify which companies he was referring to.

Speaking generally about allegations levelled at betting companies at the inquiry, Responsible Wagering Australia chief executive Kai Cantwell described the allegations as "egregious" but said the wagering industry "strongly refutes" the claims.

"If these claims are true, we strongly recommend complaints are levelled with the individual operators as well as law enforcement and regulators, so that clearly illegal behaviours can be properly investigated," he said.

In a fiery exchange with Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young on Tuesday, Sportsbet insisted that "most" customers gambled "responsibly and recreationally".

Senator Hanson-Young warned the company was on "very thin ice" with the Australian public.

"Your industry only gets to survive on the social licence you have," she said.

Kai Cantwell says the industry rejects the allegations levelled during the inquiry. (ABC News: Dave Sciasci)

Children appear in online gambling ad

Senator David Pocock showed the inquiry screenshots from an online ad by wagering company Bet365 which included young children dressed in branded T-shirts competing in a race.

The ad has since disappeared from Racing.com.

An ad from betting agency Bet365 which was promoted on Racing.com and has since been taken down. (Supplied: Racing.com)



He also raised an example of gambling ads playing between Disney songs on a Spotify playlist. He also raised an example of gambling ads playing between Disney songs on a Spotify playlist.

Mr Norton Selzer said it was "absolutely not" the company's intention to advertise to children, and said it had wound back its advertising on free-to-air TV to reduce exposure.

He also defended the Spotify ad, saying an adult had curated the playlist.

"This was an adult on an adult playlist," he said.

Senator Pocock accused Mr Norton Selzer of "BS", asking if the company wanted "every seven-year-old to have their own Spotify account."

Mr Cantwell said concerns about underage exposure to gambling ads were legitimate.

"I'm not going to shy away from the fact that you have presented me with children wearing gambling products," he said.

"Has the industry always got everything right? No. We are presented with cases where we may have got things wrong."

The proposed legislation does not include a total ban on s.

There are currently partial restrictions on gambling advertising, and the proposed bill would go further in stopping children's exposure to branding and promotions.

It is not illegal for gambling ads to appear in the ways described by Senator Pocock.

Julian Whealing says TAB has about 400 customers it considers VIPs. (ABC News: Dave Sciasci)

Industry claims VIPs not chosen for high spend

TAB spokesperson Julian Whealing said the company had 800,000 active customers, inlcuding about 400 they considered VIP.

He said the operator had stringent "know your customer" requirements in an effort to avoid criminals using their services.

"We do want to help our customers where we can," he said.

Neither Sportsbet nor TAB was able to say how many account managers serviced their VIP customers.

Sportsbet said it provided "tailored offers" to some customers, with Mr Norton Selzer saying those customers were selected based on "engagement" rather than betting volume.

Ex-NRL player alleges gambling staff offered drugs as he lost thousands Luke Bateman says gambling company employees unofficially offered him illicit drugs in order to cultivate a relationship with him when he was high-spend punter.

When pressed on what constituted sufficient engagement, he said it could relate to "a range of things", including customers enjoying "different products".

"It is not necessarily about volume," he said.

Mr Norton Selzer also defended Sportsbet's use of inducements, which he described as "promotions" which rewarded "customer loyalty".

"It's about trying to ultimately retain our customers," he said.

Advocates are pushing for a total ban on inducements, which was a key finding of the 2023 You Win Some, You Lose More report by late Labor MP Peta Murphy, and is not included in the proposed legislation.

Regulator can't say what a 'notable person' is

The communications watchdog also appeared before the inquiry where officials struggled to answer questions about how the legislation would be implemented if it passed parliament.

A tense exchange unfolded between Senator Hanson-Young and the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) over the bill's "notable person" provision, which is intended to regulate gambling promotion by public figures and influencers.

Senator Sarah Hanson-Young questioned the communications watchdog over its ability to regulate the proposed reforms. (ABC News: Dave Sciasci)

Senator Hanson-Young repeatedly questioned the regulator about who would fall within the definition.

A representative of ACMA said it had "not formed the precise definition" but was considering case studies.

Sportsbet was also critical of the lack of clarity, claiming that "anyone with an Instagram account" could be considered a notable person included in the current draft.

The regulator confirmed it had not received additional funding to enforce the proposed advertising regime.

Punters may turn to illegal overseas markets

Sportsbet, TAB and Responsible Wagering Australia told the inquiry they were broadly supportive of the government's changes, but warned other proposals, including a complete gambling ad ban, would accelerate the movement of punters to illegal offshore gambling streams.

Mr Norton Selzer described the proposed legislation as "substantial" and warned additional advertising bans would create "significant funding issues" for sport, racing and broadcasting while having a "disproportionate impact relative to the policy objectives of the bill".

Mr Cantwell said licensed online wagering companies already operated in one of the "most highly regulated gambling markets in the world" and contributed $6 billion in economic activity each year.

"We are not and have never been anti-reform," he said.

"70 per cent of Australians enjoy a punt, and the key question is where they gamble.

"If the regulated market becomes less visible, harder to access or less competitive, consumers don't stop gambling … the evidence proves that they will move to illegal offshore operators."

World.title: US vow to dismantle the International Criminal Court labelled 'very worrying'
World.content:
At the turn of the century, more than a hundred countries voted in favour of establishing a court that would investigate and prosecute individuals accused of the gravest international crimes.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) was established to act as a court of last resort, trying individuals charged with genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and aggression.

Back in 1998, the United States was one of seven countries that voted against its foundation.

Now, its leaders are vowing to dismantle the court "brick by brick", describing the ICC as an intolerable threat to US sovereignty.

It is a move that has drawn fierce criticism from around the world, with Amnesty International condemning the campaign as reprehensible.

While the campaign is in line with the Trump administration's America-first rhetoric, analysts say the renewed focus on fighting the ICC is predominantly for domestic politics purposes, with upcoming mid-term elections in November, and the looming spectre of a presidential race.

US says it's battling 'lunatics and crazies'

Since taking office for the second time in January 2025, US President Donald Trump has taken anti-international sentiment to the extreme, according to John Bellinger, a former adviser to the State Department during the George W Bush administration.

The US has cut funding to dozens of international organisations, permanently shuttered the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and exited the Paris Agreement, an international treaty on climate change.

These moves are "part and parcel of the same sort of anti-international sentiment" that has long been present in the Republican party, Mr Bellinger said.

"The Trump administration has simply taken it to the highest level ever," he said.

The International Criminal Court tries individuals charged with genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and aggression. (Reuters: Geert Vanden Wijngaert)

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced in mid-July that the US would wage a campaign to systematically disable the ICC's ability to function.

"We have lunatics and crazies involved in the ICC that are talking about charging members of the US military, maybe even the president or a future president," he said.

"We are not members of that; we never signed on to that treaty; they need to understand that.

"Now, they're going to see the consequences of ignoring us."

The Trump administration was unhappy about the ICC's 2024 arrest warrant issued for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other Israeli officials, and imposed sanctions on 11 ICC officials in response.



Mr Trump late last week said the fresh efforts to dismantle the ICC were not not aimed at defending himself, and that there was "no indication" the court was seeking to investigate or prosecute him.

"There's no information that they're after me. It could happen. I wouldn't be surprised," he said.

"[Rubio] is not trying to defend me. He is trying to defend Bibi [Mr Netanyahu] and various other people."

Since Mr Rubio's open declaration of war on the ICC, Venezuela and Chad have both announced plans to withdraw from the court, which is based in The Hague in the Netherlands.

Venezuela's plans to exit the court had already been in motion, according to Mr Bellinger, who is also an adjunct senior fellow in international law at the Council on Foreign Relations

"I'm sure that the US, which is essentially now running Venezuela, put pressure on the new government to finish that process," he said.

'Perplexing' declaration motivated by domestic politics

Mr Bellinger said the Secretary of State's "scorched earth campaign" was perplexing and driven by domestic political concerns, rather than any foreign policy priority.

"The ICC has not done anything to provoke the United States directly in the last six years," he said.

He said the US had been unhappy with the ICC's arrest warrants for members of the Israeli cabinet, but noted that happened nearly two years ago.

"It's really not at all clear why Secretary Rubio decided to announce right now that the US is launching a campaign to dismantle the ICC," he said.

Trump's jokes fuel Vance vs Rubio succession speculation At times, Donald Trump appears to be harking back to his days hosting reality TV show The Apprentice as he leans into speculation about who he will anoint as his successor.

Mr Bellinger said Mr Rubio's own political ambitions may be playing a large part in the decision to wage war against the ICC.

"The Secretary of State, who is obviously a potential candidate for president in 2028, is trying to bolster his credentials among conservatives in the United States," he said.

He said Mr Rubio could claim success if he manages to persuade other countries to withdraw.

"By simply announcing a campaign and taking some actions as part of that campaign, he can now point to this and say, 'Look, I have stood up to protect Americans and the United States.'"

But Mr Bellinger said he doubted the Secretary of State would have luck persuading major European nations, or countries like Australia, to withdraw.

"It's just going to cause friction between the United States and our closer Western allies."

Analysts say Marco Rubio is trying to boost his "credentials among conservatives in the United States". (Reuters: Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Record-low approval ratings for Mr Trump and the Republican Party are a major factor in the push to dismantle the ICC, according to associate professor Carrie McDougall from the University of Melbourne Law School, an expert on the ICC.

"What we've often seen in history is that when an administration, particularly one that has authoritarian tendencies, starts to get in trouble, is that it starts trying to identify external enemies," she said.

"And I think the Trump administration has said expressly that they have very little regard for international law and international institutions. So it makes [the ICC] a very obvious target as part of Trump's rhetoric."

US history with the ICC

Before Mr Trump started attacking the ICC during his first administration, the US had already had a complicated relationship with the international court.

Dr McDougall said various administrations had often criticised it publicly while providing behind-the-scenes support, but added that the complex relationship had become "increasingly hostile" under Mr Trump.

His administration imposed sanctions on the ICC prosecutor in June 2020, after an investigation into US personnel in Afghanistan was announced.

Those sanctions were lifted by then-president Joe Biden in 2021. Later that year the new ICC prosecutor Karim Khan, who has now been removed over sexual misconduct allegations, decided not to investigate US forces and the CIA for war crimes in Afghanistan.

"We can really only speculate about the reasons behind that deprioritisation," Dr McDougall said.

"It could be, as some have suggested, that it was a reflection of US pressure put on the office of the prosecutor, but I think it's very plausible that it is very difficult to investigate historic allegations when the states concerned are not cooperating."

The United States protested when the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Benjamin Netanyahu. (AP: Alex Brandon)

She said it was yet to be seen whether the US would find any traction in pressuring its allies to follow suit and reject the ICC beyond Venezuela, but added that prospect was "very worrying".

"I think it's absolutely critical that ICC state parties stand up for the court," she said.

Mr Bellinger said although the ICC was a "flawed and politicised institution", it was ultimately the only venue for seeking justice for the worst international crimes.

The Australian government has reaffirmed its commitment to the ICC.

In a statement to the ABC, a spokesperson for the Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said Australia was a longstanding supporter of the International Criminal Court.

"We respect the court's independence and the important role it plays in upholding international law," they said.

World.title: Mine's ex-bosses forced into bankruptcy over allegedly misappropriated funds
World.content:
The former chief executive and chairman of the Hellyer mine in north-west Tasmania have failed to set aside a bankruptcy ruling in the federal court.

Brad Monks and Rodger Johnston have been ordered to repay a combined $8.5 million in allegedly misappropriated funds, as well as interest, and the court has ordered their estates be sequestered.

Mr Monks and Mr Johnston both denied the allegations, but in a ruling handed down on Monday, federal judge Kylie Downes found the conduct of the two men during the drawn-out proceedings was "improper", and they had not provided enough evidence to raise a "real question of fact concerning [their] knowledge of, and possible assent to, the impugned transactions".

New owners took over the Hellyer mine in early 2024. (Google Earth)

The transactions in question took place in 2022, when Mr Monks and Mr Johnston were both directors of Hellyer subsidiary Pieman Resources.

At that time, $2.9 million was transferred from a Pieman trust account to two related entities of Mr Monks, Corporate Hustle and Wilson Street Capital.

Separately, another subsidiary, Hellyer Gold Mines (HGM), alleged Mr Monks had misappropriated a further $2.4 million by way of further payments to related entities and unauthorised credit card expenses.

New owners took over the Hellyer mine in early 2024 and commenced proceedings against Mr Monks and Mr Johnston in the federal court in July that year, claiming damages for "breaches of their statutory and fiduciary duties as directors in causing company funds to be misappropriated for their own benefit".

In January 2025, the Hellyer entities obtained bankruptcy notices for a combined $8.5 million in a court judgement that criticised the defendants' conduct as "bordering on bizarre" and apparently "deliberately delaying the proceedings".

Brad Monks declined to comment on the ruling, which may be subject of an appeal. (LinkedIn)

The bankruptcy notice against Mr Monks was for $5,474,241.86, and $3,016,025.95 for Mr Johnston.

Mr Monks and Mr Johnston subsequently sought to have those bankruptcy notices set aside and filed a series of affidavits.

They argued that Corporate Hustle and Wilson Street Capital were owed the money, and that the trust account transfers were consented to by the relevant company boards by circular resolution, and the funds were used for the benefit of the broader Hellyer group.

Justice Downes rejected those arguments on Monday, finding they lacked detail and were not supported by documentary evidence.

"The improper conduct of the respondents in the first proceeding is inconsistent with the conduct of a party that has a genuine and bona-fide defence to a claim, and was the reason that they were denied a hearing on the merits," Justice Downes wrote.

"That improper conduct continued in these proceedings."

She concluded: "I am not persuaded that sufficient reason has been shown by the respondents for questioning whether behind the judgement there is in truth and reality a debt due by each of the respondents to Pieman and HGM".

The mine resumed operations this year, recommencing shipments out of Burnie Port. (ABC News: Sandy Powell)

Mr Johnston and Mr Monks declined to comment on the ruling, which may be subject to an appeal.

Hellyer Metals was placed in liquidation earlier this year as part of a corporate restructure after the state government issued a three-week stop-work order in October 2025, over alleged compliance failures and unpaid mining royalties.

The mine's current owners, who have rebranded the mine as Celestial Pacific, have claimed the stop-work caused in excess of $50 million in financial damages.

The mine has resumed operations this year, recommencing shipments out of Burnie Port.

World.title: Bystanders deprived Canberra man of 'any chance of survival' after overdose
World.content:
An ACT coroner found a Canberra man was deprived of "any chance of survival" after bystanders from a drug harm minimisation organisation waited hours to call an ambulance following an overdose.

Coroner Ken Archer handed down his findings into the 2021 death of Felipe Esteban Alvarez, identifying broader public safety issues with the Canberra Alliance for Harm Minimisation and Advocacy's (CAHMA) peer-worker model and governance.

The inquest examined the organisation because two of its trained peer workers were present when Mr Alvarez overdosed.

Hours before help was called

Felipe Alvarez, 48, died after injecting heroin and methylamphetamine at his Taylor home in March 2021.

A group of people, including two off-duty CAHMA employees, were present when he collapsed.

The two support workers were not at the unit in an official capacity, but had been trained by the organisation to respond to opioid overdoses — including administering naloxone, which can rapidly reverse the effects of an overdose.

Coroner Ken Archer found the support workers deprived Felipe Alvarez of "any chance of survival" by not contacting emergency services sooner. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Despite showing signs of an overdose, losing consciousness and stopping breathing, an ambulance was not called for what the coroner found was "probably several hours".

Instead, those present left Mr Alvarez to "sleep it off" before Triple Zero (000) was finally called.

An autopsy revealed Mr Alvarez died from toxicity caused by a combination of methamphetamine and morphine, with an underlying heart condition contributing to his death.

Due to a non-publication order by the court, the two support workers and the other people present at the unit cannot be identified, and were not called to give evidence during the coronial process.

Mr Alvarez had moved to Canberra in 2020 hoping for a fresh start, after spending a significant time in a New South Wales jail for robbery-related offences.

The Ngunnawal and Chilean man had battled drug addiction and was a client of CAHMA at the time of his death.

In statements to the court, his sisters described him as a "beautiful complex soul" and a "gentle giant" who was trying to rebuild his life after years of trauma and incarceration.

'Morally blameworthy' conduct

In his report, the coroner found it was apparent Mr Alvarez was experiencing a medical emergency and should have received immediate medical assistance, with the group's actions depriving him of "any chance of survival" he may have had after his initial collapse.

"The conduct of the group in not calling for medical help immediately upon Mr Alvarez's initial collapse, and providing misleading information to the ACT Ambulance Service, was morally blameworthy," Mr Archer said.

" [The group's conduct] showed a chilling indifference to the possibility of a loss of a life. "

He found self-interest, including concern about possible police involvement, was likely one of the reasons an ambulance was not called sooner.

ACT Coroner Ken Archer said the inquest had raised broader public safety concerns about CAHMA's peer-worker model and governance. (ABC News: Michael Barnett)

Despite those findings, Mr Archer said he would not again refer the matter to the director of public prosecutions.

The circumstances had previously been referred to prosecutors, who decided not to lay charges, and the coroner found no fresh evidence during the inquest that warranted reconsidering that decision.

Public safety concerns

In delivering his findings, the coroner said the inquest raised broader public safety concerns about CAHMA's peer-worker model and governance.

The ACT and federal government-funded service aims to reduce the harms of drug use. It employs both former and active drug users to provide services and programs to support other users.

Mr Archer said CAHMA played an important role in reducing the harms associated with illicit drug use, but warned the model relied on "the integrity of peer and peer support workers and appropriate governance structures".

He said one of the risks was that "public monies can become an indirect support for the drug taking practices of peer workers and their clients".

Despite being trained by the organisation to respond to overdoses, and it being anticipated drug use would be taking place, neither had naloxone available when Mr Alvarez collapsed.

Mr Archer found CAHMA had also failed to properly apply its own integrity processes by not obtaining Working with Vulnerable People registrations or criminal history checks for the two workers.

Both peer workers had extensive criminal histories.

The support workers were both trained to administer naloxone to reverse the effects of an opioid overdose, but neither had any available when Felipe Alvarez collapsed. (ABC News: Antoinette Radford)

While the coroner said it was not possible to determine whether they should have been employed, he found their suitability "should have been determined on the basis of a rigorous application of established screening and eligibility tools".

The two employees were terminated shortly after Mr Alvrez's death for unrelated reasons, including poor performance.

The coroner also determined that the organisation's justifications for not conducting an internal investigation into Mr Alvrez's death was influenced "to some degree" by concerns about reputational damage.

Mr Archer found the failure to investigate exposed future clients and users of the service who interacted with those peer workers to potential risk.

He recommended the ACT and federally funded service review its overdose response training to ensure "the goal of saving life is identified as the primary goal", and strengthen collaboration with health agencies, ambulance services and police.

World.title: Inside 'Kraken's' sting that led to Sydney underworld figure's arrest
World.content:
These are the pictures that show Australian underworld figure Sam Amine's underling caught in the act of supplying a gun and more than 1 kilogram of drugs to an undercover police officer.

Amine, 39, remains wanted in Fiji over a record drug haul but is awaiting sentence in the NSW District Court after pleading guilty to brokering the supply of the drugs and firearm.

Court documents obtained as part of the case against Amine show how he organised the sale and how his nephew physically handed the gun and drugs over.

What they did not know was that they were walking into a NSW Police sting and their buyer, using the Threema handle "Kraken", was an undercover operative.

'Light but very strong'

Sam Amine told the undercover officer the MDMA on offer was "light but very strong". (Supplied: District Court of NSW)

The operation that snared Amine and his associates began with a simple message from Kraken to Amine on the encrypted app in April 2024.

A statement of facts tendered to court detailed Amine telling the undercover officer that the 500 grams of MDMA on offer was "light but very strong".

Two days later, surveillance images presented in court show Amine's nephew Nabil Allouche getting into the police officer's car outside the Greenacre McDonald's.

Nabil Allouche met police in a car park. (Supplied: NSW District Court)

Court documents state the drugs referenced by Amine were exchanged for $20,000.

When police forensically examined the drugs they found the MDMA had a purity level of 77.5 per cent.

'Any luck with the shooters?'

An image of the gun and ammuntion was tendered in court. (Supplied: NSW District Court)

By May, Kraken had another request for Amine.

"Hey brother! Any luck with the shooters?" he asked. "What exactly are you looking for? You need it loaded … 30k bro," Amine replied under the handle DK, according to court documents.

Along with the message was an image of a .45 calibre pistol.

Two days after the message, police surveillance captured the moment the undercover officer picked up the firearm in exchange for $28,000.

Surveillance image of the undercover officer collecting the gun. (Supplied: NSW District Court)

A week later, court documents state Amine brokered the sale of 986 grams of MDMA and 56 grams of cocaine to the undercover police officer.

This time police swooped on Allouche after the $48,000 exchange and Amine is arrested a short time later.

Trouble in paradise

In April the ABC's Foreign Correspondent revealed Amine is separately wanted in Fiji over an unrelated record 4-tonne methamphetamine seizure.

The country's High Court labelled him a "drug kingpin" last year as nine Fijians were given the most severe sentences ever handed down for a drug crime in the nation's history.

Amine left Fiji and four months later, in May 2024, was charged with selling drugs and a firearm to an undercover officer on a suburban Sydney street.

Vision of his arrest shows officers dressed in tactical uniform storming his waterfront Sans Souci mansion as the anti-gangs Raptor Squad arrested Amine in Ramsgate.

The NSW Crime Commission has also seized $10 million worth of his assets.

A judge called him a 'drug kingpin'. Now Fiji Police want this Australian on trial Key insiders from Fiji's largest-ever meth bust say the drug import had alarming links to organised crime in Australia.

Amine's associations with the city's gangland milieu saw him kidnapped and tortured during one bloody ordeal over several days for a $3 million ransom in 2021.

A previous bail hearing heard he had connections to the Alameddine crime family and the KVT, a Western Sydney street gang of Fijian-Australians.

Amine has pleaded guilty to supplying a large commercial quantity of drugs and supply of a firearm.

He is due to be sentenced over the drug and pistol offences in the Downing Centre District Court next week.

World.title: No supervision for man who stockpiled chemicals and fantasised about mass killings
World.content:
A young man who fantasised about bombing universities and shooting students at his old school will be freed into the community with no supervision, after a judge said he had been "punished enough" by two years in jail.

The man, who pleaded guilty to two explosives possession charges, stored a cache of chemicals in his home and created a manifesto where he discussed taking "revenge" on former classmates, police alleged.

Today, a psychiatrist said the man spent a lot of time "living in a fantasy world" and that his fixation on chemistry was "not going to go away".

Soon after, County Court Judge Douglas Trapnell convicted the now-21-year-old and discharged him entirely.

It means he will be able to return home to live with his parents and will not be subjected to further supervision or reporting conditions.

County Court Judge Douglas Trapnell convicted the now-21-year-old Melbourne man this week and discharged him entirely. ( ABC News: Danielle Bonica )

Due to an ongoing suppression order granted on mental health grounds, the ABC is unable to reveal the Melbourne man's name, suburb or the institutions he planned on targeting.

The man has been in custody since 2024, when he was denied bail by a local magistrate.

Today, the judge accused prosecutors of "dithering around" with the case after the man offered to plead guilty last year.

He has spent 677 days in custody, a period the judge considered too long for the offences he was charged with.

"He's been punished enough," Judge Trapnell said.

" I don't want him there for another minute. "

The judge rejected calls from prosecutor Jordan O'Toole for a sentence that included compulsory therapeutic treatment for the man.

"This young man with no prior convictions who has been languishing in [protective custody] for 677 days and you stand there wanting me to give him something more, well it's not happening," the judge said.

Psychologist Michael Davis said the man had autism spectrum disorder and Schizotypal personality disorder, conditions that affected his ability to have empathy and socialise with others.

He said the man had "a degree of grandiosity" and was attracted to far-left and far-right ideologies.

"As long as it's extreme, he's drawn to it," Mr Davis said.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) found disturbing posts the man made online and alerted Australian police in 2024.

"Senior Class of 2023 … they don't know that they're all gonna die for bullying me and ignoring me. This is the day when I finally take revenge," one post read.

During two police raids of the man's house, officers found precursor explosives chemicals, some of which were purchased on eBay and Etsy.

Other items located included chemistry glassware, a tactical military vest, hundreds of rounds of ammunition, walkie-talkies, electronic shock collars and coded, handwritten notes.

According to 2024 court documents, the notes included plans to "commit several bombings at a university", derail a train and poison members of the public.

Judge Trapnell said he was powerless to revoke the suppression order over the man's name, first granted by Magistrate Luisa Bazzani in 2024, because of the way the order had been worded.

It would fall to the media or other parties to go back to her court to request a review of the order, he said.

World.title: Labor to tip another $950 million into new Mandurah Hospital
World.content:
NationalWAHospitals Labor to tip another $950 million into new Mandurah Hospital Michael Philipps August 4, 2026 — 4:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

West Australian Health Infrastructure Minister John Carey claims there “is always capacity in the budget for health” as construction officially begins on the new Mandurah Hospital site. The latest announcement for the hospital is set to see the government spend a further $950 million on the site, in addition to around $150 million already committed on water and electricity infrastructure. Health Infrastructure Minister John Carey. Holly Thompson The health infrastructure spend also coincides with the pledge of $1 million allocated to a master plan for the future of the Rockingham General Hospital. “Never before have you seen so many hospital projects under way,” Carey said on Tuesday.



“This is a massive construction program. A new women’s and babies’ hospital, the new Royal Perth Hospital build, this build, Bunbury, a number of regional projects. “We have never seen this type of hospital construction in the state’s history.” However, asked if it was a coincidence that the dual health infrastructure announcements, in areas that flanked the Secret Harbour electorate, coincided with an upcoming byelection, Carey said the government couldn’t win. “Whoopee doodah – we’ve got to build hospitals,” he said. “Can we get real here? You can’t win.



“The message we receive is to invest in hospital infrastructure. “So, by George, that’s what we are doing and it is a massive program. You have never seen it before.” Carey said he expected the build of the Mandurah Hospital site to be completed by early 2029, and made no apologies about the “record” investment. “This is the cost. We have an office that is very thorough in the procurement process,” he said. “We go way beyond to get value for taxpayers, but I do believe that no one is going to complain because we are undertaking a record investment to build a new Mandurah Hospital.”



Tree breaks silence after not making a sound in weekend media events Meanwhile, Labor’s candidate for the seat of Secret Harbour, Georgia Tree, has fronted journalists after the party faced criticism for not allowing her to speak at a series of recent media events. Addressing the press pack at Mandurah Hospital announcement, Tree said she had answered more questions than any other candidate in the by-election. Asked why she had not spoken at the announcement of funding for the Karnup train station, Tree repeated the premier’s words that a tight schedule had prevented her from addressing media. “We had to get to Lark Hill because we were announcing $3 million in flood lighting, so little kids can train at night, and we had to get there for the community groups and sporting groups that were there,” she said.



“I then had a field rally where over 100 volunteers came out to support me and go out door knocking in Singleton that afternoon. Related Article WA election WA’s attorney-general and transport minister spoke at Secret Harbour media events. But Labor’s candidate didn’t “So it was a packed schedule.” Tree added that throughout her door-knocking campaign within the electorate, the topic of the Karnup station was a key focus for voters. “It’s something I’ve been fighting for all the way along this campaign and feeding back community feedback to the government,” she said.



“And I’m so glad that they’ve brought the announcement forward, so I can campaign on it, so voters know what they’re getting when they go to the polls on the 29th of August. “The main thing for me is that Karnup’s getting built.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: NBL star Xavier Cooks serves month-long ban for positive drug test
World.content:
Breaking SportBasketballNBL NBL star Xavier Cooks serves month-long ban for positive drug test Jon Pierik August 4, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney Kings championship forward Xavier Cooks has apologised to teammates and supporters after serving a one-month suspension for a positive test to cannabis. The Kings revealed on Tuesday that Cooks, 30, and one of the league’s highest-paid players, had been banned by Basketball Australia after an in-competition doping control test detected the metabolite of Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the main psychoactive compound of cannabis. “I want to sincerely apologise to my teammates, our fans, the club, and everyone who has supported me. I take full responsibility for my actions and understand the disappointment and frustration this has caused,” Cooks, a three-time NBL champion and Australian Boomer, said. Served his ban: Sydney Kings star Xavier Cooks was suspended for a second time. Getty Images “I am grateful to [Kings owners] Hoops Capital for the support they have continued to provide me throughout this process.”



Related Article Drugs in sport NBL star Xavier Cooks tested positive to cocaine Cooks’ ban expired on July 4. The Kings told this masthead Cooks, a former NBL most valuable player and one of the league’s most athletic stars, was tested after a game last season. Hoops Capital chief executive Mark Thompson said Cooks would be given the wellbeing and educational support he needed. “We acknowledge and respect the outcome of the Basketball Australia and Sport Integrity Australia process,” Thompson said. “We hold ourselves to strong professional standards. When those standards are not met, we respond appropriately and work to ensure our people receive the support, education and guidance they need – not only through the successes but also the challenges that come with professional sport.



“Xavier has completed his period of ineligibility and is back on court with his teammates as pre-season commences. Our focus is now on supporting him and the team as we prepare for the upcoming season.” Sport Integrity Australia did not wish to comment when contacted by this masthead. Basketball Australia confirmed the ban but did not wish to comment further. The Kings would not divulge if Cooks faced further punishment from the club. Happy days: Xavier Cooks and teammate Makuach Maluach celebrate the Kings’ championship series win over the Adelaide 36ers this year. Getty Images It is the second time Cooks has been suspended for taking an illegal substance. In February 2025, Cooks received an immediate provisional suspension from BA and the NBL after returning an adverse analytical finding for cocaine, an out-of-competition illicit substance. He served a one-month ban from February 7 to March 7, 2025, missing the Kings’ play-off run.



Cooks has represented Australia at FIBA tournaments, and logged NBA 10 games for the Washington Wizards in the 2022-23 season. View post on X The Kings begin their NBL championship defence against the Cairns Taipans on September 20. Sports news, results and expert commentary.

Day two of former 2GB broadcaster Alan Jones’ lengthy indecent assault and sexual touching trial has concluded in the NSW Local Court.

Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, commenced her cross-examination of the first witness in the trial, complainant “J”, this afternoon. He will return to the witness box on Wednesday morning.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Sam Mooy

“J”, a former teen athlete, spent from 10am to 4pm in the witness box today after starting his evidence on Monday afternoon.

“J” gave evidence about one occasion when he stayed at Jones’ Southern Highlands property and said the broadcaster told him to wear a robe “and nothing else” before indecently assaulting him.

Jones vehemently denies the allegations.

Court will resume at 10am tomorrow.

World.title: BoM orders independent review after $96m website backlash
World.content:
PoliticsFederalExtreme weather BoM orders independent review after $96m website backlash Rob Harris August 4, 2026 — 4:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Bureau of Meteorology has ordered an independent review of its operations after a turbulent period that included the botched rollout of its $96 million website upgrade and mounting scrutiny over whether the agency is meeting the needs of Australians. The review, commissioned by bureau chief executive Stuart Minchin in consultation with Environment Minister Murray Watt, will examine everything from the agency’s public communications and customer service to its reputation, strategic direction and whether its services are keeping pace with the changing needs of the public. Bureau of Meteorology chief executive Stuart Minchin. Alex Ellinghausen It follows one of the organisation’s most difficult periods in recent years after last year’s website overhaul sparked widespread anger from farmers, emergency service volunteers, mariners and weather enthusiasts who struggled to access forecasts during severe weather. The bureau was eventually forced to make changes after the backlash, while chief customer officer and former acting chief executive Dr Peter Stone – who oversaw the customer experience during the rollout – has since retired.



Former Murray-Darling Basin Authority chief executive Phillip Glyde will lead the inquiry, with the panel reporting back by March next year as the bureau prepares its next long-term strategy. Related Article Meteorology Weather bureau executive quits months after $96m website bungle The review will assess whether the bureau’s services match the needs of Australians, how effectively it communicates with the public, whether it is maintaining public trust and where it faces growing competition or unmet demand. Watt said the review would provide an outside assessment of one of the country’s most relied-upon public agencies. He said the work the organisation did every day was “complex” and staff faced a range of pressures, adding the review would bring an independent perspective to understanding the services being delivered and how that value could be strengthened.



“BoM’s role in keeping Australia safe, informed and prepared in a changing climate has never been more vital,” he said. “Maintaining trust in, and ensuring the effectiveness of, BoM’s information and services is essential.” “Many Australians rely on BoM to make decisions on farm, at work and in severe weather, and I know we’re all committed to ensuring that future services meet people’s needs and expectations.” Related Article Meteorology BOM restores old rain radar after widespread backlash of ‘flawed’ website The organisation has faced previous criticism over its public image. In 2022, amid devastating floods across NSW and Victoria, it announced it wanted to be referred to as “the Bureau” rather than “BoM”. Then environment minister Tanya Plibersek dismissed the move as “ridiculous”, saying Australians cared about timely weather warnings rather than a $220,000 rebrand during a natural disaster. Minchin said the review was intended to shape the bureau’s next decade.



“The development of our next strategy is a significant opportunity to take a fresh look at what matters most to the Australian community and to ensure we are well positioned to meet future challenges and opportunities,” adding he “deeply valued” the public trust placed in the organisation. “This review will help the Bureau of Meteorology better understand current and future customer needs and ensure our strategy and services are squarely focused on the things that are important to the Australian community, our customers and partners.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Stark testimony highlights weakness of government’s gambling reforms
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGambling Editorial Stark testimony highlights weakness of government’s gambling reforms The Herald's View Editorial August 4, 2026 — 4:19pm

August 4, 2026 — 4:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Allegations that betting companies routinely use drugs, escorts and bonus bets to woo gambling addicts are an embarrassing counterpoint to the Albanese government’s dogged refusal to outlaw inducements in its tepid attempt at gambling law reform. The government is refusing to bend despite the landmark report by the parliamentary committee headed by late Labor MHR Peta Murphy in 2023 that recommended full prohibition of betting inducements, a gambling advertising blackout and a national regulator. Gambling reform advocates say the government’s legislation is inadequate. Jason South Instead, Labor’s reforms will include fewer gambling ads across various media, including none during television broadcasts, a ban on “pocket pokies” and improved financial counselling. The latest allegations came to light when Luke Bateman, a former Canberra Raiders player turned TikTok influencer, told a Senate inquiry he was flown interstate for race days by betting companies, where he was plied with alcohol and offered his choice of drugs. He also said he would steal from his mother, partner and siblings to feed his gambling addiction.



Related Article Exclusive

Gambling Labor’s millions in gambling donations revealed amid last-ditch push for reform Bateman did not identify the betting company. He had already told part of his story to this masthead’s Good Weekend magazine. On Monday, he was joined by gambling reform advocates to highlight what they regard as the inadequacies of the government’s reform legislation. Alliance for Gambling Reform chief Tim Costello said the legislation had some good aspects, but it was line ball if it was better than the status quo. He spoke of a man who stole $12.3 million from his company. “He was the TAB’s biggest customer in that time. They were giving him $50,000 bonus bets,” Costello said. “He was also Sportsbet’s biggest customer. They were flying him to grand finals. They were offering him escorts, drugs, whatever he wanted. He was doing turnover of more than $20 million a month.” Gambling industry representatives have rejected the claims.



Sportsbet’s Jules Norton Selzer just told the inquiry on Tuesday: “I also want to make it very clear that we have zero evidence of the allegations made by Reverend Costello yesterday. We have no tolerance for that kind of deplorable conduct and information, and no information has been provided to us beyond what was referenced yesterday, and we would gladly investigate it.” Related Article Gambling ‘Pretty egregious claims’: Betting companies deny wooing clients with drugs, escorts Tabcorp’s head of government affairs, Julian Whealing, said: “Tabcorp has zero tolerance for this behaviour. We are Australia’s most regulated wagering company and we take our responsibilities to compliance seriously.” Kai Cantwell, who represents the peak body Responsible Wagering Australia, disputed the “pretty egregious claims” and said if they were true, complainants should contact operators and authorities. But there is no denying that the personal stories of addicts and their perception of how their weaknesses were preyed upon have been heard for years in various royal commissions and government inquiries conducted into the impact of gambling on Australian lives.



Their lived experiences have mostly been ignored. The Senate evidence captures the tragic vulnerability of addicts and should fuel a growing consensus across the political spectrum to force the Albanese government to toughen its milksop gambling reforms. World.title: The fancy dress work party that sparked a massive police response
World.content:
It was a Monday afternoon in Sydney, when the people who keep the city’s nightlife going through the weekend typically find time to have a little fun themselves. Jacopo Mastrocinque and colleagues at the Italian restaurant he manages were dressed up to go bowling. The theme? Heroes v villains. Arriving at Strike Bowling in the Entertainment Quarter about 1.45pm, Mastrocinque was seen on CCTV leaving about 2.20pm. It’s not clear when or whether he returned. By 4.45pm, the 35-year-old was seen smoking a cigarette outside a nearby Oporto restaurant, concerning onlookers enough that they had to call police. Loading While other guests at the party came as ghosts, superheroes and Pokémon, Mastrocinque’s “hero” outfit – purchased from a Mascot costume shop – included a ballistic vest bearing the American flag, a fake badge, plastic handcuffs and a replica firearm. “We saw a gun on his chest, but we were like, is he wearing a costume, is it real?” one onlooker told news crews at the scene.



“It was terrifying.” According to the solicitor who represented Mastrocinque in court on Tuesday, his client was at a loss to understand what happened next, and had been reduced to tears as he recounted the story. Jacopo Mastrocinque took a break from a “heroes v villians” costume party to smoke a cigarette before he was arrested in a large-scale police operation. Nine News “He went outside for a cigarette, had [a] pistol pointed [at him] by police, has been arrested and is in custody overnight,” solicitor Cassy Giudice told the court on Tuesday. General duties and specialist officers – their ballistic vests bearing NSW Police insignias rather than American flags, and their guns real – swarmed the precinct. Police vehicles, marked and unmarked, sped down Driver Avenue. Mastrocinque and his 39-year-old roommate were taken into custody.



Wearing the army-style jacket he was arrested in, Mastrocinque told the court that he was at a “staff party from the restaurant that I work with”. “You can ask everyone who was there,” he said as his hearing was adjourned. “My manager, my general manager, you can ask them.” Mastrocinque, 35, is a restaurant manager with a long career in Sydney’s dining scene. Facebook The police prosecutor told the court that Mastrocinque had chosen to dress as a “hero” for the costume party. A man told officers on the scene that the man they had just arrested was attending the event, the prosecutor informed the court. Barrister Wali Shukoor appeared for Mastrocinque on Tuesday afternoon, conceding that his client made a “very poor and foolish decision to attend the event the way he did”, but arguing that his otherwise perfect record supported his release.



Judge Daniel Covington granted Mastrocinque bail on the condition that he move to his partner’s North Ryde address, avoid the Entertainment Quarter and surrender his passport. His matter will next be heard on August 18 at the Downing Centre. Jacopo Mastrocinque was arrested at Sydney’s Entertainment Quarter after a massive police operation. NSW Police The swift response, including specialist officers, did not occur in a vacuum. Just months on from the worst terrorist attack in Australia’s history, a few kilometres away at Bondi Beach, onlookers were “genuinely concerned and alarmed” by the sight of a man walking around with a firearm in a public place, NSW Police Detective Superintendent Peter Glynn said. “It’s a timely reminder regarding the heightened concerns the community have about public safety,” Glynn said on Tuesday afternoon.



“Any calls to police regarding threats to public safety will be taken very seriously. Mastrocinque allegedly wore a ballistic vest with the US flag on the front, and carried a police badge and plastic handcuffs. A cardboard box marked “hard drugs” was also seized. NSW Police “People need to be mindful about how they dress and they act and they behave in public, particularly if they’re carrying firearms or imitation firearms ... that could be seen as genuine.” Mastrocinque’s seized costume also included a more DIY accessory – a cardboard box marked “hard drugs”. Arrested alongside him, Mastrocinque’s roommate was charged with drug possession after he was searched at Surry Hills police station. He is due to face court on August 20.



Mastrocinque has worked in the Sydney hospitality scene since arriving in Australia in 2014. The permanent resident managed the Bel & Brio Italian restaurant in Barangaroo before its 2022 closure, co-founded catering business The Italian Fellas, and now operates a pizza shop. He was interviewed by the Herald in November 2021 about the challenges of returning to business at Bel & Brio after the COVID lockdowns, when he said a “lazy mindset” from hospitality workers had dampened the success of the venue’s reopening. Mastrocinque at Bel & Brio in October 2021. Edwina Pickles Mastrocinque also appeared in a 2024 documentary titled Covid Safe Domestic Violence by the State in which “owners of small Sydney businesses explain how they had their livelihoods stripped away from them” during the lockdowns, according to IMDb. He was credited as a small business manager in the film. Be the first to know when major news happens.

Addressing the press pack at Mandurah Hospital announcement, Tree said she had answered more questions than any other candidate in the by-election. Asked why she had not spoken at the announcement of funding for the Karnup train station, Tree repeated the premier’s words that a tight schedule had prevented her from addressing media. “We had to get to Lark Hill because we were announcing $3 million in flood lighting, so little kids can train at night, and we had to get there for the community groups and sporting groups that were there,” she said.



“I then had a field rally where over 100 volunteers came out to support me and go out door knocking in Singleton that afternoon. Related Article WA election WA’s attorney-general and transport minister spoke at Secret Harbour media events. But Labor’s candidate didn’t “So it was a packed schedule.” Tree added that throughout her door-knocking campaign within the electorate, the topic of the Karnup station was a key focus for voters. “It’s something I’ve been fighting for all the way along this campaign and feeding back community feedback to the government,” she said.



“And I’m so glad that they’ve brought the announcement forward, so I can campaign on it, so voters know what they’re getting when they go to the polls on the 29th of August. “The main thing for me is that Karnup’s getting built.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: NBL star Xavier Cooks serves month-long ban for positive drug test
World.content:
Breaking SportBasketballNBL NBL star Xavier Cooks serves month-long ban for positive drug test Jon Pierik August 4, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney Kings championship forward Xavier Cooks has apologised to teammates and supporters after serving a one-month suspension for a positive test to cannabis. The Kings revealed on Tuesday that Cooks, 30, and one of the league’s highest-paid players, had been banned by Basketball Australia after an in-competition doping control test detected the metabolite of Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the main psychoactive compound of cannabis. “I want to sincerely apologise to my teammates, our fans, the club, and everyone who has supported me. I take full responsibility for my actions and understand the disappointment and frustration this has caused,” Cooks, a three-time NBL champion and Australian Boomer, said. Served his ban: Sydney Kings star Xavier Cooks was suspended for a second time. Getty Images “I am grateful to [Kings owners] Hoops Capital for the support they have continued to provide me throughout this process.”



Related Article Drugs in sport NBL star Xavier Cooks tested positive to cocaine Cooks’ ban expired on July 4. The Kings told this masthead Cooks, a former NBL most valuable player and one of the league’s most athletic stars, was tested after a game last season. Hoops Capital chief executive Mark Thompson said Cooks would be given the wellbeing and educational support he needed. “We acknowledge and respect the outcome of the Basketball Australia and Sport Integrity Australia process,” Thompson said. “We hold ourselves to strong professional standards. When those standards are not met, we respond appropriately and work to ensure our people receive the support, education and guidance they need – not only through the successes but also the challenges that come with professional sport.



“Xavier has completed his period of ineligibility and is back on court with his teammates as pre-season commences. Our focus is now on supporting him and the team as we prepare for the upcoming season.” Sport Integrity Australia did not wish to comment when contacted by this masthead. Basketball Australia confirmed the ban but did not wish to comment further. The Kings would not divulge if Cooks faced further punishment from the club. Happy days: Xavier Cooks and teammate Makuach Maluach celebrate the Kings’ championship series win over the Adelaide 36ers this year. Getty Images It is the second time Cooks has been suspended for taking an illegal substance. In February 2025, Cooks received an immediate provisional suspension from BA and the NBL after returning an adverse analytical finding for cocaine, an out-of-competition illicit substance. He served a one-month ban from February 7 to March 7, 2025, missing the Kings’ play-off run.



Cooks has represented Australia at FIBA tournaments, and logged NBA 10 games for the Washington Wizards in the 2022-23 season. View post on X The Kings begin their NBL championship defence against the Cairns Taipans on September 20. Sports news, results and expert commentary.

Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, commenced her cross-examination of the first witness in the trial, complainant “J”, this afternoon. He will return to the witness box on Wednesday morning.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Sam Mooy

“J”, a former teen athlete, spent from 10am to 4pm in the witness box today after starting his evidence on Monday afternoon.

During his cross-examination, “J” was asked repeatedly by Bashir if he read news articles in 2023 detailing similar allegations about Jones before he made his own report to police after the former broadcaster’s arrest in November 2024. He said he did not.

Jones vehemently denies the allegations.

World.title: A special announcement about Melbourne’s future
World.content:
NationalVictoriaNote From The Editor A special announcement about Melbourne’s future Patrick Elligett August 4, 2026 — 4:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“It was a glorious farce.” That was how advertising executive and social commentator Phillip Adams once described a 1978 public competition aiming to transform Melbourne’s most prominent eyesore into a landmark worthy of the place it occupied at the gateway to Melbourne’s CBD. Adams was one of eight judges attempting to find a defining public monument to satisfy the vision of then premier Rupert Hamer, who wanted to replace the Gas and Fuel Corporation Towers opposite Flinders Street Station with something more befitting a city on the rise. Rupert Hamer wanted Melbourne’s answer to the Opera House. What we got was something far less ostentatious but more suitable: Federation Square. Photograph by Chris Hopkins He and his fellow judges pored over a flood of entries that could be variously described as bold, courageous, absurd and offensive. As journalists Jewel Topsfield and Royce Millar wrote in this excellent 2023 series, the competition failed to identify a standout entry and no winner was declared.



The Age hosted the competition and published the many suggestions put forward. While it didn’t identify a winning idea, it succeeded in prompting a wave of debate in its black-and-white pages. That conversation spilled out into the city’s offices, shopfronts and kitchen tables, as Victorians considered the best use for the site now acknowledged as the beating heart of a healthy metropolis. The result of that conversation was the creation of the meeting place we now call Federation Square, and the modernisation of the nearby spaces along the Yarra River that hug the back of the world-renowned Flinders Street Station. When The Age is at its best, it is leading the conversation about the future of the city, with the input of the people whose lives it will change. Hamer wanted a world-class monument, Melbourne’s answer to the Opera House. What we received − eventually − was something far less ostentatious than most competition entries promised, but far more suitable for this great city of congregation. We received a meeting place − a fitting tribute to a state that is both “going places” and whose citizens like to go places: a footy game, a concert, a lecture, a meal, a play or an exhibition. Fed Square gave us another place to bring Melburnians together. The key ingredient in the Federation Square recipe was that other great Melbourne pastime: spirited public debate. It is with those two great Melbourne traditions top of mind that I announce today the launch of an exciting new initiative from The Age: Melbourne Assembly. A forum bringing together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. To be held from October 19-21, it will, fittingly, take place at The Edge in Federation Square − a nod to Melbourne’s lust for progress.



The Assembly will bring together globally renowned city-shapers and Melbourne’s leading thinkers to tackle four topics crucial to our future: shaping the city, education and innovation, healthy places and people, and how to make the most of our status as the nation’s leading city for sport and the arts. Former New York mayor Bill de Blasio will be one of the headline speakers at Melbourne Assembly. Bloomberg Melbourne Assembly is being presented in partnership with the University of Melbourne which, like The Age, recognises the value in honest public conversations that help lay the groundwork for progress. Thanks to their support, we have been able to secure two leading international experts on cities as the headline speakers for this event. Carlos Moreno, pioneer of the 15-Minute City concept adopted by governments around the world, will provide his unique insights on Melbourne and its future direction as part of the event. Moreno will be joined by Bill de Blasio, former mayor of New York City, whose legacy includes meaningful action to address affordable housing and homelessness, reform of the justice system and early childhood education.



Keep an eye on The Age this week for more on De Blasio and Moreno’s conversation-starting thoughts on Melbourne’s future. As we count down to the Assembly in October, The Age will take an in-depth look at each of the forum’s four topics to consider their role in our city’s evolution. Related Article City life 350 parking spots to vanish from Chapel Street in one fell swoop Moreno and De Blasio will be joined by leading thinkers from Melbourne and around Australia, who we will announce in the coming weeks. As an Age subscriber, you have early access to tickets to this event at a substantial discount, before they go on sale to the general public next week. Click on this link to see the offers available for various parts of the Assembly or enter the code ‘EditorNote’ to apply the subscriber discount. Further information will become available at the Melbourne Assembly website. Stay tuned for updates. As was the case in the late ’70s, our city is on the cusp of profound change. We are set to become Australia’s largest city (by some measures, we already are) and a metropolis the size of present-day London by the 2050s. The questions of how we get there, and indeed whether that is where we want to go, have largely been held behind closed doors by a small group of powerful people. It is time to recapture the public conversation and invite Melburnians to help chart the course of their city.



In the shadow of a November state election, Victorians are being asked to consider two distinct visions for the kind of city and state we want. As de Blasio told The Age today, that conversation is too precious to be left to governments alone. It requires the participation of a new generation of civic leadership across Melbourne’s business, education and cultural sectors. It needs a generation of leaders and thinkers to step forward and participate in the discussion about the kind of city we want Melbourne to be − not just the one we’re told we should be. Related Article City life Anger over push to turn one of Australia’s oldest orphanages into apartments It is not just The Age and the University of Melbourne who share that vision and believe in the value of facilitating discussion and debate. Other local institutions have come on board to back this important event. Health insurer Bupa and Melbourne’s leading sport and entertainment precinct, Melbourne Park, share the desire to recapture the public conversation about Melbourne’s successes and opportunities. Leaders at both organisations have demonstrated their commitment to that mission and I’m grateful for their support in this endeavour as major partners. Our supporting partners, Right Angle, City of Melbourne and the Committee for Melbourne, have also embraced this mission and have been instrumental in preparing the Melbourne Assembly. Thanks also to Future Events Lab, The Langham and MapCo for partnering with The Age to help host this essential conversation.



As was the case in the late ’70s, when Melbourne was on the cusp of a new wave of growth and change, it is time to draft its next chapter through stimulating conversation and robust debate. Leadership is required to make that happen. Leadership from The Age, its partners and, crucially, our readers and subscribers. When Topsfield and Millar wrote their article in 2023 to mark Federation Square’s 21st birthday, they asked The Age’s former editor-in-chief Ranald Macdonald why he chose to involve the publication in the 1978 competition. “We thought The Age should be a centre for ideas,” he said. “The concept was to see if there was any great idea that Melbourne could embrace.” Macdonald was right then. And in 2026, the situation is no different. When The Age is at its best, it is leading the conversation about the future of the city, with the input of the people whose lives it will change. That’s what we hope to achieve in October.

World.title: BoM orders independent review after $96m website backlash
World.content:
PoliticsFederalExtreme weather BoM orders independent review after $96m website backlash Rob Harris August 4, 2026 — 4:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Bureau of Meteorology has ordered an independent review of its operations after a turbulent period that included the botched rollout of its $96 million website upgrade and mounting scrutiny over whether the agency is meeting the needs of Australians. The review, commissioned by bureau chief executive Stuart Minchin in consultation with Environment Minister Murray Watt, will examine everything from the agency’s public communications and customer service to its reputation, strategic direction and whether its services are keeping pace with the changing needs of the public. Bureau of Meteorology chief executive Stuart Minchin. Alex Ellinghausen It follows one of the organisation’s most difficult periods in recent years after last year’s website overhaul sparked widespread anger from farmers, emergency service volunteers, mariners and weather enthusiasts who struggled to access forecasts during severe weather. The bureau was eventually forced to make changes after the backlash, while chief customer officer and former acting chief executive Dr Peter Stone – who oversaw the customer experience during the rollout – has since retired.



Former Murray-Darling Basin Authority chief executive Phillip Glyde will lead the inquiry, with the panel reporting back by March next year as the bureau prepares its next long-term strategy. Related Article Meteorology Weather bureau executive quits months after $96m website bungle The review will assess whether the bureau’s services match the needs of Australians, how effectively it communicates with the public, whether it is maintaining public trust and where it faces growing competition or unmet demand. Watt said the review would provide an outside assessment of one of the country’s most relied-upon public agencies. He said the work the organisation did every day was “complex” and staff faced a range of pressures, adding the review would bring an independent perspective to understanding the services being delivered and how that value could be strengthened.



“BoM’s role in keeping Australia safe, informed and prepared in a changing climate has never been more vital,” he said. “Maintaining trust in, and ensuring the effectiveness of, BoM’s information and services is essential.” “Many Australians rely on BoM to make decisions on farm, at work and in severe weather, and I know we’re all committed to ensuring that future services meet people’s needs and expectations.” Related Article Meteorology BOM restores old rain radar after widespread backlash of ‘flawed’ website The organisation has faced previous criticism over its public image. In 2022, amid devastating floods across NSW and Victoria, it announced it wanted to be referred to as “the Bureau” rather than “BoM”. Then environment minister Tanya Plibersek dismissed the move as “ridiculous”, saying Australians cared about timely weather warnings rather than a $220,000 rebrand during a natural disaster. Minchin said the review was intended to shape the bureau’s next decade.



“The development of our next strategy is a significant opportunity to take a fresh look at what matters most to the Australian community and to ensure we are well positioned to meet future challenges and opportunities,” adding he “deeply valued” the public trust placed in the organisation. “This review will help the Bureau of Meteorology better understand current and future customer needs and ensure our strategy and services are squarely focused on the things that are important to the Australian community, our customers and partners.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: The fancy dress work party that sparked a massive police response
World.content:
It was a Monday afternoon in Sydney, when the people who keep the city’s nightlife going through the weekend typically find time to have a little fun themselves. Jacopo Mastrocinque and colleagues at the Italian restaurant he manages were dressed up to go bowling. The theme? Heroes v villains. Arriving at Strike Bowling in the Entertainment Quarter about 1.45pm, Mastrocinque was seen on CCTV leaving about 2.20pm. It’s not clear when or whether he returned. By 4.45pm, the 35-year-old was seen smoking a cigarette outside a nearby Oporto restaurant, concerning onlookers enough that they had to call police. Loading While other guests at the party came as ghosts, superheroes and Pokémon, Mastrocinque’s “hero” outfit – purchased from a Mascot costume shop – included a ballistic vest bearing the American flag, a fake badge, plastic handcuffs and a replica firearm. “We saw a gun on his chest, but we were like, is he wearing a costume, is it real?” one onlooker told news crews at the scene.



“It was terrifying.” According to the solicitor who represented Mastrocinque in court on Tuesday, his client was at a loss to understand what happened next, and had been reduced to tears as he recounted the story. Jacopo Mastrocinque took a break from a “heroes v villians” costume party to smoke a cigarette before he was arrested in a large-scale police operation. Nine News “He went outside for a cigarette, had [a] pistol pointed [at him] by police, has been arrested and is in custody overnight,” solicitor Cassy Giudice told the court on Tuesday. General duties and specialist officers – their ballistic vests bearing NSW Police insignias rather than American flags, and their guns real – swarmed the precinct. Police vehicles, marked and unmarked, sped down Driver Avenue. Mastrocinque and his 39-year-old roommate were taken into custody.



Wearing the army-style jacket he was arrested in, Mastrocinque told the court that he was at a “staff party from the restaurant that I work with”. “You can ask everyone who was there,” he said as his hearing was adjourned. “My manager, my general manager, you can ask them.” Mastrocinque, 35, is a restaurant manager with a long career in Sydney’s dining scene. Facebook The police prosecutor told the court that Mastrocinque had chosen to dress as a “hero” for the costume party. A man told officers on the scene that the man they had just arrested was attending the event, the prosecutor informed the court. Barrister Wali Shukoor appeared for Mastrocinque on Tuesday afternoon, conceding that his client made a “very poor and foolish decision to attend the event the way he did”, but arguing that his otherwise perfect record supported his release.



Judge Daniel Covington granted Mastrocinque bail on the condition that he move to his partner’s North Ryde address, avoid the Entertainment Quarter and surrender his passport. His matter will next be heard on August 18 at the Downing Centre. Jacopo Mastrocinque was arrested at Sydney’s Entertainment Quarter after a massive police operation. NSW Police The swift response, including specialist officers, did not occur in a vacuum. Just months on from the worst terrorist attack in Australia’s history, a few kilometres away at Bondi Beach, onlookers were “genuinely concerned and alarmed” by the sight of a man walking around with a firearm in a public place, NSW Police Detective Superintendent Peter Glynn said. “It’s a timely reminder regarding the heightened concerns the community have about public safety,” Glynn said on Tuesday afternoon.



“Any calls to police regarding threats to public safety will be taken very seriously. Mastrocinque allegedly wore a ballistic vest with the US flag on the front, and carried a police badge and plastic handcuffs. A cardboard box marked “hard drugs” was also seized. NSW Police “People need to be mindful about how they dress and they act and they behave in public, particularly if they’re carrying firearms or imitation firearms ... that could be seen as genuine.” Mastrocinque’s seized costume also included a more DIY accessory – a cardboard box marked “hard drugs”. Arrested alongside him, Mastrocinque’s roommate was charged with drug possession after he was searched at Surry Hills police station. He is due to face court on August 20.



Mastrocinque has worked in the Sydney hospitality scene since arriving in Australia in 2014. The permanent resident managed the Bel & Brio Italian restaurant in Barangaroo before its 2022 closure, co-founded catering business The Italian Fellas, and now operates a pizza shop. He was interviewed by the Herald in November 2021 about the challenges of returning to business at Bel & Brio after the COVID lockdowns, when he said a “lazy mindset” from hospitality workers had dampened the success of the venue’s reopening. Mastrocinque at Bel & Brio in October 2021. Edwina Pickles Mastrocinque also appeared in a 2024 documentary titled Covid Safe Domestic Violence by the State in which “owners of small Sydney businesses explain how they had their livelihoods stripped away from them” during the lockdowns, according to IMDb. He was credited as a small business manager in the film. Be the first to know when major news happens.
